stem: Which ADM phase is specifically responsible for developing the Target Business Architecture?

options.text: Phase A: Architecture Vision
Phase B: Business Architecture
Phase C: Information Systems Architecture
Phase E: Opportunities and Solutions

rationale: Phase B develops the Baseline and Target Business Architectures. Phase A only creates a high-level vision. Phase C covers Data and Application architectures. Phase E identifies work packages to bridge the gap.

stem: In TOGAF, which of the four architecture domains is concerned with the structure of logical and physical data assets?

options.text: Business Architecture
Application Architecture
Data Architecture
Technology Architecture

rationale: Data Architecture defines the structure of an organisation's logical and physical data assets and data management resources. Application Architecture deals with individual applications and their interactions. Technology Architecture covers hardware and software infrastructure.

stem: Which of the following best describes the purpose of the Enterprise Continuum?

options.text: A governance framework for managing architecture change requests
A view of the Architecture Repository classifying assets from generic to organisation-specific
A database storing all project deliverables and work packages
A migration plan for transitioning from Baseline to Target Architecture

rationale: The Enterprise Continuum provides a classification scheme for architectures and solutions, ranging from Foundation Architectures (most generic) through Common Systems and Industry Architectures to Organisation-Specific Architectures. It is a view of the Architecture Repository.

stem: The Architecture Repository contains six classes of architectural information. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.text: Standards Information Base
Governance Log
Project Management Office Records
Architecture Capability

rationale: The six classes in the Architecture Repository are: Architecture Metamodel, Architecture Capability, Architecture Landscape, Standards Information Base, Reference Library, and Governance Log. PMO Records are not part of the Architecture Repository.

stem: In TOGAF terminology, what is the difference between a View and a Viewpoint?

options.text: A View is a set of stakeholders; a Viewpoint is a specific concern
A View is what you see; a Viewpoint is the specification of conventions for constructing that view
A View is a governance artefact; a Viewpoint is a migration plan
They are synonymous terms used interchangeably in TOGAF

rationale: A View is a representation of a system from the perspective of a set of related concerns. A Viewpoint is the specification of conventions for constructing and using a view — it defines what can be in a view and how to express it.

stem: Which ADM phase produces the Statement of Architecture Work?

options.text: Preliminary Phase
Phase A: Architecture Vision
Phase B: Business Architecture
Phase G: Implementation Governance

rationale: The Statement of Architecture Work is a key output of Phase A: Architecture Vision. It defines the scope of the architecture work, the approach, and obtains formal sign-off. The Preliminary phase establishes the framework; Phase B develops the Business Architecture.

stem: Requirements Management in TOGAF ADM is best described as:

options.text: A one-time activity performed only in Phase A
A continuous process that feeds requirements into and from all ADM phases
A sub-phase within Phase B: Business Architecture
The responsibility of the project management office, not the architecture team

rationale: Requirements Management is a continuous process at the centre of the ADM wheel. It manages the identification, storage, and feeding of requirements into and out of relevant ADM phases throughout the architecture lifecycle.

stem: Which phase of the ADM is primarily responsible for developing the Architecture Roadmap?

options.text: Phase D: Technology Architecture
Phase E: Opportunities and Solutions
Phase F: Migration Planning
Phase G: Implementation Governance

rationale: Phase E: Opportunities and Solutions generates the initial Architecture Roadmap. It identifies work packages and Transition Architectures. Phase F refines and finalises the detailed Migration Plan and Architecture Roadmap.

stem: An Architecture Contract in TOGAF is best described as:

options.text: A legal agreement between the enterprise and an IT vendor
A joint agreement between development partners and sponsors on deliverables, quality, and fitness-for-purpose
A document produced in Phase A that authorises the architecture project
A compliance checklist used during architecture reviews

rationale: An Architecture Contract is a joint agreement between development partners and sponsors on the deliverables, quality, and fitness-for-purpose of an architecture. It is established in Phase G: Implementation Governance to ensure ongoing conformance.

stem: In the TOGAF Architecture Landscape, which level addresses the detailed building blocks needed to support a particular business unit?

options.text: Strategic Architecture
Segment Architecture
Capability Architecture
Foundation Architecture

rationale: Capability Architecture shows how the enterprise needs to be organised to deliver a specific outcome or respond to a strategic driver. Segment Architecture addresses a specific area of the enterprise (e.g., a business unit). Strategic Architecture provides the long-term direction.

stem: A technology director tells her team: 'We use TOGAF so all our architectural decisions must comply with The Open Group's vendor recommendations.' Which aspect of this statement is incorrect?

options.text: TOGAF does not belong to The Open Group
TOGAF is vendor-neutral and does not make vendor recommendations
Architectural decisions are not governed by TOGAF
The Open Group is a commercial software company

rationale: TOGAF is explicitly vendor-neutral — it does not endorse, recommend, or favour any specific products, tools, or technology vendors. The Open Group is a vendor-neutral industry consortium, not a vendor itself.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF's vendor neutrality is a foundational characteristic. The Open Group deliberately maintains independence from commercial vendors so that TOGAF can be adopted without creating technology lock-in. No part of TOGAF recommends specific products.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is false — TOGAF is owned and maintained by The Open Group. C is false — TOGAF governance does constrain architectural decisions through principles and compliance requirements. D is false — The Open Group is a vendor-neutral consortium, not a software company.
explanation.examTip: When you see statements pairing TOGAF with vendor recommendations or product preferences, the answer is always that TOGAF is vendor-neutral. This principle is tested across multiple question types.

stem: Which of the following most accurately describes the relationship between TOGAF and ITIL?

options.text: TOGAF replaces ITIL for organisations doing large-scale digital transformation
ITIL is a subset of TOGAF, covered within the ADM's operational phases
TOGAF and ITIL address different concerns and can be used together
TOGAF's Preliminary Phase eliminates the need for a separate ITSM framework

rationale: TOGAF covers architecture development; ITIL covers IT service management and operations. They are complementary — TOGAF defines how services should be architecturally designed; ITIL governs how they are run and improved operationally.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF explicitly recognises other management frameworks and is designed to coexist with them. The Preliminary Phase specifically addresses how TOGAF integrates with ITIL, COBIT, and PRINCE2.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — TOGAF never claims to replace project management or service management frameworks. B is wrong — ITIL is an independent framework, not contained within TOGAF. D is wrong — the Preliminary Phase defines integration points, not replacements.
explanation.examTip: Any question suggesting TOGAF 'replaces' another named framework is wrong. TOGAF's standard answer to coexistence questions is: complementary, not competing.

stem: An organisation's Head of Strategy says: 'We need our Enterprise Architecture to start with what the business wants to achieve — not with what IT has available.' Which TOGAF domain most directly reflects this priority?

options.text: Technology Architecture — it defines the infrastructure strategy
Application Architecture — it maps systems to business processes
Business Architecture — it describes strategy, governance, and key business processes
Data Architecture — it governs how enterprise information assets are managed

rationale: Business Architecture is the domain that covers business strategy, governance, organisation structure, and key business processes. It is explicitly the first domain developed in the ADM (Phase B), because business needs drive all subsequent architecture decisions.

explanation.whyCorrect: The BDAT sequence exists precisely for this reason: Business Architecture establishes what the enterprise needs to do before Data, Application, or Technology decisions are made. Starting with Business Architecture is the TOGAF mechanism for ensuring business drives IT.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Technology Architecture (A) is the last domain developed — it responds to the others, not leads them. Application Architecture (B) maps systems to already-defined business processes. Data Architecture (D) governs information, which itself is defined by business need.
explanation.examTip: Whenever a question emphasises business primacy in architecture, Business Architecture and the BDAT sequence are the correct anchors.

stem: A TOGAF practitioner describes the ADM as 'the prescriptive cookbook that organisations must follow step-by-step to produce valid architectures.' Which part of this description requires correction?

options.text: The ADM is not part of TOGAF
The ADM is iterative and must be tailored to the organisation's context — it is not a rigid sequential prescription
The ADM does not produce architectures — it only produces governance documents
The term 'cookbook' accurately describes the ADM's intent

rationale: TOGAF explicitly states that the ADM must be adapted and tailored. It is iterative, not linear. Organisations select applicable phases, adjust artefact requirements, and adapt processes to their context. Treating it as a rigid step-by-step prescription misrepresents TOGAF's design intent.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Preliminary Phase is dedicated to tailoring TOGAF. ADM iteration (architecture iteration, transition iteration, landscape iteration) is a documented feature, not an exception. 'Must follow step-by-step' contradicts core TOGAF guidance.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is false — the ADM is the core of TOGAF. C is false — ADM phases produce architecture deliverables including the Architecture Definition Document. D is false — the 'cookbook' metaphor implies rigid prescription, which TOGAF explicitly rejects.
explanation.examTip: Questions testing ADM flexibility follow a pattern: a statement about rigid application is incorrect; the correct answer emphasises tailoring, iteration, and adaptation.

stem: An enterprise has three subsidiaries each operating different Architecture Frameworks. The group CTO wants to adopt TOGAF as the group standard while allowing subsidiaries to retain local practices where appropriate. Which TOGAF concept most directly supports this requirement?

options.text: Architecture Partitioning — dividing the architecture landscape into Strategic, Segment, and Capability levels
Architecture Principles — establishing enterprise-wide rules that subsidiaries must follow
The Enterprise Continuum — classifying assets from generic to organisation-specific
ADM tailoring — adapting TOGAF to integrate with existing subsidiary frameworks

rationale: The Preliminary Phase's tailoring capability directly supports integration with existing frameworks. TOGAF can be adapted to coexist with other architecture methods — tailoring the terminology, process steps, and governance processes to align with what each subsidiary already uses.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF's tailoring guidelines explicitly address integration with other frameworks, including adapting TOGAF's terminology and process to match existing practices. This is precisely the Preliminary Phase's purpose.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Architecture Partitioning (A) addresses governance levels, not framework integration. Architecture Principles (B) set rules but don't resolve framework coexistence. The Enterprise Continuum (C) classifies assets, not frameworks.
explanation.examTip: Framework integration and coexistence scenarios almost always point to the Preliminary Phase's tailoring and integration activities.

stem: A banking IT team is looking for an existing security architecture reference model that applies broadly across the financial services industry, before designing their own. At which level of the Enterprise Continuum should they search?

options.text: Foundation Architectures — they contain the most generic and reusable patterns
Organisation-Specific Architectures — they are most directly applicable
Industry Architectures — they provide sector-specific reference models
Common Systems Architectures — they address cross-industry technical concerns

rationale: Industry Architectures are specific to a vertical sector (e.g., BIAN for banking, HL7 for healthcare). For a bank seeking a financial services security architecture, the Industry level is the most directly applicable starting point.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Enterprise Continuum levels progress from generic (Foundation) to sector-specific (Industry) to enterprise-specific (Organisation-Specific). A bank seeking a financial services reference model should look at Industry Architectures first.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Foundation (A) is too generic — it applies to any industry. Organisation-Specific (B) is the bank's own architecture, not a starting reference. Common Systems (D) addresses cross-industry IT patterns, not financial services specifically.
explanation.examTip: Match the specificity of the search to the Continuum level. Sector-specific = Industry. Any industry = Common Systems. Any enterprise anywhere = Foundation.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the Enterprise Continuum and the Architecture Repository?

options.text: The Architecture Repository is a sub-component of the Enterprise Continuum
The Enterprise Continuum is a classification view of what is stored in the Architecture Repository
They are independent TOGAF concepts with no formal relationship
The Enterprise Continuum replaces the Architecture Repository in TOGAF 10

rationale: The Enterprise Continuum is a view of the Architecture Repository — it is a way of classifying the assets stored in the Repository according to how generic or specific they are. The Repository stores; the Continuum classifies.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF defines this relationship explicitly: the Enterprise Continuum provides a classification scheme for architectures and solutions, and these assets are stored in the Architecture Repository. The Continuum is how you understand the Repository's contents.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A reverses the relationship — the Repository isn't inside the Continuum. C is incorrect — they have a formal, documented relationship. D is false — both concepts exist in TOGAF 10.
explanation.examTip: Remember the analogy: the Repository is the library; the Continuum is the catalogue system that tells you where to find things based on how generic they are.

stem: An architect finds that the Architecture Repository's Standards Information Base contains an approved open-source API gateway. A project team requests to use a commercial alternative. Where should the outcome of this governance decision be recorded?

options.text: Standards Information Base — updating the approved standards list
Architecture Landscape — as a new application component
Governance Log — recording the dispensation decision
Reference Library — as a new architecture pattern

rationale: Governance decisions — including dispensations from approved standards — are recorded in the Governance Log class of the Architecture Repository. The Governance Log is specifically designed to hold records of compliance reviews, dispensations, and Architecture Board decisions.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Governance Log exists precisely for this scenario: a project deviating from an approved standard (SIB) with Architecture Board approval. The decision, its justification, and its time limit must be documented there.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: The SIB (A) holds approved standards, not governance decisions. The Architecture Landscape (B) holds architecture descriptions, not governance outcomes. The Reference Library (C) holds patterns and templates, not decisions.
explanation.examTip: Governance decisions, dispensations, and compliance review outcomes always go in the Governance Log. It is the audit trail of architecture governance.

stem: An enterprise has an Organisation-Specific Architecture for its customer identity platform. A new subsidiary acquisition brings a different identity platform. The EA team wants to assess both against common patterns before deciding on a target. Which direction of the Enterprise Continuum should guide this analysis?

options.text: From Organisation-Specific toward Foundation — seeking common patterns to compare both platforms against
From Foundation toward Organisation-Specific — specialising a generic pattern for each platform
Across Industry Architectures only — since identity is a cross-industry concern
Within the Solutions Continuum only — since both platforms are deployed solutions

rationale: When comparing two organisation-specific solutions, moving toward more generic levels (Common Systems or Foundation) identifies common patterns that both can be assessed against. This provides a neutral architectural reference point for the comparison.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Enterprise Continuum runs from Foundation (generic) to Organisation-Specific (particular). Moving left (toward Foundation) finds common ground. Both identity platforms can be assessed against a Common Systems identity architecture pattern as a neutral reference.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Option B describes the normal specialisation direction for creating new architecture, not comparison. Option C limits search unnecessarily. Option D is too narrow — understanding architectural intent requires the Architecture Continuum, not just the Solutions Continuum.
explanation.examTip: For comparison exercises, move toward the generic end of the Continuum. For creation exercises, move from generic toward specific.

stem: An architect states: 'The Requirements Repository is a separate system from the Architecture Repository.' A colleague disagrees. Who is correct and why?

options.text: The architect is correct — requirements are managed in a dedicated requirements management tool outside TOGAF
The colleague is correct — the Requirements Repository is part of the Architecture Landscape class within the Architecture Repository
Both are partially correct — requirements can be stored either inside or outside the Architecture Repository depending on organisational preference
The colleague is correct — requirements are stored in the Standards Information Base class of the Architecture Repository

rationale: The Requirements Repository is part of the Architecture Landscape class of the Architecture Repository. It is not a separate system — requirements are architecture assets and are stored within the formal Architecture Repository structure.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF positions requirements as architectural assets. The Architecture Landscape class holds descriptions of the architecture at different levels — and requirements are part of that landscape. Storing them elsewhere would break traceability.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — TOGAF is clear that the Requirements Repository sits within the Architecture Repository. D is wrong — the SIB holds approved standards, not requirements. C introduces ambiguity that TOGAF doesn't support.
explanation.examTip: Requirements in TOGAF are always architecture assets stored in the Architecture Landscape class of the Architecture Repository — not in external tools or the SIB.

stem: Which component of an Architecture Principle provides the business justification for why the principle exists?

options.text: Name
Statement
Rationale
Implications

rationale: The Rationale component of an Architecture Principle provides the business justification — explaining why the enterprise has adopted this principle and what benefits it delivers. This distinguishes Rationale from Implications, which describe the practical consequences of the principle.

explanation.whyCorrect: Rationale answers 'why does this principle exist?' and provides the business case for it. For example: 'Data is an enterprise asset — Rationale: shared data reduces redundancy, improves quality, and enables cross-enterprise reporting.'
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Name (A) is just the short identifier. Statement (B) declares what the principle requires. Implications (D) describe the consequences of adopting it — costs, organisational changes, constraints. Implications are often confused with Rationale but they answer 'what happens as a result?' not 'why does this principle exist?'
explanation.examTip: Rationale = the justification (the 'why it was adopted'). Implications = the consequences (the 'what must change as a result'). This distinction is one of the most frequently tested on OGEA-101.

stem: A principle states: 'All enterprise applications must use standard REST APIs for system integration.' The consequence is that three teams must replace their existing proprietary integration protocols, and a new API governance function must be established. This consequence represents which component?

options.text: The Rationale — it justifies why the principle was adopted
The Statement — it declares the principle
The Implications — it describes the practical consequences of adopting the principle
The Name — it identifies the principle concisely

rationale: Implications describe the practical consequences of adopting a principle — what must change, what must be invested in, and what constraints are created. Replacing proprietary protocols and establishing governance are consequences of adoption, making this the Implications component.

explanation.whyCorrect: Implications answer: 'If we adopt this principle, what concrete changes must happen?' They typically include costs, organisational changes, technology investments, and operational constraints. They are the most operationally important component.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Rationale (A) would be something like: 'Standard APIs reduce integration cost and enable ecosystem interoperability.' Statement (B) is the principle declaration itself. Name (D) would be something like 'API-First Integration'.
explanation.examTip: When a question presents a consequence or cost of a principle — what must be done as a result — that is always Implications. The exam frequently presents scenarios requiring you to classify principle components.

stem: During a programme review, a project team argues that their solution should be exempt from the enterprise's 'Cloud First' architecture principle because on-premise hosting is cheaper for their specific workload. What is the architecturally correct response?

options.text: Accept the exemption — cost is always a valid override for architectural principles
Escalate to the Architecture Board for a formal dispensation assessment with documented justification
Update the principle immediately to include a cost exception clause
Allow the project to proceed — principles are guidelines, not mandatory rules

rationale: Architecture Principles are fundamental rules, not preferences. Deviating from a principle requires formal governance approval via the dispensation process — not unilateral project decisions or immediate principle revision.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF's governance process provides the dispensation mechanism for exactly this situation. The Architecture Board reviews the case — assessing the justification, risk, and time period — and either approves or rejects the exception. The decision is documented in the Governance Log.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — cost alone doesn't override principles; the governance process must decide. C is wrong — revising a principle because of one project's constraint undermines the principle's stability. D is wrong — principles are specifically described as fundamental rules, not guidelines.
explanation.examTip: Any scenario where a project wants to deviate from a principle should trigger your 'dispensation' response. The Architecture Board decides; the Governance Log records it.

stem: An enterprise has twelve architecture principles. A review reveals that Principle 3 ('Maximise reuse of existing components') conflicts with Principle 9 ('All new solutions must use cloud-native patterns'). Some existing components are not cloud-native. Which quality of good Architecture Principles does this situation violate?

options.text: Understandable — the principles are too complex for non-architects to apply
Stable — the principles change too frequently to be relied upon
Consistent — principles should not internally contradict each other
Complete — the principles do not cover all relevant architectural concerns

rationale: A set of Architecture Principles must be consistent — no principle should contradict another. When two principles pull in opposite directions, architects cannot apply them both, which undermines governance. Conflicts must be resolved by defining priority rules or reconciling the principles.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF's five qualities of good principles include Consistent: the principles must not conflict with each other. Where genuine tensions exist, the principles should define how to resolve them. An unresolved conflict leaves architects unable to make governed decisions.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Understandable (A) relates to clarity for non-technical stakeholders. Stable (B) relates to frequency of change. Complete (D) relates to whether all major architectural concerns are addressed. None of these relate to internal contradiction.
explanation.examTip: The five principle qualities are: Understandable, Robust, Complete, Consistent, Stable. Map each quality to its specific concern — Consistent specifically addresses internal contradictions.

stem: An enterprise architect argues: 'We should update our Architecture Principles every time a new programme reveals a gap.' A governance consultant disagrees. Which of the following best supports the consultant's position?

options.text: Principles should never be updated — they are permanent commitments
Updating principles per-programme would undermine their Stability quality, making them unreliable as enterprise-wide rules
Principles are documents, not rules, so updating them has no governance consequence
The Architecture Board cannot update principles — only The Open Group can

rationale: One of the five qualities of good principles is Stability — they should not change with every new project or programme. Frequent updates undermine the principle's value as an enterprise-wide rule that all decisions are made against consistently.

explanation.whyCorrect: Principles can evolve — but through a deliberate, governed process when the enterprise strategy genuinely changes, not as a reaction to individual programme gaps. Frequent per-programme updates mean the principles are no longer stable enterprise-level constraints.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — principles can legitimately evolve when enterprise strategy changes. C is wrong — principles are governance rules, and updating them has real architectural consequences. D is wrong — organisations create and update their own principles; The Open Group has no role.
explanation.examTip: Stability in principles means they persist across multiple programmes. The test is: does this change reflect a genuine enterprise strategy shift, or just one programme's convenience? The former can justify a principle update; the latter should not.

stem: A CFO has expressed concern that the proposed architecture will increase operational costs without providing clear business benefit reporting. In TOGAF terminology, what is this?

options.text: A stakeholder requirement
A stakeholder concern
An architecture principle
A compliance assessment criterion

rationale: A concern is a stakeholder's area of interest, worry, or responsibility in the architecture. The CFO's worry about cost and benefit visibility is a concern — it is broader and less formally structured than a requirement, and it motivates the creation of views to address it.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF defines a concern as an interest that pertains to the system's development, operation, or any aspect of the system's objectives. The CFO's worry about costs and benefits is exactly this — an interest that the architecture must address.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A requirement (A) is a specific, formally stated need derived from a concern — more precise than a concern. A principle (C) is a governance rule. A compliance criterion (D) is used in Phase G reviews.
explanation.examTip: Concerns are the raw material that stakeholders bring. Requirements are derived from concerns through Business Scenarios. Concerns → Scenarios → Requirements is the TOGAF chain.

stem: An architect creates a document defining the notation, content, and conventions for representing a system's security architecture for a risk and compliance audience. A colleague uses this document to produce an actual security architecture diagram for the current programme. What has each person produced?

options.text: The architect produced an architecture view; the colleague produced an architecture viewpoint
The architect produced an architecture viewpoint; the colleague produced an architecture view
Both produced architecture views — one is the template, one is the instance
Both produced architecture viewpoints — views are only produced during Phase D

rationale: A viewpoint is the specification — the definition of conventions for constructing a type of view. A view is the actual representation produced by applying a viewpoint to specific architecture content. The architect defined the template; the colleague produced the instance.

explanation.whyCorrect: Viewpoint = recipe (how to build this type of view). View = the dish (the actual view built for this architecture). The first architect defined the specification; the colleague applied it to produce a specific view.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A reverses the definitions. C is wrong — a viewpoint is not a 'template view'; it is a specification of conventions. D is wrong — views are produced in all domain phases (A through D), not only Phase D.
explanation.examTip: Viewpoint = specification/recipe. View = instance/result. One viewpoint can generate many views across different architectures. This distinction is reliably tested.

stem: During Phase A, the architecture team produces a high-level diagram showing how the proposed transformation will affect the enterprise's core business capabilities. This diagram is targeted at senior business executives. What type of artefact is this, and what purpose does it serve?

options.text: An architecture principle — establishing the rules for the transformation
An architecture view — representing the architecture from a specific stakeholder perspective
An architecture viewpoint — defining conventions for future views
A compliance assessment — reviewing the architecture against standards

rationale: An architecture view is an actual representation of the architecture from a specific stakeholder perspective — in this case, a business capability view for senior executives. It presents selected architectural content in a format accessible and relevant to that audience.

explanation.whyCorrect: Views are the deliverables — the actual diagrams, documents, and models produced for specific audiences addressing their specific concerns. A business capability diagram for executives is a view addressing executives' strategic concerns.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A principle (A) is a governance rule, not a diagram. A viewpoint (C) is the specification for how to build this type of diagram — not the diagram itself. A compliance assessment (D) is a Phase G governance activity.
explanation.examTip: Any concrete architecture representation produced for a specific audience is a view. The specification that defined how to produce it would be a viewpoint.

stem: Two architecture views of the same enterprise show different owners for the 'Customer Master Record' data entity. One shows the Sales department as owner; the other shows the Data Governance team. What does this indicate?

options.text: Different views are expected to show different information — this is normal
The viewpoints used were inappropriate for the respective audiences
There is an unresolved inconsistency in the underlying architecture that must be corrected
The Data Architecture view should take precedence and the Sales view should be deleted

rationale: All views of an architecture must be consistent — they are different presentations of the same underlying architectural truth. Conflicting information between views indicates an unresolved architectural problem, not a communication issue.

explanation.whyCorrect: Views are windows onto a single underlying architecture. When two windows show contradictory information, the architecture itself has a flaw — in this case, the data ownership model is unresolved. This must be corrected in the underlying architecture, not papered over by choosing one view over the other.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — different views present different aspects, but they must be consistent. B is wrong — the viewpoints may be correct; the problem is the underlying architecture. D is wrong — deleting a view doesn't fix the architectural inconsistency.
explanation.examTip: View inconsistency = architecture problem, not a communication problem. The fix is always in the underlying architecture, not in the views.

stem: An architecture programme produces a single 250-page document containing every architectural detail for all stakeholder audiences. The document is technically accurate but receives no approvals from the steering committee. What does this situation most likely indicate about the architecture communication approach?

options.text: The architecture is too complex for the steering committee — it should be simplified
The architecture lacks appropriate views — different stakeholders need targeted representations addressing their specific concerns
The steering committee should be replaced by architects on the approval board
A 250-page document is insufficient — more detail is needed to achieve approval

rationale: Architecture views exist to address specific stakeholder concerns in appropriate formats. A single document for all audiences fails to address any audience's specific concerns effectively. Different stakeholders (CFO, CTO, Operations) need different views — not different versions of one document.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the core value proposition of views and viewpoints: architecture communication must be tailored to each audience's concerns. An executive view focuses on business value and risk; a technical view focuses on component interactions. One document serves none well.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A misidentifies the problem — the issue isn't complexity, it's audience targeting. C is impractical and contrary to TOGAF governance. D is wrong — more detail makes the targeting problem worse, not better.
explanation.examTip: When architecture documents fail to get approval, consider whether the right views have been produced for the right audiences. Architecture communication effectiveness = stakeholder concern addressed + appropriate format.

stem: A compliance regulator is identified as a stakeholder with concerns about audit trail completeness and data retention. The EA team argues this regulator 'isn't really a stakeholder' because they are external and not part of the programme. Which TOGAF concept most clearly refutes this argument?

options.text: Architecture Principles — which require regulatory compliance as a standard principle
TOGAF's definition of a stakeholder — which includes any individual, team, or organisation with an interest in the architecture, regardless of whether they are internal
Phase G compliance reviews — which only address internal governance, not external regulatory compliance
The Architecture Vision — which limits stakeholder scope to the sponsoring organisation

rationale: TOGAF defines a stakeholder as any individual, team, or organisation that has an interest in — or concern about — the architecture. External parties, including regulators, auditors, and partner organisations, fully qualify as stakeholders if the architecture affects their interests.

explanation.whyCorrect: The TOGAF definition of stakeholder is deliberately broad. Regulators who will audit the system post-implementation have a direct interest in how the architecture handles audit trails and data retention. Excluding them from stakeholder analysis creates governance risk.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is irrelevant — principles don't define who is a stakeholder. C is wrong — Phase G compliance reviews can and do address regulatory requirements. D is wrong — the Architecture Vision must address all stakeholders' concerns, not just the sponsor's.
explanation.examTip: When a question proposes limiting stakeholders to 'internal' or 'project' people, the answer is always that TOGAF's stakeholder definition is broader. Regulators, end users, future maintainers, and partner organisations can all be stakeholders.

stem: A project team says: 'We produced ten architecture views, so we have addressed all stakeholder concerns.' The architecture governance review rejects this claim. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Ten views exceed the maximum permitted by TOGAF governance
The number of views is irrelevant — the question is whether every significant stakeholder concern is addressed by at least one view
Views must be approved before they count — unapproved views have no governance status
Views can only be produced in Phases B through D — Phase A views are not recognised

rationale: The governance criterion for views is not quantity — it is coverage. Every significant stakeholder concern must be addressed by at least one architecture view. Ten views could leave some concerns unaddressed, or thirty views might not cover a critical concern.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF's view creation objective is stakeholder concern coverage. The governance review would check whether each identified concern has a corresponding view addressing it — not count views.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is false — TOGAF has no maximum view count. C conflates view production with view approval — both matter, but the quantity argument is still wrong. D is false — views are produced in Phase A (Architecture Vision views) and in all domain phases.
explanation.examTip: The quality test for views is always: 'Does each significant stakeholder concern have a corresponding view addressing it?' Volume of views is irrelevant.

stem: An architect specifies that a 'Notification Service' building block must support email, SMS, and push notifications, expose a REST API, and process 10,000 messages per hour. No specific product is mentioned. What type of building block is this?

options.text: A Solution Building Block (SBB) — it is a specific implementation
An Architecture Building Block (ABB) — it is an abstract specification of required capability
A Foundation Architecture building block — it is the most generic type
A Technology Building Block only — since it addresses infrastructure concerns

rationale: An Architecture Building Block (ABB) is an abstract specification of what a component must do — its required capabilities and interfaces — without specifying a concrete implementation. The described notification service defines capabilities without naming a specific product.

explanation.whyCorrect: ABBs answer 'what must it do?' SBBs answer 'what product or system does it?' This is an ABB — it specifies the required capability (email/SMS/push, REST API, 10k msg/hr) but leaves the implementation choice open.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: An SBB (A) would be a specific product — e.g., 'Amazon SNS configured for enterprise use'. Foundation architecture (C) refers to the most generic Continuum level, not an ABB type. Technology Building Block (D) isn't wrong as a description, but ABB is the more precise answer.
explanation.examTip: Abstract capability specification = ABB. Concrete product or implementation = SBB. This distinction is one of the most tested in the Architecture Content domain.

stem: In which ADM phase are Solution Building Blocks (SBBs) primarily selected to fulfil Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs)?

options.text: Phase B: Business Architecture
Phase D: Technology Architecture
Phase E: Opportunities and Solutions
Phase G: Implementation Governance

rationale: Phase E is specifically where ABBs are mapped to SBBs — concrete products, platforms, or bespoke solutions that fulfil the abstract architectural specifications. This is the transition from architectural intent to implementation reality.

explanation.whyCorrect: Phase E's role as the bridge between architecture and implementation includes selecting SBBs. The ABBs from Phases A–D define what is needed; Phase E identifies what will implement it (retained existing systems, commercial products, or bespoke development).
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Phase B (A) defines Business Architecture ABBs but doesn't select SBBs. Phase D (B) defines Technology ABBs but SBB selection comes in Phase E. Phase G (D) governs conformance of SBBs to ABBs — it doesn't select them.
explanation.examTip: ABBs in Phases A–D; SBBs in Phase E. Phase G checks that delivered SBBs conform to their ABB specifications. This timeline is reliably tested.

stem: An enterprise has defined an ABB for 'Payment Processing' specifying PCI-DSS compliance, support for VISA and Mastercard, and a REST interface. Subsidiary A implements this with Stripe; Subsidiary B implements it with Braintree. Which statement best describes this situation?

options.text: This is an architectural inconsistency — both subsidiaries must use the same SBB
This is architecturally valid — one ABB can be fulfilled by different SBBs in different contexts
The ABB is invalid because it can be implemented in more than one way
Both subsidiaries need a dispensation because neither is using the enterprise-standard implementation

rationale: One of the key benefits of the ABB/SBB model is that an ABB can be fulfilled by different SBBs in different contexts. Both Stripe and Braintree can satisfy the same ABB specification — this is architecturally sound, not inconsistent.

explanation.whyCorrect: ABBs define requirements; SBBs implement them. Multiple valid SBBs can satisfy the same ABB — this is the power of the model. Both subsidiaries comply with the ABB (PCI-DSS, VISA/Mastercard, REST) while using different products.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — the ABB standard is being met by both SBBs. C is wrong — the ability to have multiple implementations is a feature, not a flaw. D is wrong — dispensations are for deviations from standards, not legitimate alternative implementations.
explanation.examTip: The ABB/SBB model explicitly supports context-appropriate implementation variety. If both SBBs satisfy the ABB specification, both are valid — no dispensation needed.

stem: An architect is designing a new enterprise integration platform. She specifies that all integration components must 'interact through well-defined interfaces and have no internal dependencies on each other's implementation details.' Which building block characteristic is she enforcing?

options.text: Purposeful — each building block has a defined purpose
Standards-compliant — building blocks use open standards
Loosely coupled — building blocks interact through interfaces, not internal assumptions
Measurable — building blocks have testable specifications

rationale: Loose coupling — interacting through well-defined interfaces without internal dependencies — is the characteristic that enables building blocks to be reused, replaced, or changed independently. This is precisely what the architect is enforcing.

explanation.whyCorrect: Loose coupling is the characteristic that makes building blocks genuinely reusable. Without it, changing one component requires changing all components that depend on its internals. Well-defined interfaces are the mechanism of loose coupling.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Purposeful (A) relates to having a clear purpose. Standards-compliant (B) relates to open standards usage. Measurable (D) relates to having clear, testable specifications. Each is a distinct characteristic.
explanation.examTip: Loose coupling is the most critical characteristic for reuse. If a question mentions 'interfaces', 'no internal dependencies', or 'independently replaceable', the answer is loose coupling.

stem: A Phase G compliance review finds that an implementation team has delivered a customer authentication component that satisfies all the functional requirements in the ABB but used a tightly-coupled design that makes it impossible to replace without significant rework. What is the most accurate architectural assessment?

options.text: The component is Fully Conformant — all functional requirements are met
The component is Non-conformant — tight coupling violates building block design principles
The component is Compliant — it meets the spirit of the architecture
Coupling is an implementation concern, not an architectural concern

rationale: Loose coupling is an architectural characteristic of building blocks, not just an implementation preference. A tightly coupled component fails to meet the architectural specification even if functional requirements are met. This is a non-conformance requiring remediation.

explanation.whyCorrect: If the ABB specification includes loose coupling as a requirement — which good building block ABBs should — then tight coupling is a violation of the ABB, not just a design preference. Architecture includes non-functional and structural requirements, not just functional ones.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Fully Conformant (A) requires all mandatory architecture requirements to be met — tight coupling violates a structural requirement. Compliant (C) would mean it broadly follows the approach. D is wrong — coupling is an architectural quality, not just an implementation detail.
explanation.examTip: Architecture requirements include structural qualities (coupling, cohesion, scalability) as well as functional capabilities. Meeting functional requirements while violating structural requirements is non-conformance.

stem: An organisation's Architecture Repository contains a 'Payment Gateway' ABB from three years ago. A new programme is designing payment capabilities. The architect wants to start from scratch because 'technology has changed significantly.' Which TOGAF principle should guide this decision?

options.text: Start from scratch — outdated ABBs should not be used as they create technical debt
First check the Repository ABB, assess its currency, and either update/reuse it or formally replace it — not ignore it
Only Foundation-level building blocks from the Enterprise Continuum should be used as starting points
ABBs are permanently valid once published — they cannot be replaced without Architecture Board approval

rationale: The Enterprise Continuum and Architecture Repository exist specifically to promote reuse. The correct approach is always to check the Repository first, assess whether existing assets can be used or updated, and only create new ones when necessary. Ignoring existing Repository assets defeats the purpose of the Repository.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF's reuse principle: check the Repository first. The existing ABB may need updating (if technology has changed), but the assessment process, the specification structure, and any still-valid requirements should be incorporated rather than discarded.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A contradicts TOGAF's reuse ethos. C is too restrictive — organisation-specific and industry ABBs are valuable starting points too. D is wrong — ABBs can be updated through governance, but the correct process is to update, not ignore.
explanation.examTip: Enterprise Continuum + Repository = reuse over rebuild. Always check what exists before creating new. This is a foundational TOGAF principle.

stem: A programme is implementing an enterprise integration hub. Phase E has selected RabbitMQ as the SBB for the 'Message Broker' ABB. During Phase G, an integration developer proposes replacing RabbitMQ with Apache Kafka because it is better suited for the programme's eventual streaming requirements. What is the most appropriate architectural response?

options.text: Approve the change — developers understand technology better than architects
Assess whether Kafka satisfies the Message Broker ABB specification; if it does, the SBB can be changed through the Architecture Board with documented justification
Reject the change — SBBs selected in Phase E cannot be changed once implementation begins
Accept the change without governance — SBB selection is an implementation concern, not architectural

rationale: SBBs can be changed — but through architectural governance. The key question is whether the proposed SBB (Kafka) satisfies the same ABB specification as the original (RabbitMQ). If it does, and the Architecture Board approves the change with documented justification, it is architecturally valid.

explanation.whyCorrect: The governance process allows SBB changes when they can be justified and when the new SBB satisfies the ABB. The architect's role is to assess ABB conformance and process the change through the Architecture Board, not block or blindly approve it.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A bypasses governance. C is wrong — SBBs can change through governance. D is wrong — SBB selection is an architectural decision because SBBs must satisfy ABB specifications.
explanation.examTip: SBB changes are permitted with governance. Always check: (1) does the new SBB satisfy the ABB? (2) is the change approved by the Architecture Board? (3) is it documented?

stem: An enterprise architecture team is asked to scope a new initiative. The CTO says: 'We should cover the entire global enterprise, all four architecture domains, at full specification depth, for a 10-year horizon.' The Chief Architect advises against this scope. What TOGAF guidance supports the Chief Architect's position?

options.text: TOGAF limits architecture work to a maximum of two domains at a time
Architecture scoping guidelines advise calibrating breadth, depth, time period, and domains to the engagement objective — over-scoping is as harmful as under-scoping
Global enterprise architecture is prohibited under TOGAF — it must be partitioned by geography
A 10-year horizon exceeds the maximum permitted by the ADM

rationale: TOGAF's ADM scoping guidelines explicitly address the four dimensions of scope — breadth, depth, time period, and domains — and advise that each should be calibrated to what is actually needed. Over-ambitious scope produces waste, delays, and stakeholder disengagement.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF's guidance on scoping exists precisely to prevent the 'boil the ocean' failure pattern. A global, full-depth, all-domain, 10-year architecture engagement would take years and likely never produce anything usable. Calibrated scope is better architecture practice.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is false — TOGAF has no domain count limit. C is false — global architectures are permitted; partitioning is recommended for governance but not a prohibition. D is false — TOGAF sets no maximum time horizon.
explanation.examTip: Over-scoping questions always have the same answer structure: TOGAF's scoping guidelines advise calibrating all four dimensions to the engagement objective. Excessive scope is explicitly a risk to address.

stem: An architect discovers an existing application reference architecture in the Architecture Repository that was used by a different business unit. She wants to reuse it for a new programme in a third business unit, adapting it for local context. Which Enterprise Continuum concept most directly enables and encourages this approach?

options.text: Foundation Architecture — the most generic level should be the starting point
Architecture Continuum — storing architectural descriptions from generic to specific enables discovery and reuse
Solutions Continuum — existing deployed solutions should be the starting point
The Standards Information Base — approved standards restrict what can be reused

rationale: The Architecture Continuum (part of the Enterprise Continuum) stores architectural descriptions from generic to organisation-specific. Its purpose is to enable discovery and reuse — architects can find relevant existing architectures and specialise them rather than starting from scratch.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Architecture Continuum is the classification of architectural descriptions. Finding an existing architecture from another business unit and adapting it is exactly the reuse pattern the Continuum enables — the existing architecture sits at a certain Continuum level; the adaptation moves it toward more-specific.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Foundation Architecture (A) is the most generic level — useful for absolute starting points, not for finding domain-specific references. The Solutions Continuum (C) contains implementations, not architectural descriptions. The SIB (D) contains standards, not reusable architectures.
explanation.examTip: Reuse of architectural descriptions = Architecture Continuum. Reuse of deployed solutions = Solutions Continuum. Different purposes, different contents.

stem: An enterprise's Architecture Principles were last reviewed and approved by the Architecture Board three years ago. A new CTO questions whether they are still valid. Which quality of good Architecture Principles is most relevant to this review, and what should the review assess?

options.text: Stability — principles should never change, so the review should confirm them unchanged
Robustness — the review should assess whether the principles can withstand challenge
Stability — the review should assess whether enterprise strategy has changed enough to justify a principle update, not update principles reactively
Completeness — the review should add new principles for all technology trends in the last three years

rationale: Stability means principles should persist over time — not that they never change, but that changes are strategic and deliberate, not reactive. The review should assess whether the enterprise strategy has genuinely shifted enough to warrant updates, not update principles because time has passed.

explanation.whyCorrect: Stability in principles means they endure across multiple programmes and change only when enterprise strategy genuinely shifts. A time-based review is appropriate, but the threshold for change should be 'has the enterprise strategy changed?' not 'have three years passed?'
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A misunderstands Stability — it doesn't mean 'never change', it means 'change deliberately'. B is relevant but not the primary consideration for a periodic review. D is wrong — adding principles for every technology trend would undermine stability.
explanation.examTip: Stability ≠ permanence. It means strategic persistence with deliberate, governed change. The review question is: 'has the strategic context changed enough to justify a principle update?'

stem: An architecture team has identified 22 stakeholder groups and 67 concerns. A programme director says: 'We need a view for every concern — that's 67 views.' The Chief Architect disagrees. What is the architecturally correct approach?

options.text: The programme director is correct — every concern must have its own dedicated view
Group related concerns that can be effectively addressed by a single viewpoint; one view can address multiple concerns for the same audience
A maximum of ten views should be produced regardless of the number of concerns
Only the top five stakeholder groups should have views — the rest receive the main architecture document

rationale: Views address concerns, but one view can address multiple related concerns for the same audience. Related concerns from the same stakeholder group can often be addressed in a single, well-structured view. The goal is concern coverage, not one-to-one mapping.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF's guidance is that views must address significant stakeholder concerns — but efficiency means grouping related concerns into targeted views. A security and compliance view might address five concerns from the risk team simultaneously.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A would produce an unwieldy and often redundant set of views. C is arbitrary — TOGAF has no maximum view count. D is wrong — all identified significant stakeholder concerns must be addressed, not just a subset.
explanation.examTip: The test is concern coverage, not view count. Group related concerns into coherent viewpoints; one good view can address many related concerns from the same audience.

stem: A newly appointed Enterprise Architect says: 'TOGAF tells us what architecture to build — we just need to follow the phases and our architecture will be correct.' An experienced colleague corrects her. What is the most important correction?

options.text: TOGAF phases must be followed in strict alphabetical order, not sequential phase order
TOGAF is a framework and method that tells you how to approach architecture work — it does not prescribe what the architecture should be
TOGAF only covers IT architecture — business architecture must be determined independently
The ADM phases guarantee correct architecture if followed carefully

rationale: TOGAF is a framework for doing architecture work — it provides methods, vocabulary, and governance. It does not dictate what the architecture should contain. The architecture content is determined by the enterprise's context, strategy, and requirements.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is perhaps TOGAF's most fundamental characteristic. The ADM provides the process; architects and stakeholders provide the content. Following the ADM correctly ensures the process is sound — not that the output is predetermined.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is false — phases are labelled Preliminary, A–H, not alphabetically. C is false — TOGAF explicitly covers Business Architecture in Phase B. D is wrong — the ADM ensures process quality, not outcome correctness.
explanation.examTip: TOGAF = how to do architecture, not what to architect. This framing appears in many question forms. The framework provides process and governance; organisations provide content.

stem: An organisation has a strategic-level Architecture Landscape description covering the entire enterprise, and a capability-level description covering a specific shared services function. A new segment-level programme is starting for the finance division. In which part of the Architecture Landscape should this new programme's outputs be stored?

options.text: Within the Strategic Architecture — because it affects the whole enterprise
Within the Capability Architecture — because it details specific building blocks
Within the Segment Architecture — because it covers a specific business area
In the Standards Information Base — because it will establish new standards

rationale: Segment Architecture covers a specific significant area of the enterprise — a business division, a major function, or a strategic programme. A finance division programme sits at the segment level, between the enterprise-wide strategic view and the specific capability level.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Architecture Landscape has three levels: Strategic (whole enterprise, long horizon), Segment (business area or major function, medium horizon), and Capability (specific capability or building block, short horizon). A finance division programme is Segment-level.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Strategic (A) is for whole-enterprise, board-level architecture — a finance division programme is more specific. Capability (B) is for specific capabilities within a programme. SIB (D) stores approved standards, not architecture descriptions.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Landscape levels: Strategic = enterprise. Segment = division/domain. Capability = specific system/building block. Match the scope of the programme to the appropriate level.

stem: An architecture principle states: 'All customer data must remain within EU data centres.' The principle was established when the enterprise operated only in Europe. The enterprise has now expanded to serve customers in the Asia-Pacific region. Which of the following best describes the appropriate response?

options.text: The principle is immutable — all Asia-Pacific customer data must be stored in EU data centres
The expansion makes the principle automatically void — architecture principles expire when business context changes
Review the principle through the Architecture Board; the strategic context change may justify an update to address APAC requirements alongside EU requirements
Allow each APAC project to decide individually whether to follow the principle

rationale: Architecture Principles can legitimately evolve when enterprise strategy genuinely changes. A geographic expansion into APAC is exactly the kind of strategic change that may require a principle to be updated — not abandoned, but revised through governance to reflect the new context.

explanation.whyCorrect: Stability means principles don't change reactively per project — not that they never change when enterprise strategy shifts. An APAC expansion is a strategic context change. The Architecture Board should review and potentially update the principle to address both EU and APAC requirements.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — forcing APAC data to EU data centres may violate APAC regulations. B is wrong — principles don't automatically expire; they require governance to update. D is wrong — per-project decisions undermine enterprise governance.
explanation.examTip: Principle updates require governance and strategic justification — not project convenience. Genuine strategic changes (new markets, new regulations) are valid triggers for principle review through the Architecture Board.

stem: An architecture team is starting Phase A for a major transformation. The programme manager argues: 'We don't need to identify stakeholders — we know who cares about this.' The Enterprise Architect insists on a formal stakeholder analysis. Which TOGAF concept most strongly supports the architect's position?

options.text: Architecture Principles require all stakeholders to be consulted
Stakeholder analysis drives the communication plan and view creation — missing stakeholders means missing concerns and gaps in the architecture
TOGAF requires a minimum of ten identified stakeholders per programme
Stakeholder analysis is mandatory only for programmes above a defined cost threshold

rationale: Stakeholder analysis in Phase A is the foundation of the entire communication strategy and view creation plan. Missing a stakeholder group means their concerns are not identified, no views are created to address them, and the architecture will have gaps.

explanation.whyCorrect: Unidentified stakeholders = unaddressed concerns = architecture gaps. In practice, 'we know who cares' typically misses peripheral stakeholders (regulators, end users, future maintainers, partner organisations) whose concerns are critical but not immediately obvious.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is relevant but overly general. C is false — TOGAF has no minimum stakeholder count. D is false — stakeholder analysis applies to all architecture engagements.
explanation.examTip: Stakeholder analysis → concerns → views. Missing any step breaks the chain. The Phase A stakeholder analysis is the mandatory starting point for architecture communication.

stem: An ABB for an 'Authentication Service' specifies: OAuth2 support, MFA capability, response time under 200ms, and 99.9% uptime SLA. A delivered implementation supports OAuth2 and MFA but cannot meet the 200ms response time under load. Which conformance level best describes this implementation?

options.text: Conformant — the core functional requirements (OAuth2, MFA) are met
Compliant — the implementation follows the spirit of the architecture
Non-conformant — a mandatory ABB requirement (200ms SLA) is not satisfied
Fully Conformant — close enough to the specification

rationale: If 200ms response time is a mandatory ABB requirement, failing to meet it makes the implementation non-conformant — regardless of how many other requirements are met. Non-functional requirements specified in ABBs are architecture requirements, not optional targets.

explanation.whyCorrect: ABB specifications include non-functional requirements (performance SLAs, availability) as mandatory as functional ones. Failing a mandatory requirement = Non-conformant, requiring remediation or a formal dispensation.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Conformant (A) means all architecture requirements are met — this one isn't. Compliant (B) means broadly following the approach — but violating a specific mandatory SLA is a specific non-conformance. Fully Conformant (D) requires all mandatory requirements to be satisfied.
explanation.examTip: Non-functional requirements in ABBs (SLAs, performance, availability) are as mandatory as functional ones. Failure to meet them = Non-conformant.

stem: A CTO argues: 'TOGAF is designed for large enterprises — organisations with fewer than 1,000 employees don't need it and couldn't benefit from it.' What is the most accurate assessment of this claim?

options.text: The CTO is correct — TOGAF explicitly targets organisations with more than 500 IT staff
The CTO is incorrect — TOGAF is a foundational framework designed to be scaled and adapted to any size of enterprise
The CTO is partially correct — TOGAF's ADM is only useful for enterprises with 3+ architecture domains
The CTO is correct — the ADM's phase complexity makes it unsuitable for small organisations

rationale: TOGAF is explicitly described as a foundational framework applicable to any kind of architecture in any context. It is designed to be scaled — smaller organisations use fewer phases, simpler governance, and lighter artefact sets. There are no size prerequisites.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF's tailoring guidelines exist precisely to enable organisations of any size to adopt what is appropriate for their context. A small organisation might run a simplified ADM with one architect and a lightweight Repository.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is false — TOGAF has no staff size prerequisite. C is false — even a single-domain architecture engagement can benefit from TOGAF's discipline. D is wrong — the ADM is explicitly designed to be adapted for smaller engagements.
explanation.examTip: TOGAF's applicability is universal. Size-based exclusions don't exist in TOGAF — but the appropriate level of adoption varies with context, which is why tailoring is mandatory.

stem: An Architecture Review Board is assessing the Architecture Repository. They find: the Governance Log has 45 entries from last year. The Reference Library has not been updated in 18 months. The Architecture Metamodel was last reviewed 3 years ago. The Architecture Landscape has comprehensive current-state descriptions. Which of these findings indicates the highest governance risk?

options.text: An outdated Reference Library — architects will not have access to current patterns
An outdated Architecture Metamodel — architectures may be described using inconsistent concepts and relationships
The high number of Governance Log entries — too many governance decisions are being made
The comprehensive Architecture Landscape — this creates excessive maintenance burden

rationale: The Architecture Metamodel defines the schema of all architectural descriptions — what entities and relationships can be described. An outdated Metamodel means newer architectures may use concepts not in the schema, creating inconsistencies that undermine cross-architecture analysis and governance.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Metamodel is the foundational schema of the entire Architecture Repository. If it is out of date, all architectures created against it may be using inconsistent or undefined concepts, making governance, comparison, and integration impossible.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: An outdated Reference Library (A) reduces efficiency but doesn't undermine governance integrity. The Governance Log (C) having 45 entries is expected activity — not a risk. A comprehensive Landscape (D) is positive — that's what the Landscape is for.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Repository health priority: Metamodel consistency > Governance Log > Landscape > Reference Library. The Metamodel is the schema — without it, nothing else in the Repository can be trusted.

stem: Which of the following best describes an Architecture Building Block (ABB)?

options.text: A specific technology product selected to implement a capability
An abstract specification defining what a component must do, without specifying how it is implemented
A reusable architecture pattern retrieved from the Foundation Architecture level of the Enterprise Continuum
A governance document produced in Phase G to assess implementation conformance

rationale: An ABB is an abstract specification of capability — it defines what a component must do, what interfaces it must expose, and what quality attributes it must satisfy. It deliberately avoids specifying any particular implementation.

explanation.whyCorrect: ABBs describe architectural intent without implementation. 'The authentication service must support OAuth2, enforce MFA, and respond within 200ms' is an ABB — it defines requirements, not solutions.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A describes a Solution Building Block (SBB). C conflates ABBs with Foundation Architecture patterns — ABBs exist at all Continuum levels, not just Foundation. D describes a Compliance Assessment artefact.
explanation.examTip: ABB = abstract 'what'. SBB = concrete 'how'. This distinction is tested in both direct recall and scenario-based questions.

stem: An enterprise defines an ABB for an 'API Gateway' with mandatory requirements: OAuth2 authentication, rate limiting, and request logging. Division A implements this with Kong; Division B uses AWS API Gateway. Both satisfy all three mandatory requirements. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Division A is non-conformant because Kong is not an enterprise-approved standard
Both implementations are architecturally valid — one ABB can be fulfilled by multiple SBBs in different contexts
Division B needs a dispensation because cloud-hosted services require Architecture Board approval
The ABB is flawed if two different products can satisfy it — ABBs should specify a single implementation

rationale: The ABB/SBB model is specifically designed to allow context-appropriate implementation flexibility. Provided both SBBs satisfy the mandatory ABB requirements, both are architecturally valid. This is a strength of the model, not an inconsistency.

explanation.whyCorrect: ABBs define 'what'; SBBs define 'how'. Multiple valid 'how' options can satisfy the same 'what'. Division A and B each chose the SBB most appropriate for their context while satisfying the enterprise's architectural intent.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A introduces a standard not stated in the scenario. C invents a dispensation requirement with no basis. D misunderstands the model — the ability to support multiple SBBs is intentional and valuable.
explanation.examTip: When multiple SBBs satisfy the same ABB specification, all are valid. Dispensations are for deviations FROM the specification, not for choice WITHIN it.

stem: During Phase D, an architect identifies that the application architecture requires a high-availability database cluster. She documents the required characteristics: active-passive failover, automated backups, and point-in-time recovery. No vendor is specified. What has she produced?

options.text: A Solution Building Block — because it describes a database system
An Architecture Building Block — because it specifies required capabilities without naming a product
An Architecture Principle — because it establishes rules for database design
An Architecture Requirement — because it specifies what the technology must do

rationale: An ABB specifies required capabilities, interfaces, and quality attributes without naming a specific implementation. 'Active-passive failover, automated backups, point-in-time recovery' describes what the database capability must provide — this is an ABB.

explanation.whyCorrect: The absence of a vendor or product name is the key signal. The specification defines requirements for a capability type, which is precisely what an ABB does.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: An SBB (A) would name a specific product (e.g., 'PostgreSQL 15 on AWS RDS'). A principle (C) is an enterprise governance rule, not a technical specification. An architecture requirement (D) is technically valid but less precise — TOGAF specifically uses ABB for this type of capability specification.
explanation.examTip: Capability specification + no product name = ABB. Capability specification + specific product = SBB. This pattern appears repeatedly in exam questions.

stem: A building block for 'Document Management' was designed to support a core HR application. A new Finance programme wants to reuse it but needs the building block to also support digital signatures. What should the architect do?

options.text: Create a new, separate Document Management building block for Finance — each domain needs its own
Enhance the existing ABB to include digital signature capability and update the Architecture Repository
Finance must use the existing building block without modification to maintain architectural consistency
Document the digital signature need as an Architecture Principle for future programmes

rationale: Building blocks are designed to be evolved and enhanced. Adding digital signature capability to the existing ABB — and updating the Repository — extends the reusable asset for the whole enterprise while maintaining consistency. This is the preferred TOGAF approach.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF's reuse model includes the ability to enhance existing building blocks when requirements grow. Updating the ABB and storing the enhanced version in the Repository means all future programmes benefit from the enhancement.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A creates fragmentation — Finance and HR end up with separate Document Management components that will diverge. C prevents Finance from meeting its needs. D misclassifies a capability requirement as a principle.
explanation.examTip: Building blocks are living architectural assets — they can be enhanced, refined, and extended through governance. Duplication to avoid modification is an anti-pattern TOGAF explicitly discourages.

stem: An architect argues that building blocks should be 'tightly integrated to ensure reliability — loose coupling introduces unnecessary abstraction layers.' What is the main flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: Tight integration is acceptable as long as building blocks are documented in the Repository
Tight coupling prevents reuse and replacement — building blocks must interact through defined interfaces to be genuinely reusable
The argument is correct for Infrastructure building blocks but not Application building blocks
Reliability and loose coupling are independent concerns — both can be achieved simultaneously

rationale: Loose coupling is not just a design preference — it is one of the defining characteristics of a well-formed building block. Tight coupling makes it impossible to replace or reuse a building block without changing everything that depends on it, defeating the purpose of building blocks entirely.

explanation.whyCorrect: Loose coupling — interaction through well-defined interfaces rather than internal dependencies — is what makes building blocks genuinely reusable and replaceable. Without it, 'reuse' means copying the whole dependency chain.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — documentation doesn't compensate for tight coupling. C introduces a false distinction between infrastructure and application building blocks; the principle applies universally. D avoids the issue — while reliability and loose coupling can coexist, the architect's claim that tight integration is preferable for reliability is the flaw to identify.
explanation.examTip: The five characteristics of building blocks: purposeful, measurable, standards-compliant, loosely coupled, reusable. Loose coupling is what enables the last one — without it, 'reuse' is not achievable in practice.

stem: A Phase G compliance review reveals that the delivered 'Customer Notification' SBB fully satisfies the functional and performance requirements in the ABB, but uses an internal proprietary messaging protocol rather than the open standard REST API specified. What is the appropriate conformance classification and action?

options.text: Compliant — functional requirements are met, so the protocol choice is an implementation detail
Fully Conformant — all user-facing requirements are satisfied
Non-conformant — the ABB specifies REST as mandatory; using a proprietary protocol is a direct violation requiring remediation or a dispensation
Conformant — the system works correctly, which is the only architectural criterion that matters

rationale: The ABB specifies REST as a mandatory interface requirement. Using a proprietary protocol instead is a direct non-conformance — not an implementation detail. API standards are architectural requirements because they affect integration, interoperability, and replaceability.

explanation.whyCorrect: ABBs include interface specifications as mandatory architectural requirements. REST vs proprietary protocol is not an implementation detail — it affects every consumer of the service and directly impacts the building block's standards-compliant and loosely coupled characteristics.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Compliant (A) would mean broadly following the architectural approach — using a proprietary protocol instead of the specified REST API is a specific violation, not a minor deviation. Fully Conformant (B) requires ALL mandatory requirements to be met. Conformant (D) would mean satisfying the defined architectures — the interface standard is part of that definition.
