explanation.examTip: Interface standards in ABBs are architectural requirements — not implementation preferences. Violating a specified interface standard = non-conformant, even if functional requirements are met.

stem: An enterprise architect is reviewing the Architecture Repository and discovers that 34 of the 47 ABBs in the Architecture Landscape have not been updated in four years. Technology has evolved significantly. What is the most appropriate architectural response?

options.text: Delete outdated ABBs — they create confusion and programmes should start from scratch
Mark them all as deprecated and create entirely new ABBs for every capability
Conduct a structured review: assess currency of each ABB, update those still relevant with technology changes, formally retire those that are superseded, and preserve those still valid
ABBs do not expire — they remain valid architectural guidance regardless of technology changes

rationale: The Architecture Repository requires active maintenance. Outdated ABBs should be reviewed individually — some may be updated with technology changes, some formally retired (with documentation of what replaced them), and others may remain valid. Blanket deletion or blanket preservation are both wrong.

explanation.whyCorrect: Architecture Repository management is an ongoing responsibility. TOGAF's Phase H (Architecture Change Management) and the Architecture Capability framework both address the need for continuous Repository maintenance. A structured review, with individual assessment of each ABB, is the governed approach.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A loses institutional knowledge and traceability. B creates unnecessary duplication work and orphans existing implementations. D is wrong — ABBs can become outdated and must be maintained.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Repository maintenance is a governance activity. Outdated assets should be reviewed, updated, or formally retired — never ignored or mass-deleted. This reflects Phase H thinking applied to Repository management.

stem: In the TOGAF Content Framework, which of the following correctly describes a 'deliverable'?

options.text: Any diagram or model produced during an ADM phase
A work product that is formally reviewed, governed, and signed off — it has contractual significance
A reusable building block component stored in the Architecture Repository
A technical specification produced by the implementation team in Phase G

rationale: A deliverable is a formal architecture work product that is contractually specified — it is reviewed by governance, signed off by appropriate stakeholders, and enters the Architecture Repository upon completion. It has a formal governance status that artefacts do not.

explanation.whyCorrect: Deliverables are the formal governance outputs — Statement of Architecture Work, Architecture Definition Document, Architecture Roadmap — each requiring formal review and sign-off. Their status as deliverables gives them governance authority.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A describes an artefact, not a deliverable. C describes a building block. D describes an implementation output from Phase G, not an architecture deliverable in the Content Framework sense.
explanation.examTip: Three Content Framework categories: Deliverables (formal/governance), Artefacts (content elements), Building Blocks (reusable components). Deliverables have formal sign-off; artefacts are within them.

stem: An architect produces a structured list of all applications in the enterprise's current landscape, including each application's owner, primary business function, and lifecycle status. What type of artefact is this?

options.text: A matrix — it shows relationships between elements
A diagram — it visually represents the application landscape
A catalog — it is a structured inventory of architectural elements
A deliverable — it is a formal governance output

rationale: A catalog is a structured list of architectural elements — in this case, an Application Catalog listing all applications with their attributes. Catalogs answer 'what exists?' A matrix would show relationships between elements; a diagram would provide a visual representation.

explanation.whyCorrect: Catalogs are one of the three TOGAF artefact types. They are structured inventories answering 'what exists?' — listing entities with their attributes. An application list with owner, function, and status is a classic Application Catalog.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A matrix (A) would show relationships between applications and other elements (e.g., which applications support which business functions). A diagram (B) would be visual — like an application interaction diagram. A deliverable (D) is a formal governance output; a catalog is typically a component within a deliverable.
explanation.examTip: Three artefact types: Catalogs (lists of things), Matrices (relationships between things), Diagrams (pictures of things). Match the question description to the right type.

stem: An architect produces a grid showing which of the enterprise's 15 applications create, read, update, or delete each of the 20 core data entities. What type of artefact is this, and in which ADM phase is it most likely produced?

options.text: A catalog produced in Phase B: Business Architecture
A matrix produced in Phase C: Information Systems Architectures
A diagram produced in Phase D: Technology Architecture
A deliverable produced in Phase E: Opportunities and Solutions

rationale: A grid showing relationships between applications and data entities — an Application/Data CRUD matrix — is a matrix artefact. It is produced in Phase C (Information Systems Architectures) where both Data and Application Architectures are developed and their interactions mapped.

explanation.whyCorrect: Matrices show relationships between catalogue items. 'Applications × Data Entities' is an Application/Data Matrix — produced in Phase C where both application and data architectures are in scope. CRUD analysis (Create/Read/Update/Delete) is a classic Phase C matrix technique.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A catalog (A) would list applications or data entities separately, not their relationships. A diagram (C) would be visual. A deliverable (D) is a formal output, not a specific artefact type.
explanation.examTip: Matrix artefacts always show relationships between two types of catalogue items. The phase is determined by which domains are being developed — Application × Data = Phase C.

stem: What does the TOGAF Enterprise Metamodel define?

options.text: The sequence of phases in the ADM cycle
The types of architectural entities that can be described and the permitted relationships between them
The format and content of the Architecture Definition Document
The governance rules applied by the Architecture Board during compliance reviews

rationale: The Enterprise Metamodel is the schema of the architecture — it defines what types of entities (Business Process, Application Component, Data Entity, Technology Service) can be described and what relationships (supports, implements, runs on) are permitted between them.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Metamodel is the vocabulary and grammar of the architecture. It ensures that when an architect in one team says 'Application Component' and another says 'Service', they are referring to the same concept with the same permitted relationships.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: The ADM phase sequence (A) is covered by the ADM itself, not the Metamodel. The ADD format (C) is defined by the Content Framework's deliverable specifications. Architecture Board governance rules (D) are in the Architecture Governance Framework.
explanation.examTip: Metamodel = schema of what can be described. Think of it as the 'grammar' of the architecture language. Stored in the Architecture Metamodel class of the Architecture Repository.

stem: An architect is working in Phase B: Business Architecture. She produces: a list of all business capabilities, a grid showing which organisational units are responsible for each capability, and a flow diagram showing how value moves through the enterprise. Which set of artefact types has she produced?

options.text: Three diagrams — all represent visual information about the business
A catalog, a matrix, and a diagram — one of each artefact type
Three catalogs — all list business elements
A deliverable, an artefact, and a building block — one of each Content Framework category

rationale: The business capability list is a catalog (structured inventory). The capability/organisation grid is a matrix (showing relationships between two types of element). The value flow diagram is a diagram (visual representation). Each represents one of the three TOGAF artefact types.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a perfect illustration of the three artefact types working together in a single phase: Catalog answers 'what capabilities exist?', Matrix answers 'which units own which capabilities?', Diagram answers 'how does value flow?'
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — a list is a catalog, not a diagram. C is wrong — the grid and flow diagram are not catalogs. D incorrectly applies the broader Content Framework categories (deliverable, artefact, building block) when the question asks about artefact types within that framework.
explanation.examTip: The three artefact types always map to: list/inventory = Catalog; relationship grid = Matrix; visual = Diagram. In Phase B, all three types appear regularly.

stem: A programme director argues: 'We don't need the Enterprise Metamodel — architects are experienced enough to apply consistent terminology without a formal schema.' An architecture governance review disagrees. What is the strongest argument against the director's position?

options.text: The Metamodel is mandatory under TOGAF certification requirements
Without a shared Metamodel, the same term (e.g., 'Application') may mean different things in different teams' architectures, making cross-domain analysis and governance impossible
The Metamodel is needed to generate automated diagrams from the Architecture Repository tooling
Individual architect experience is unreliable — only formal documentation ensures quality

rationale: The Enterprise Metamodel's primary value is ensuring terminological and structural consistency across all architecture work in the enterprise. Without it, 'Application' in one team's model may be a very different concept from 'Application' in another's, making integration analysis, impact assessment, and governance impossible.

explanation.whyCorrect: In a large enterprise with multiple architecture teams, informal terminological consistency breaks down. The Metamodel is the shared schema that allows architecture work from different teams to be compared, combined, and governed coherently.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is too compliance-focused and doesn't address the practical argument. C is a tool-specific benefit, not the primary governance argument. D is unnecessarily personal and doesn't make the strongest case for the Metamodel.
explanation.examTip: The Metamodel's governance value: consistent vocabulary + consistent relationship types = comparable, governable architectures across the enterprise. This is its primary purpose.

stem: In the TOGAF Content Framework, what is the correct relationship between a deliverable and an artefact?

options.text: A deliverable is a type of artefact — they are in the same category with deliverables being more formal
An artefact is a building block — they can be used interchangeably in the Content Framework
A deliverable is a formal governance output that typically contains one or more artefacts as its content
Artefacts are produced in delivery phases; deliverables are produced in architecture phases

rationale: Deliverables are the formal governance containers — they have contractual status and require sign-off. Artefacts are the specific content elements (catalogs, matrices, diagrams) that live inside deliverables. The Architecture Definition Document (a deliverable) contains many artefacts.

explanation.whyCorrect: The relationship is hierarchical: deliverable > artefact. The Architecture Definition Document (deliverable) contains an Application Catalog, a Data Flow Diagram, and an Application/Data Matrix (all artefacts). The deliverable is signed off; the artefacts are the substance within it.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A blurs the distinction — deliverables and artefacts are different categories in the Content Framework, not sub-types of each other. B incorrectly conflates artefacts with building blocks. D introduces a false phase-based distinction.
explanation.examTip: Deliverable = the envelope (formal, signed). Artefact = what's inside the envelope (the actual diagrams, lists, matrices). One deliverable can contain many artefacts.

stem: An architecture programme has produced the following: (1) a system context diagram, (2) a list of all business services, (3) a technology component deployment diagram, (4) a grid mapping applications to business functions. In the TOGAF artefact taxonomy, these are respectively classified as:

options.text: Diagram, Catalog, Diagram, Matrix
Catalog, Catalog, Diagram, Matrix
Diagram, Diagram, Catalog, Matrix
Matrix, Catalog, Diagram, Diagram

rationale: (1) System context diagram = Diagram (visual). (2) List of business services = Catalog (structured inventory). (3) Deployment diagram = Diagram (visual representation of technology layout). (4) Grid mapping applications to business functions = Matrix (showing relationships between two sets).

explanation.whyCorrect: Apply the three rules: list/inventory = Catalog; relationship grid = Matrix; visual/picture = Diagram. (1) A context diagram is visual = Diagram. (2) A list of services is an inventory = Catalog. (3) A deployment diagram is visual = Diagram. (4) A grid of App × Function relationships = Matrix.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B incorrectly classifies the context diagram as a Catalog. C incorrectly classifies the business services list as a Diagram. D misclassifies multiple items.
explanation.examTip: Train yourself on the three categories: if it's a visual picture = Diagram; if it's a list of things = Catalog; if it's a grid showing how things relate = Matrix. Apply this mechanically to classify any artefact.

stem: The Architecture Metamodel is described as 'the schema governing architecture descriptions.' A new programme team proposes to extend the enterprise Metamodel to add a new entity type for 'AI Model' that doesn't currently exist. What is the correct governance process?

options.text: Each programme team can extend the Metamodel independently to meet their needs
The Metamodel cannot be extended — it is a fixed TOGAF standard
The proposed extension should be reviewed by the Architecture Board, approved through the tailoring process, and the updated Metamodel stored in the Architecture Repository
AI Models should be described using the existing Application Component entity type — no extension is needed

rationale: The Enterprise Metamodel is a governance artefact stored in the Architecture Metamodel class of the Architecture Repository. Changes to it require Architecture Board approval — it is not programme-specific and cannot be changed unilaterally. Once approved, the update benefits all future programmes.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Metamodel is an enterprise-wide governance artefact. Programme-level extensions that aren't approved create inconsistency. The Architecture Board governs Metamodel changes as part of the tailoring process, ensuring enterprise-wide coherence.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A allows fragmentation — every programme with a different Metamodel defeats the purpose of having one. B is too restrictive — TOGAF explicitly supports Metamodel tailoring to organisational context. D may be pragmatic but doesn't address whether the Metamodel should formally recognise AI Models.
explanation.examTip: Metamodel changes = governance process. The Architecture Board approves, the Preliminary Phase's tailoring mechanism handles it, and the Repository stores the result. Never unilateral programme-level changes.

stem: Which ADM deliverable formally authorises the architecture engagement, defines its scope and approach, and requires sign-off from the sponsoring organisation?

options.text: Architecture Vision
Architecture Definition Document
Statement of Architecture Work
Architecture Contract

rationale: The Statement of Architecture Work formally authorises the architecture engagement. It defines scope, approach, team, schedule, and success criteria — and must be signed off by the sponsoring organisation before architecture development begins.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Statement of Architecture Work is the 'mandate document' for the architecture engagement — analogous to a project initiation document. Without a signed SAW, the architecture team has no formal authority to proceed.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: The Architecture Vision (A) communicates strategic direction but doesn't authorise the engagement. The ADD (B) contains the architecture content. The Architecture Contract (D) is a Phase G governance agreement for implementation teams, not an engagement authorisation.
explanation.examTip: Authorisation document = Statement of Architecture Work. Communication document = Architecture Vision. Both are Phase A outputs but they serve completely different purposes.

stem: The Architecture Definition Document is described as 'the primary deliverable container for architecture content.' By the end of which phase does it contain completed descriptions for all four architecture domains?

options.text: Phase A: Architecture Vision
Phase C: Information Systems Architectures
Phase D: Technology Architecture
Phase E: Opportunities and Solutions

rationale: The ADD grows progressively: Phase B adds Business Architecture, Phase C adds Data and Application Architectures, Phase D adds Technology Architecture. By the end of Phase D, all four domain architectures are complete in the ADD.

explanation.whyCorrect: The ADD accumulates content phase by phase: B adds Business, C adds Data+Application, D adds Technology. Phase D is the last domain architecture phase, so the ADD reaches completion there.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Phase A (A) produces the Architecture Vision — the ADD content doesn't begin until Phase B. Phase C (B) completes Data and Application but Technology Architecture is still missing. Phase E (D) uses the complete ADD as input; it doesn't add domain content.
explanation.examTip: ADD completion timeline: Phase B = Business done. Phase C = Data + Application done. Phase D = Technology done = ADD complete. This progressive accumulation is tested frequently.

stem: A steering committee receives the Architecture Vision document for a new cloud transformation programme. A board member asks: 'Where are the detailed system specifications, the vendor choices, and the integration designs?' The Chief Architect explains this is inappropriate for the Architecture Vision. Why?

options.text: Architecture Vision is a Phase A deliverable — those details require Phase B approval first
Architecture Vision is intentionally high-level and aspirational — detailed specifications belong in the Architecture Definition Document produced across Phases B–D
System specifications are vendor-specific and excluded from TOGAF deliverables entirely
Those details would be produced in the Statement of Architecture Work, not the Architecture Vision

rationale: The Architecture Vision is deliberately high-level — it communicates strategic direction and builds stakeholder alignment before detailed architecture work begins. Detailed specifications, vendor choices, and integration designs are produced in the Architecture Definition Document across Phases B through D.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Architecture Vision exists to build executive understanding and secure approval to proceed — not to specify technical details. Adding system-level specifications to a Vision bypasses the governance steps in Phases B, C, and D that ensure those decisions are made with proper analysis.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A has the right phase reference but the wrong explanation. C is incorrect — TOGAF deliverables absolutely include system specifications (in the ADD). D is wrong — the SAW defines scope and approach, not architecture specifications.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Vision = aspirational, strategic, executive-facing. Architecture Definition Document = detailed, technical, domain-specific. This is the most frequently tested deliverable distinction on OGEA-101.

stem: An implementation team has completed delivery and asks: 'What architectural document should we check our work against to verify conformance?' The architect refers them to two specific deliverables. Which pair is correct?

options.text: Architecture Vision and Statement of Architecture Work
Architecture Definition Document and Architecture Requirements Specification
Architecture Roadmap and Implementation and Migration Plan
Architecture Contract and Architecture Roadmap

rationale: Conformance is assessed against the Architecture Definition Document (what the architecture looks like) and the Architecture Requirements Specification (the measurable requirements it must satisfy). Together they define what was architected and at what quality standard.

explanation.whyCorrect: Phase G compliance assessments check implementation against the ADD (architecture descriptions) and ARS (testable requirements). The ADD tells you what should have been built; the ARS tells you whether it meets the quality criteria.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Architecture Vision (A) and SAW are Phase A documents — they set direction and scope, not detailed specification. Roadmap and Migration Plan (C) describe the delivery sequence, not the architecture to conform to. Architecture Contract (D) governs the implementation obligations but references the ADD/ARS rather than replacing them.
explanation.examTip: Conformance check = ADD + ARS. The ADD describes the architecture; the ARS provides the measurable test criteria. These two deliverables together define what 'conformant' means.

stem: Which deliverable contains the sequence of Transition Architectures and work packages that describe how the enterprise will move from its Baseline to its Target Architecture over time?

options.text: Architecture Definition Document
Implementation and Migration Plan
Architecture Roadmap
Architecture Vision

rationale: The Architecture Roadmap is the deliverable that shows the architectural journey from Baseline to Target — the sequence of Transition Architectures and work packages. It is first produced in Phase E and finalised in Phase F.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Architecture Roadmap is an architectural view of the transformation sequence. It shows which Transition Architectures will be delivered, in what order, and why — communicating the architectural logic of the journey.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: The ADD (A) describes the Baseline and Target architectures but not the journey between them. The Implementation and Migration Plan (B) provides the detailed, costed delivery plan — more granular than the Roadmap. The Architecture Vision (D) is a high-level Phase A view of the Target only.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Roadmap = architectural view of the journey (Transition Architectures, work packages, sequence rationale). Migration Plan = detailed delivery plan (resources, costs, timelines). Both are needed; they serve different audiences.

stem: A programme manager receives the Architecture Roadmap and says: 'I'll use this as our project plan — it tells us what to do and when.' The Enterprise Architect corrects her. What is the key distinction she needs to explain?

options.text: The Roadmap is produced by architects, not project managers — it has a different owner
The Roadmap is an architectural view of the transformation sequence; it does not contain resource assignments, costs, or delivery timelines — the Implementation and Migration Plan provides those
The Roadmap is a governance document — it cannot be used for project planning
The Roadmap covers the full 5-year horizon; the project plan covers only 12 months

rationale: The Architecture Roadmap is an architectural view — it shows the sequence and rationale for Transition Architectures and work packages. It does not contain the resources, costs, timelines, and risk assessments needed for project delivery. The Implementation and Migration Plan (Phase F) provides those.

explanation.whyCorrect: The distinction is level of detail and audience. The Roadmap is for Architecture Board and executive audiences — communicating architectural logic. The Migration Plan is for programme and project managers — providing delivery-ready specifications.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A focuses on ownership, not the substantive difference in content. C overstates — the Roadmap informs delivery but isn't purely a governance document. D introduces an arbitrary time distinction that isn't the core issue.
explanation.examTip: Roadmap = what to build and in what architectural order (why). Migration Plan = how to build it (who, what cost, when, what risk). The Roadmap precedes and informs the Plan.

stem: An Architecture Contract is established for a cloud migration programme. Three months later, the implementation team's technical lead states: 'The Architecture Contract was for the architecture team — it doesn't bind us.' What is wrong with this statement?

options.text: Nothing — Architecture Contracts are internal architecture team documents
An Architecture Contract is a joint agreement between development partners AND sponsors — implementation teams are development partners and are bound by its terms
Architecture Contracts bind only external vendors, not internal teams
The Architecture Contract is advisory — only the Statement of Architecture Work is binding

rationale: An Architecture Contract is explicitly a joint agreement between development partners (the teams doing implementation) and the sponsoring organisation. The implementation team is a development partner — the contract exists precisely to define their architectural obligations.

explanation.whyCorrect: TOGAF defines the Architecture Contract as the document that formalises implementation teams' architectural obligations. It is not an internal architecture document — it is an agreement that the implementation team has entered into and is bound by.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is completely wrong — the Architecture Contract explicitly governs implementation teams. C introduces a false internal/external distinction. D is wrong — Architecture Contracts are governance documents with real authority in Phase G.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Contract parties: development partners (implementation teams) + sponsoring organisation (Architecture Board and sponsors). Both parties are bound. This is its entire governance purpose.

stem: An Architecture Requirements Specification has been produced for a new trading platform. The CTO asks: 'How is this different from the Architecture Definition Document?' What is the most accurate explanation?

options.text: They are different names for the same document — the ARS is an older term for the ADD
The ADD describes what the architecture looks like; the ARS specifies the measurable criteria the architecture must satisfy
The ADD covers business and data domains; the ARS covers application and technology domains
The ARS is produced in Phase A; the ADD is produced in Phase E

rationale: The ADD describes the architecture (what it is) — Baseline and Target descriptions across all four domains. The ARS specifies the measurable, testable requirements the architecture must satisfy. They complement each other: the ADD is the design; the ARS is the acceptance criteria.

explanation.whyCorrect: ADD = architecture description (diagrams, models, component specifications). ARS = requirements specification (measurable criteria: 'response time < 500ms', 'availability > 99.9%'). Together they define both the architecture and how to test whether it has been achieved.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — they are distinct deliverables with different contents and purposes. C introduces a false domain split; both cover all four domains. D is wrong — both begin to be produced from Phase B onwards, not Phase A and E respectively.
explanation.examTip: ADD = design. ARS = test criteria. Both are produced across Phases B–D and both are used in Phase G compliance assessments. Never confuse them.

stem: A governance audit examines a completed enterprise transformation programme. The auditors find: an Architecture Vision document, a Statement of Architecture Work, and an Architecture Definition Document for three of the four domains. The Technology Architecture domain has no ADD section. What governance risk does this create?

options.text: No risk — the ADD is optional for the Technology domain if the infrastructure is standard
The programme cannot be closed — all deliverables must be approved before programme closure
Phase D outputs are missing — Phase G compliance assessments for technology implementation have no architecture baseline to assess against
The programme team must redo Phase B through D before the programme can proceed

rationale: The Technology Architecture section of the ADD is the baseline against which Phase G compliance assessments evaluate infrastructure and platform implementations. Without it, implementation teams have no architectural specification to conform to, and compliance reviews cannot be conducted.

explanation.whyCorrect: Phase G assesses conformance against the ADD and ARS. If the Technology Architecture section is missing, technology implementations cannot be formally assessed. This creates invisible technical debt — infrastructure choices made without architectural governance.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — TOGAF does not make the Technology domain optional. B is technically true but doesn't identify the substantive governance risk. D overstates — the missing section needs to be produced, but not necessarily starting from Phase B.
explanation.examTip: Every domain architecture phase must produce its ADD section. Missing Technology Architecture = no foundation for Phase G technology compliance assessment = ungoverned infrastructure decisions.

stem: An architecture programme produced an Architecture Vision, Architecture Definition Document, and Architecture Requirements Specification. No Architecture Roadmap was produced. Phase F planning has begun. What is the consequence of this omission?

options.text: No consequence — the Architecture Roadmap is optional if the programme has a project plan
Phase F cannot produce a complete Implementation and Migration Plan without the Roadmap providing the architectural sequencing logic and Transition Architecture definitions
The Architecture Board must void the entire programme and restart from Phase A
The Roadmap should have been in Phase A — it cannot be created retrospectively

rationale: The Architecture Roadmap (produced in Phase E) provides the architectural sequencing — which Transition Architectures, in what order, with which work packages. Phase F's Implementation and Migration Plan is built from this Roadmap. Without the Roadmap, the Migration Plan has no architectural basis for sequencing.

explanation.whyCorrect: Phase F takes the Phase E Roadmap and adds detail: resources, costs, risk assessments, timelines. The Roadmap is the input to Phase F. Producing a Migration Plan without a Roadmap means Phase F has no architectural sequencing logic — it risks violating dependency constraints and missing Transition Architecture coherence requirements.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — the Roadmap is a mandatory Phase E output, not optional. C is disproportionate. D is wrong — the Roadmap is a Phase E deliverable, not Phase A.
explanation.examTip: Phase E → Architecture Roadmap → Phase F → Implementation and Migration Plan. These are sequential dependencies. Phase F cannot complete without the Phase E Roadmap.

stem: An architecture review finds that three separate project teams each have their own 'Statement of Architecture Work' for overlapping scopes within the same enterprise programme. The Architecture Board is concerned. What governance issue does this indicate?

options.text: Each project needs its own SAW — this is normal and expected
Multiple SAWs for overlapping scopes indicate the programme lacks a properly scoped engagement authorisation — separate projects may be duplicating or conflicting architectural work
The SAW should be replaced by Architecture Contracts for each project
The SAW is reissued for each ADM phase — three phases have completed, hence three SAWs

rationale: The Statement of Architecture Work is produced at the start of an architecture engagement to define scope, prevent overlap, and authorise one coherent programme of work. Multiple overlapping SAWs suggest scope was not properly defined — different teams may be architecting the same areas without coordination.

explanation.whyCorrect: The SAW's explicit purpose is to define and bound the architecture engagement scope. Overlapping scopes in separate SAWs means the scoping exercise failed — creating risk of duplicated effort, conflicting architectures, and missed dependencies.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — multiple overlapping SAWs represent a governance failure, not normal practice. C conflates the SAW (engagement authorisation) with Architecture Contracts (implementation obligations). D is wrong — the SAW is produced once per engagement, not per phase.
explanation.examTip: The SAW is a scope-defining, authorisation document produced once per engagement. Multiple overlapping SAWs in the same programme = scope governance failure = conflict risk.

stem: An architecture programme produces an 'Application Interaction Diagram' showing how eight applications communicate in the target state, what protocols they use, and what data they exchange. In which ADM phase is this most likely produced, and what type of artefact is it?

options.text: Phase B (Business Architecture) — Matrix
Phase C (Information Systems Architectures) — Diagram
Phase D (Technology Architecture) — Catalog
Phase E (Opportunities and Solutions) — Deliverable

rationale: An Application Interaction Diagram showing application communications, protocols, and data exchanges is a visual representation (Diagram) produced in Phase C Application Architecture. Application-level interactions are defined as part of the Application Architecture, which is Phase C's second sub-phase.

explanation.whyCorrect: Application interactions are a core Phase C Application Architecture concern. A diagram showing application communication patterns is visual = Diagram artefact type. Phase C is correct because it is specifically where application interactions are architecturally defined.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Phase B (A) covers business processes and capabilities, not application interactions. Phase D (C) covers infrastructure hosting and networking, not application-level interaction design. Phase E (D) synthesises outputs from earlier phases but doesn't produce domain architecture diagrams.
explanation.examTip: Application interaction diagrams = Phase C Application Architecture. Technology infrastructure diagrams = Phase D. Business capability maps = Phase B. Match the diagram content to its domain phase.

stem: An architect is tasked with producing Phase B Business Architecture artefacts. She produces: (1) a business capability heat map, (2) a value stream map, (3) a business process flow diagram, (4) a Role/Responsibility matrix. Which artefact types have been produced?

options.text: Diagram, Diagram, Diagram, Matrix
Catalog, Diagram, Diagram, Matrix
Diagram, Diagram, Catalog, Diagram
Matrix, Catalog, Diagram, Matrix

rationale: (1) Business capability heat map = visual representation of capabilities with colour coding = Diagram. (2) Value stream map = visual flow diagram = Diagram. (3) Business process flow = visual workflow diagram = Diagram. (4) Role/Responsibility matrix = grid showing relationships between Roles and Responsibilities = Matrix.

explanation.whyCorrect: Heat maps, value stream maps, and process flows are all visual representations = Diagrams. A Role/Responsibility grid shows relationships between two types of entity = Matrix. Three diagrams and one matrix.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B incorrectly classifies the capability heat map as a Catalog — a heat map is a visual representation, not a list. C misclassifies the value stream map as a Catalog. D misclassifies multiple items.
explanation.examTip: Key classification rule: if it's primarily visual (even if structured), it's a Diagram. A heat map, despite having structured content, is fundamentally a visual representation. Only flat lists without visual elements are Catalogs.

stem: A post-implementation review reveals that the delivered system satisfies 95% of requirements but uses a deployment topology fundamentally different from the Technology Architecture specified in the ADD. What should the architecture team do?

options.text: Update the ADD to match the delivered system — it is now the new baseline
Raise a Phase G non-conformance finding; assess whether a retrospective dispensation is appropriate or remediation is required
Accept the deviation — 95% requirement satisfaction is sufficient for architecture conformance
Initiate a full new ADM cycle to redesign the Technology Architecture

rationale: A fundamental deviation from the ADD's Technology Architecture topology is a non-conformance, regardless of functional requirement satisfaction. The governance process requires this to be formally assessed — either a retrospective dispensation (with documented justification) or remediation.

explanation.whyCorrect: Phase G governance applies throughout implementation, not just at functional milestones. A fundamentally different topology may have implications for resilience, scalability, security, or future development that the Architecture Board must assess.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A normalises the deviation without governance assessment — this is how undocumented architectural drift accumulates. C incorrectly treats requirement satisfaction percentage as an architectural conformance criterion. D is disproportionate.
explanation.examTip: Deviations from the ADD discovered post-implementation are still governance events. The options are: retrospective dispensation (if justifiable) or remediation. Neither 'accept quietly' nor 'restart the programme' is the right answer.

stem: An organisation's Phase E has identified eight work packages but produced no Architecture Roadmap. The team argues: 'The Migration Plan we'll produce in Phase F serves the same purpose.' What is the most important reason this argument is flawed?

options.text: The Architecture Roadmap and Migration Plan are different documents with different owners

The Architecture Roadmap provides the architectural sequencing rationale — defining Transition Architectures and work package ordering. Without it, the Migration Plan lacks architectural justification for its sequence
The Migration Plan requires Architecture Board approval; the Roadmap does not
The Roadmap is required for TOGAF certification compliance; the Migration Plan is not

rationale: The Architecture Roadmap is the architectural justification for the transformation sequence — it explains why Transition Architectures are ordered the way they are, based on architectural dependencies and coherence. A Migration Plan without this rationale is a delivery schedule that could inadvertently violate architectural dependencies.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Roadmap and Plan serve different purposes. The Roadmap provides the 'why' of sequencing (architectural coherence, dependencies, Transition Architecture definitions). The Plan provides the 'how' (resources, costs, timelines). The Plan should derive from the Roadmap — not replace it.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A focuses on ownership, which is not the most important issue. C inverts governance reality — both require Architecture Board input. D is a compliance argument that doesn't address the substantive issue.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Roadmap = architectural logic and justification for sequence. Migration Plan = delivery mechanics. The Plan DEPENDS on the Roadmap — it translates architectural sequencing into delivery reality.

stem: During a Phase C review, the architecture team has produced catalogs of data entities and applications, matrices showing application/data relationships, and data flow diagrams. A governance reviewer argues: 'All these separate documents should be combined into one master document.' The Chief Architect disagrees. What is the strongest architectural reason to maintain them separately?

options.text: Separate documents are required by TOGAF certification

Different artefact types serve different analytical purposes — catalogs for inventory, matrices for relationship analysis, diagrams for visual communication. Combining them would obscure their distinct governance value
Each artefact must be approved by a different stakeholder — combining them creates approval conflicts
TOGAF limits the number of artefacts per deliverable to a fixed maximum

rationale: The three artefact types serve distinct analytical purposes. Catalogs provide the inventory foundation; matrices reveal relationships between catalogue items; diagrams communicate architecture visually to stakeholders. Each type answers different questions and is consumed differently. Combining them collapses these distinct analytical lenses.

explanation.whyCorrect: In architectural governance, catalogs enable machine-readable analysis (impact assessment, compliance checking), matrices enable relationship analysis (dependency mapping, CRUD analysis), and diagrams enable stakeholder communication. These purposes are better served by maintaining distinct, structured artefacts.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is a compliance argument that doesn't address the substance. C invents an approval rule. D is false — TOGAF has no fixed maximum artefact count per deliverable.
explanation.examTip: The three artefact types are complementary analytical instruments, not just different ways to present the same information. Their distinct structure enables different types of analysis — this is why they are maintained separately.

stem: An architecture programme has produced both an Architecture Roadmap and an Implementation and Migration Plan. The Architecture Board is reviewing both. A board member asks: 'If we already have the Migration Plan, why do we need the Roadmap?' What is the complete and correct answer?

options.text: The Roadmap is produced earlier — it is superseded by the Migration Plan once Phase F is complete
The Roadmap and Migration Plan serve different audiences: architects review the Roadmap; project managers review the Migration Plan

The Roadmap shows the architectural logic and coherence of the transformation sequence — including Transition Architecture definitions. The Migration Plan translates this into delivery. Both are needed because the Roadmap justifies the sequence the Plan implements
The Roadmap covers the future; the Migration Plan covers the past and present state

rationale: The Roadmap and Migration Plan are both needed because they serve different purposes within a coherent pair. The Roadmap provides architectural justification and Transition Architecture definitions. The Migration Plan translates that architectural structure into delivery mechanics. Removing either leaves the transformation with either no delivery plan or no architectural rationale.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Roadmap is the 'why' and 'what' of architectural sequencing — it defines Transition Architectures and justifies their order architecturally. The Plan is the 'how' — the funded, resourced, risk-assessed delivery schedule that implements the Roadmap. They are complementary, not redundant.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — the Roadmap remains a maintained deliverable throughout the programme. B is partially true but incomplete — audience difference is a consequence, not the full explanation. D is wrong — both cover future state.
explanation.examTip: The Roadmap is the architecture; the Plan is the delivery. The Plan should derive from and remain consistent with the Roadmap. Neither can fully substitute for the other.

stem: An organisation tailors TOGAF and decides to combine the Architecture Definition Document and Architecture Requirements Specification into a single document called the 'Architecture Specification.' Supporters argue it reduces document overhead. Critics from the Architecture Board argue against this. What is the strongest architectural governance argument against combining them?

options.text: TOGAF prohibits combining deliverables during tailoring

The ADD and ARS serve fundamentally different governance purposes — the ADD describes what was designed; the ARS specifies testable acceptance criteria. Combining them blurs the distinction between design and requirements, complicating compliance assessments
A combined document cannot be approved by the Architecture Board
The combined document would be too large to maintain effectively

rationale: The ADD and ARS serve distinct governance purposes in Phase G: the ADD is the design reference; the ARS is the test specification. In a compliance assessment, reviewers need to distinguish 'what was architected' (ADD) from 'what measurable standard must it meet' (ARS). Combining them obscures this distinction.

explanation.whyCorrect: Phase G compliance assessments use both documents in specific ways: the ADD to assess whether what was built matches the architectural design; the ARS to assess whether it meets the measurable quality criteria. When combined, compliance reviewers cannot cleanly separate these two analytical tasks.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is wrong — TOGAF's tailoring explicitly permits deliverable combination in appropriate contexts. C is wrong — the Board approves whatever deliverable structure is defined in the Tailored Architecture Framework. D focuses on maintenance, not governance substance.
explanation.examTip: The strongest argument against combining deliverables is always about governance clarity — what distinct purpose does each serve, and does combining them obscure that purpose? ADD = design reference; ARS = test specification. These are different governance instruments.

stem: A Capability Assessment is listed as an optional deliverable in TOGAF. A programme manager asks: 'When should we produce one?' The architect explains. Which situation most strongly justifies producing a Capability Assessment?

options.text: When the programme requires more than £1 million of investment
When there is a significant gap between the enterprise's current capabilities and those needed to deliver or operate the Target Architecture
When external auditors require evidence of architecture capability maturity
When the Architecture Board requests one during Phase G compliance review

rationale: A Capability Assessment documents the current capabilities of the enterprise and assesses any gaps relative to what is needed for the Target Architecture. It is most valuable when the transformation requires significantly different capabilities — people, processes, and technologies — from what currently exists.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Capability Assessment directly feeds transformation readiness planning. If the enterprise needs capabilities it doesn't currently have, this must be recognised and planned for. It also informs Phase A's assessment of readiness for business transformation.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A uses a financial threshold that TOGAF doesn't reference. C is an external compliance trigger, not an internal architectural one. D makes it reactive to Board requests rather than driven by programme need.
explanation.examTip: Capability Assessment = current vs. required capabilities for the Target Architecture. Most useful when a significant capability gap exists. This directly informs transformation readiness and work package sequencing.

stem: Which of the following TOGAF artefacts produced in Phase D (Technology Architecture) is most likely to be a Matrix?

options.text: A network topology diagram showing how data centres connect
A platform decomposition diagram showing infrastructure layers
A technology component catalogue listing all infrastructure components
A technology/application matrix showing which applications are hosted on which platforms

rationale: A technology/application matrix — showing which application components run on which technology platforms — is a grid-format artefact showing the relationship between two types of architectural element. This is a Matrix. It is a key Phase D artefact that traces applications (Phase C output) to technology platforms (Phase D output).

explanation.whyCorrect: Matrices show relationships between catalogue items. 'Applications × Technology Platforms' is exactly a matrix — it answers 'which applications run on which infrastructure?' and directly supports deployment planning.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is a Diagram (visual network topology). B is a Diagram (visual platform decomposition). C is a Catalog (structured list of infrastructure components). Only D is a relationship grid between two entity types = Matrix.
explanation.examTip: Phase D Matrix example: Technology/Application matrix (which apps on which platforms). Phase C Matrix example: Application/Data matrix (which apps use which data). The phase context helps identify the matrix type.

stem: A Compliance Assessment is produced during Phase G. A programme director asks: 'What makes this different from just reviewing the Architecture Definition Document?' The architect explains. What is the key distinction?

options.text: A Compliance Assessment is produced by the project team; the ADD is produced by the architecture team
The ADD describes the intended architecture; a Compliance Assessment formally evaluates whether the implementation conforms to that intended architecture using defined criteria
The ADD covers all four domains; the Compliance Assessment covers only the Technology domain
A Compliance Assessment is optional; the ADD is mandatory

rationale: The ADD is the design reference — it describes what the architecture should be. A Compliance Assessment is a formal evaluation process that assesses whether what has been built actually matches the ADD. One is a specification; the other is a systematic verification of conformance against that specification.

explanation.whyCorrect: The ADD describes intent; the Compliance Assessment measures actuality against intent. The assessment uses the ADD and ARS as its reference documents — producing a formal verdict (Conformant, Non-conformant, etc.) with specific findings and required actions.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A describes a practical ownership distinction but not the substantive difference. C invents a domain restriction. D is wrong — both are formal TOGAF deliverables; neither is optional in a properly governed programme.
explanation.examTip: ADD = the design. Compliance Assessment = the verdict on whether the delivery matched the design. These are design-time and assessment-time counterparts.

stem: The TOGAF Content Framework organises architecture work products into three categories. Which of the following correctly lists all three?

options.text: Documents, Models, and Frameworks
Deliverables, Artefacts, and Building Blocks
Specifications, Standards, and Guidelines
Principles, Architectures, and Roadmaps

rationale: The TOGAF Content Framework organises architecture work products into exactly three categories: Deliverables (formal governance outputs), Artefacts (specific content elements — catalogs, matrices, diagrams), and Building Blocks (reusable capability components — ABBs and SBBs).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a foundational Content Framework fact. The three categories serve different purposes: Deliverables for governance, Artefacts for analytical content, Building Blocks for reuse. Together they cover all architecture work products.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A introduces informal terms not used in the Content Framework. C lists types of guidance documentation. D lists specific architecture elements, not the framework's organisational categories.
explanation.examTip: Three Content Framework categories: Deliverables, Artefacts, Building Blocks. If a question asks for 'the three categories' or 'how TOGAF organises work products', this is always the answer.

stem: An organisation has completed a major transformation programme. The Architecture Board proposes to archive all programme deliverables and treat them as 'completed — no longer active.' The Chief Architect objects. What is the strongest architectural argument for maintaining active access to these deliverables?

options.text: Regulatory requirements mandate retaining architecture documents for seven years
Completed programme deliverables — particularly the ADD and ARS — become the Baseline Architecture for the next programme and are required inputs for future ADM phases
The Architecture Board is responsible for document retention, not the Chief Architect
Archived deliverables cannot be retrieved in time for future programmes

rationale: When a programme completes, its Target Architecture becomes the new Baseline Architecture. The ADD from the completed programme is a primary input to future ADM Phase A (assessing current state) and Phase B onwards (developing the new Baseline description). Archiving it as 'inactive' severs this critical link.

explanation.whyCorrect: The TOGAF Architecture Repository and the ADM are continuous — each cycle's Target Architecture is the next cycle's Baseline. The ADD documents exactly what was built, making it essential for future programmes' Gap Analysis, impact assessment, and baseline documentation.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is a compliance argument that doesn't address the architectural substance. C deflects responsibility. D is an operational concern, not an architectural argument.
explanation.examTip: Architecture deliverables don't become irrelevant when a programme ends. The Target Architecture becomes the Baseline for the next cycle. This 'living architecture' principle is fundamental to TOGAF's continuous ADM model.

stem: A TOGAF architecture programme produces a deliverable described as: 'A formal evaluation of whether a proposed architecture solution complies with enterprise Architecture Principles and Standards.' This is produced mid-programme to assess a vendor's proposed solution. What deliverable is this?

options.text: Architecture Requirements Specification
Compliance Assessment
Architecture Contract
Architecture Definition Document

rationale: A Compliance Assessment is a formal evaluation of whether something (a solution, a design, an implementation) conforms to the enterprise Architecture Principles and standards. It can be produced during architecture development (assessing a vendor proposal) or during Phase G (assessing implemented work).

explanation.whyCorrect: Compliance Assessments are not exclusively Phase G deliverables — they can be produced whenever a formal conformance evaluation is needed. Assessing a vendor's proposed solution against Architecture Principles mid-programme is exactly this use case.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: The ARS (A) specifies requirements; it doesn't evaluate conformance. The Architecture Contract (C) is an agreement for implementation obligations. The ADD (D) describes the architecture design.
explanation.examTip: Compliance Assessments can be produced in multiple contexts — vendor proposal review, mid-programme milestone assessment, and Phase G post-delivery review. The trigger is always: 'does this conform to the architecture?'

stem: According to the TOGAF Standard, which of the following is explicitly listed as a valid example of an "enterprise"?

options.text: Only a whole corporation with a single unified ownership structure
A partnership or alliance of businesses working together, such as a consortium
Any organisation with more than 500 employees
Only government agencies, not private-sector organisations

rationale: The Standard explicitly lists partnerships and alliances of businesses working together, such as a consortium, as one of its named examples of a valid "enterprise" — alongside a whole corporation, a single division, or a chain of geographically distant organisations linked by common ownership.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Standard's definition is deliberately broad: an enterprise is any collection of organisations with common goals. A consortium of independent businesses fits this definition exactly as named.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is false — a single corporation is only one of several named examples, not the exclusive definition. C is false — size (employee count) is never used as the defining criterion. D is false — government agencies are one named example among several, not an exclusive category.
explanation.examTip: Any question testing 'what counts as an enterprise' should be answered with the common-goals test, not size, sector, or single-ownership tests.

stem: An architect states: "Enterprise Architecture is really just IT Architecture with a fancier name — its job is to design better IT systems." What does this statement get wrong?

options.text: Enterprise Architecture optimises the enterprise's fragmented processes into an integrated environment responsive to business strategy, not just IT system design
Enterprise Architecture only applies to enterprises with more than one IT department
Enterprise Architecture is a subset of Technology Architecture, not the other way around
Enterprise Architecture was created after IT Architecture and replaced it entirely

rationale: The Standard's executive overview explicitly frames Enterprise Architecture as addressing the fragmented legacy of business processes (manual and automated) to enable responsiveness to business strategy — not merely as "IT Architecture" focused on system design.

explanation.whyCorrect: The purpose of Enterprise Architecture is explicitly business-strategic — optimising across the whole enterprise, not confined to IT system design decisions.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B invents a scale requirement not in the Standard. C inverts the actual relationship — Technology Architecture is one of four domains within Enterprise Architecture, not the reverse. D fabricates a historical claim not supported by the Standard.
explanation.examTip: Watch for questions that try to narrow Enterprise Architecture down to just 'IT.' The Standard explicitly distinguishes EA from IT Architecture in its opening executive overview.

stem: Which of the following pairs correctly matches the two official meanings of "Architecture" in the TOGAF Standard?

options.text: A cost estimate for IT projects; and a governance policy document
A formal description of a system to guide implementation; and the structure of components with their governing principles
A diagram of the network; and a list of approved vendors
A business strategy document; and an IT service catalogue

rationale: TOGAF's official two-part definition of "Architecture" is: (1) a formal description of a system, or detailed plan at component level, to guide implementation; and (2) the structure of components, their inter-relationships, and the principles and guidelines governing their design and evolution.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own two-part definition, and both parts are commonly tested — candidates who only remember one half are vulnerable to distractor options.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A, C, and D are all plausible-sounding but fabricated definitions with no basis in the Standard's actual glossary entry for 'Architecture.'
explanation.examTip: Memorise both halves of the Architecture definition exactly — exam questions frequently test whether you know only one half or both.

stem: The Open Group's stated mission is to drive the creation of Boundaryless Information Flow™. Which best describes what this mission actually represents?

options.text: A specific software product sold by The Open Group
Access to integrated information to support business process improvements, representing a desired end-state of an enterprise's infrastructure
A certification exam separate from TOGAF Foundation and Practitioner
A mandatory technical standard that all TOGAF-certified architects must implement

rationale: Boundaryless Information Flow™ is explicitly defined as shorthand for "access to integrated information to support business process improvements" — representing a desired state of an enterprise's infrastructure, not a product, exam, or mandatory technical standard.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own glossary definition, word for word in substance. It's an aspiration/goal, not a deliverable or product.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A is false — it's a trademarked concept, not a product. C is false — it's not an exam category. D is false — TOGAF doesn't mandate specific technical implementations to achieve this goal; it's a directional aspiration the framework works toward.
explanation.examTip: Boundaryless Information Flow is the goal; TOGAF (and specifically III-RM) is one of the mechanisms working toward it. Don't confuse the aspiration with the method.

stem: A multinational corporation has twelve semi-autonomous divisions, each with its own IT department, but all sharing a common parent company and overall strategic goals. For the purpose of applying TOGAF, which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Only the parent company counts as "the enterprise"; the divisions are entirely outside TOGAF's scope
Each division must be treated as a completely separate enterprise with no shared architecture possible
The corporation may comprise multiple enterprises, each potentially requiring its own Enterprise Architecture, while still benefiting from a common framework for shared building blocks and re-use
TOGAF cannot be applied at all until the divisions are merged into a single legal entity

rationale: The Standard explicitly recognises that organisations may comprise multiple enterprises, each potentially maintaining independent Enterprise Architectures, while still having much in common — creating potential for a shared framework, common building blocks, and a shareable Architecture Repository.

explanation.whyCorrect: This scenario matches the Standard's own description of complex organisations almost exactly — multiple potential enterprises within one larger organisation, benefiting from shared architecture assets.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly excludes the divisions from TOGAF's scope entirely. B wrongly forbids any shared architecture between divisions. D fabricates a legal-merger prerequisite that doesn't exist in the Standard.
explanation.examTip: Complex, multi-division organisations are a common Part 1 exam scenario type — the correct answer usually allows for multiple enterprises coexisting with shared framework benefits, not an all-or-nothing single-enterprise view.

stem: How many free-standing documents make up the TOGAF Standard Fundamental Content?

options.text: Four
Five
Six
Eight

rationale: The TOGAF Standard Fundamental Content is presented as six free-standing documents: Introduction and Core Concepts, Architecture Development Method, ADM Techniques, Applying the ADM, Architecture Content, and Enterprise Architecture Capability and Governance.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a directly stated, frequently tested fact — six documents, named specifically in the Standard's own preface.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Four, five, and eight are all plausible-sounding distractor numbers with no basis in the Standard's actual structure.
explanation.examTip: Memorise the exact count (six) and be ready to name at least a few of the six documents by name.

stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between the TOGAF Standard and the TOGAF Library?

options.text: The TOGAF Library replaces the Standard once an organisation reaches a certain maturity level
The Standard describes the generally applicable approach to Enterprise and IT Architecture; the Library is a portfolio of additional guidance material supporting practical application
The Library is mandatory reading for OGEA-101, while the Standard is optional
The Standard and Library are two names for the same identical set of documents

rationale: The Standard explicitly describes itself as the generally applicable approach to Enterprise and IT Architecture, supplemented by the Library — a portfolio of additional guidance material supporting the practical application of the TOGAF approach in specific contexts.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own stated relationship — core method (Standard) plus supplementary situational guidance (Library).
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A fabricates a maturity-based replacement relationship. C reverses the actual OGEA-101 requirement — the Standard's fundamental content, not Series Guides, is the core exam-tested material. D falsely claims identity between two distinct things.
explanation.examTip: Standard = core, universal. Library = supplementary, situational. Don't conflate the two.

stem: Which of the six Fundamental Content documents specifically describes the TOGAF ADM as an iterative approach to developing an Enterprise Architecture?

options.text: Introduction and Core Concepts
Architecture Development Method
ADM Techniques
Applying the ADM

rationale: The TOGAF Standard — Architecture Development Method document is specifically described as describing "the TOGAF Architecture Development Method (ADM) — an iterative approach to developing an Enterprise Architecture."

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the document's own stated purpose, directly from the Standard's preface listing the six documents.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Introduction and Core Concepts covers definitions and the overview, not the ADM's detailed method. ADM Techniques covers supporting techniques used within the ADM. Applying the ADM covers adapting the ADM to specific contexts, not describing the base method itself.
explanation.examTip: Each of the six documents has a specific, distinct stated purpose — know which document 'owns' which core concept.

stem: An organisation new to TOGAF asks whether it must adopt all six Fundamental Content documents simultaneously before beginning any architecture work. Which is the most accurate response, per the Standard?

options.text: Yes, TOGAF's six documents are indivisible and must be adopted as a complete package
No — organisations new to TOGAF are expected to focus on particular constituent documents for initial adoption, with others tabled for later consideration
No — organisations must adopt exactly three of the six documents, no more, no fewer, for their first cycle
The Standard does not address this question at all

rationale: The Standard explicitly states that organisations new to TOGAF and wishing to incrementally adopt TOGAF concepts are expected to focus on particular constituent documents for initial adoption, with other areas tabled for later consideration.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is directly and explicitly stated guidance for organisations new to TOGAF — selective, incremental adoption is expected, not discouraged.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A contradicts the Standard's explicit encouragement of selective adoption. C invents an arbitrary numeric requirement not in the Standard. D is false — the Standard directly addresses this exact question.
explanation.examTip: This is a frequently tested nuance: TOGAF explicitly supports incremental, selective adoption for new organisations — don't assume 'all six at once' is required.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes TOGAF Series Guides from the six Fundamental Content documents?

options.text: Series Guides are simply older editions of the Fundamental Content documents
Series Guides are a separate collection addressing specific concerns and use cases; not all Series Guides will be relevant in every situation
Series Guides must all be adopted alongside the six Fundamental Content documents to be considered TOGAF-compliant
There is no meaningful distinction — the terms are interchangeable

rationale: The Standard explicitly structures itself as the six Fundamental Content documents plus a separate collection of TOGAF Series Guides, providing guidance to address specific concerns and use cases — explicitly noting that not all Series Guides will be relevant in every situation.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own explicit structural distinction, directly stated alongside the diagram showing Fundamental Content and Series Guides as two separate elements.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A fabricates a version-history relationship that doesn't exist. C contradicts the Standard's explicit statement that not all Series Guides are relevant in every situation. D denies a distinction the Standard itself explicitly makes.
explanation.examTip: Remember: Fundamental Content (six documents) is the core; Series Guides are optional, situational supplements — not something to claim you've 'fully adopted' as a checklist.

stem: Which ADM phase covers both Data Architecture and Application Architecture?

options.text: Phase B
Phase C
Phase D
Phase E

rationale: Phase C is titled "Information Systems Architectures" (plural) and explicitly covers both Data Architecture and Application Architecture as its two constituent parts.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is directly stated and one of the most heavily tested facts in the Foundation exam — the plural naming of the phase is itself a clue.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Phase B covers Business Architecture only. Phase D covers Technology Architecture only. Phase E covers Opportunities and Solutions, not any of the four domains directly.
explanation.examTip: If a question asks which single phase covers two domains, the answer is always Phase C (Data + Application).

stem: Does TOGAF mandate a specific order for developing Data Architecture versus Application Architecture within Phase C?

options.text: Yes, Data Architecture must always be developed first
Yes, Application Architecture must always be developed first
No — the Standard explicitly supports both sequences, with advocates for each depending on context
No — TOGAF requires both to be developed in a single simultaneous step with no distinction

rationale: Phase C involves some combination of Data and Application Architecture, in either order. The Standard explicitly notes advocates exist for both sequences — a data-driven approach (e.g., Spewak's Enterprise Architecture Planning) and an application-driven approach (common for ERP/CRM-centric organisations).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is one of the most commonly mistested nuances — many candidates assume a mandated order exists when the Standard explicitly says otherwise.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A and B both wrongly assert a mandatory single order. D wrongly claims no distinction exists between the two domains at all, which contradicts Phase C explicitly covering two separate architecture domains.
explanation.examTip: If asked which comes first, Data or Application, the safest answer acknowledging Standard nuance is: it depends on context, both orderings are valid.

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four core architecture domains TOGAF is designed to support?

options.text: Business Architecture
Security Architecture
Data Architecture
Technology Architecture

rationale: The four core architecture domains are Business, Data, Application, and Technology (BDAT). Security Architecture is not a fifth core domain — it is created by combining appropriate views across the four core BDAT domains.

explanation.whyCorrect: Security Architecture is explicitly described as a domain formed by combining views across BDAT, not a fifth standalone core domain.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Business, Data, and Technology Architecture are all explicitly named as core domains.
explanation.examTip: There is no fifth core domain. Security, Risk, and Digital Architecture are all formed by combining BDAT views, not standing alongside BDAT as equals.

stem: Which architecture domain "describes the digital architecture and the logical software and hardware infrastructure capabilities and standards" required to support business, data, and application services?

options.text: Business Architecture
Data Architecture
Application Architecture
Technology Architecture

rationale: The Standard's own definition of Technology Architecture describes exactly this — the digital architecture and logical software/hardware infrastructure capabilities and standards required to support deployment of business, data, and application services.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own verbatim-substance definition for Technology Architecture, including explicit reference to digital services, IoT, cloud, and infrastructure.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Business Architecture defines strategy/governance/processes. Data Architecture describes logical/physical data assets. Application Architecture provides a blueprint for applications and their interactions — none of these describe infrastructure capabilities and standards.
explanation.examTip: Technology Architecture is explicitly the domain that includes digital services, IoT, cloud, middleware, and networks — a distinctive, testable list.

stem: A CIO says: "We should skip developing our Business Architecture — we already know we're implementing a specific CRM platform, so let's design the Technology Architecture first and work backward." What is the strongest architectural objection to this approach?

options.text: Technology Architecture must always be developed in Phase D, and the CIO's proposal breaks phase numbering
Business Architecture defines the strategy, governance, and processes the technology must serve — skipping it risks designing technology that doesn't align with actual business needs
CRM platforms cannot be used within a TOGAF-compliant architecture at all
There is no valid objection — jumping to Technology Architecture is an accepted TOGAF shortcut

rationale: Business Architecture must come first because it defines strategy, governance, organisation, and processes that all other domains — including Technology — exist to serve. Deriving business needs backward from a pre-selected technology risks fitting the business to the tool rather than the reverse.

explanation.whyCorrect: This reflects the fundamental BDAT dependency: Business drives everything, Technology serves business needs, not the other way around.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A misidentifies the objection as merely about phase numbering rather than the substantive dependency issue. C fabricates a prohibition on CRM platforms that doesn't exist. D wrongly validates an approach the BDAT dependency logic specifically argues against.
explanation.examTip: Scenario questions describing a technology-first approach to a supposedly 'already decided' platform are testing whether you understand BDAT's dependency logic, not phase-numbering trivia.

stem: Which of the following correctly defines a TOGAF "Deliverable"?

options.text: Any diagram produced during an ADM phase
A work product that is contractually specified and formally reviewed, approved, and signed off by stakeholders
A reusable component combined with others to deliver architectures and solutions
A list of building blocks of a specific type used for governance

rationale: A Deliverable is specifically defined as a work product that is contractually specified and formally reviewed, approved, and signed off by stakeholders — distinct from artifacts and building blocks.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the precise, exam-tested definition distinguishing Deliverables from the other two content categories.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A describes something that could be an artifact (specifically a diagram), not necessarily a deliverable. C describes a Building Block. D describes a Catalog, a type of artifact.
explanation.examTip: The contractual, formally-signed-off nature is what makes something a Deliverable — not simply being produced during an ADM phase.

stem: An architect writes an ABB stating: "A network capability is required to connect all regional offices." Which statement about this ABB is correct?

options.text: It is invalid because it doesn't name a specific vendor or product
It is correctly written — ABBs describe required capability independent of implementation, and can be realised by different SBBs (e.g., a satellite hive or a small set of large satellites)
It should be reclassified as a Solution Building Block since it describes a real business need
ABBs must always specify at least the general category of technology (e.g., "satellite" or "fibre")

rationale: This is a textbook example of a well-formed ABB — describing required capability without specifying implementation. The Standard's own example uses a network requirement realised by different satellite configurations as SBBs.

explanation.whyCorrect: ABBs are meant to be implementation-independent — not naming a vendor or technology category is a feature, not a flaw.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly treats vendor-independence as invalidating rather than defining the ABB. C confuses ABB with SBB — describing a need doesn't make something an implementation choice. D fabricates a requirement to specify even a general technology category, which isn't part of the ABB definition.
explanation.examTip: The satellite network example (one ABB, two different SBB configurations) is the Standard's own illustrative example — expect it or a close variant on the exam.

stem: Which three categories are artifacts generally classified into?

options.text: Deliverables, Requirements, Standards
Catalogs, Matrices, Diagrams
Building Blocks, Components, Services
Views, Viewpoints, Models

rationale: Artifacts are generally classified as catalogs (lists of things), matrices (showing relationships between things), and diagrams (pictures of things).

explanation.whyCorrect: This CMD classification is a foundational, frequently tested fact underpinning the entire Content Framework.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A confuses artifact types with unrelated content categories. C lists building-block-related terms, not artifact classifications. D lists View/Viewpoint concepts, a related but distinct topic.
explanation.examTip: Catalog = list. Matrix = relationships. Diagram = picture. Simple memory anchor, frequently tested directly.

stem: A Programme Director asks whether a produced Application Interaction Matrix must be formally signed off by the steering committee. What determines the correct answer?

options.text: All artifacts are automatically deliverables and therefore always require formal sign-off
No artifacts ever require formal sign-off, only named deliverables like the Architecture Definition Document
Whether the artifact is a deliverable — and therefore requires sign-off — depends on the contractual specification for this specific engagement
Matrices specifically are exempt from ever being classified as deliverables, unlike catalogs and diagrams
