rationale: The Standard explicitly states an artifact may or may not be considered a deliverable based on the contractual specification — this determination isn't automatic in either direction.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the precise qualifier the Standard uses — contractual specification determines deliverable status, not the artifact type itself.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly claims universal automatic deliverable status. B wrongly claims artifacts can never be deliverables. D fabricates an exemption specific to matrices that doesn't exist in the Standard.
explanation.examTip: "May or may not be a deliverable, depending on contractual specification" is the exact qualifying language to remember — don't default to an absolute answer either way.

stem: Which best distinguishes an Architecture Pattern from a Solution Building Block?

options.text: A Pattern is a reusable idea about how, when, and why to combine building blocks in proven ways; an SBB is a specific implementation choice realising a capability
Patterns and SBBs are two names for the exact same concept
A Pattern is always a code-level construct, while an SBB is always a business-level construct
SBBs are used only in Phase A, while Patterns are used only in Phase E

rationale: A Pattern documents an idea useful in one context that will probably be useful in others — describing how, when, why, and what trade-offs apply to combining building blocks. An SBB, by contrast, is an actual implementation choice realising a required capability.

explanation.whyCorrect: Patterns are about proven combinations and context; SBBs are concrete implementation decisions — genuinely distinct concepts serving different purposes.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B falsely equates two distinct concepts. C reverses TOGAF's actual usage — TOGAF patterns concern enterprise-level structures (software, hardware, networks, people), not purely code-level constructs. D fabricates phase restrictions that don't exist for either concept.
explanation.examTip: Don't confuse a TOGAF Architecture Pattern (enterprise-level, reusable structure) with a Design Pattern (software-specific) or an SBB (a concrete implementation choice).

stem: Which four components make up the recommended format for defining an Architecture Principle?

options.text: Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications
Title, Description, Owner, Version
Goal, Objective, Measure, Target
Policy, Standard, Guideline, Procedure

rationale: The recommended template for defining principles has four components: Name, Statement, Rationale, and Implications (NSRI).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own recommended format, directly and frequently tested.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B, C, and D are all plausible-sounding but fabricated alternative structures with no basis in the Standard's actual principle template.
explanation.examTip: NSRI — Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications. Implications is the component candidates most often forget.

stem: An architect drafts a principle Name: "Adopt Microsoft Azure for All Cloud Workloads." What issue does this specifically violate?

options.text: Names should not exceed three words
Specific technology platforms should not be mentioned in the Name or Statement of a principle
Names must always start with a verb
Principle Names must be approved by the CFO before the CTO

rationale: The recommended guidance explicitly states specific technology platforms should not be mentioned in the name or statement of a principle — naming "Microsoft Azure" directly violates this.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a directly stated, specific rule in the principle-writing guidance, distinct from generic style advice.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A, C, and D are all fabricated stylistic rules with no basis in the actual guidance.
explanation.examTip: Vendor/technology names in a principle's Name or Statement is a specific, exam-tested violation — not a matter of general style preference.

stem: Which of the five qualities of a good set of principles specifically means "every potentially important principle governing information and technology management is defined"?

options.text: Understandable
Robust
Complete
Stable

rationale: Completeness specifically means every potentially important principle governing information and technology management is defined — the principles cover every situation perceived. This is a property of the whole set, not of any single principle.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the exact stated definition of the Complete quality — set-level coverage, not individual principle quality.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Understandable concerns clarity of individual principles. Robust concerns precision enabling consistent decisions. Stable concerns enduring nature with an amendment process — none of these describe set-level coverage.
explanation.examTip: Don't confuse Completeness (the SET covers every situation) with well-formed individual principles (each has clear NSRI). These are different tests.

stem: A subsidiary IT department proposes a domain principle that would weaken an overarching Enterprise Principle regarding data transparency, citing operational efficiency needs. What does the principle hierarchy require?

options.text: The subsidiary principle should be approved automatically, since operational efficiency always takes priority

Subsidiary principles must exist within the bounds of the overarching Enterprise Principles and cannot overstep their boundaries — this proposal should be rejected or revised to remain within those bounds
Enterprise Principles and subsidiary principles operate entirely independently, with no hierarchy between them
The subsidiary department can adopt the principle unilaterally without any Enterprise Principle review

rationale: The hierarchy of principles starts with Enterprise Principles; subsidiary segment principles must exist within these bounds and cannot overstep them. A principle weakening an Enterprise Principle's commitment oversteps rather than elaborates within bounds.

explanation.whyCorrect: This reflects the explicit hierarchy rule — subsidiary principles elaborate on, but cannot violate, the principles above them.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly assumes operational efficiency automatically overrides governance hierarchy. C denies a hierarchy the Standard explicitly establishes. D wrongly allows unilateral adoption bypassing the hierarchy check entirely.
explanation.examTip: Any scenario describing a subsidiary principle conflicting with an Enterprise Principle should be resolved in favour of the Enterprise Principle's bounds — subsidiary principles elaborate, never override.

stem: Who is responsible for formally approving Architecture Principles, per the Standard?

options.text: The CEO exclusively
The Architecture Board, following development by Enterprise Architects in conjunction with key stakeholders
Each individual business unit approves its own principles independently
External auditors must approve all principles before internal use

rationale: Architecture Principles are typically developed by Enterprise Architects in conjunction with key stakeholders, and are approved by the Architecture Board.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's stated governance process — EAs and stakeholders develop, the Architecture Board approves.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly assigns sole approval to a single executive role not specified in the Standard. C wrongly allows independent business-unit approval, bypassing hierarchy and Board oversight. D fabricates an external audit requirement not present in the Standard.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Board approval is the consistent, correct answer whenever formal principle sign-off is being tested.

stem: Which is the correct order of the Enterprise Continuum's four levels, from most generic to most specific?

options.text: Organisation-Specific → Industry → Common Systems → Foundation
Foundation → Common Systems → Industry → Organisation-Specific
Common Systems → Foundation → Organisation-Specific → Industry
Industry → Organisation-Specific → Foundation → Common Systems

rationale: The Enterprise Continuum progresses from generic to specific: Foundation Architecture → Common Systems Architecture → Industry Architecture → Organisation-Specific Architecture.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the exact stated progression, moving from the most generic building blocks to the most organisation-specific implementations.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A, C, and D all scramble the correct generic-to-specific order.
explanation.examTip: Foundation → Common Systems → Industry → Organisation-Specific. This exact sequence is frequently tested directly.

stem: An Organisation-Specific Solution directly incorporates a Foundation Solution component (a generic operating system) without passing through Common Systems or Industry levels first. Is this a violation of the Enterprise Continuum?

options.text: Yes — the four levels must always be traversed strictly in sequence
No — the Standard explicitly states the Continuum should not be interpreted as strictly chained relationships; Organisation-Specific Solutions could contain Foundation Solutions directly
Yes, but only for Data Architecture, not Technology Architecture
No, but only if written approval is obtained from the Architecture Board first

rationale: The Standard explicitly states the Enterprise Continuum should not be interpreted as representing strictly chained relationships — Organisation-Specific Solutions could contain Foundation Solutions directly, without needing to pass through intermediate levels.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a directly stated, specific clarification meant to prevent exactly this kind of over-strict interpretation of the Continuum.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly imposes a strict sequential requirement the Standard explicitly denies. C fabricates a domain-specific exception. D fabricates an approval requirement not part of the Continuum's actual flexibility.
explanation.examTip: This 'no strict chaining' clarification is a specific, named exam trap — don't assume the four levels must be traversed in sequence.

stem: Which Architecture Repository component provides a record of all governance activity across the enterprise?

options.text: Standards Library
Reference Library
Governance Repository
Architecture Landscape

rationale: The Governance Repository specifically provides a record of governance activity across the enterprise — distinct from the Standards Library (compliance standards) and Reference Library (reusable templates/patterns).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specifically stated purpose of the Governance Repository component, one of the eight Architecture Repository components.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Standards Library holds compliance standards. Reference Library holds reusable guidance material. Architecture Landscape represents deployed assets at a point in time — none of these are the governance activity record.
explanation.examTip: Governance Repository = governance decisions record. Don't confuse with Standards Library (compliance rules) or Architecture Landscape (deployed assets).

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Architecture Landscape from the Solutions Landscape?

options.text: They are two names for the identical concept
Architecture Landscape represents deployed architectural assets at a point in time; Solutions Landscape represents SBBs planned or deployed to support the Architecture Landscape
Architecture Landscape only applies to Business Architecture; Solutions Landscape only applies to Technology Architecture
Solutions Landscape is a subset of the Standards Library

rationale: The Architecture Landscape is the architectural representation of assets deployed within the operating enterprise at a particular point in time. The Solutions Landscape presents an architectural representation of the SBBs supporting the Architecture Landscape which have been planned or deployed.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the precise, stated distinction — design-level view (Architecture Landscape) vs. implementation-level view (Solutions Landscape) of the same underlying enterprise state.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly denies a genuine, exam-tested distinction. C fabricates a domain restriction that doesn't exist for either component. D incorrectly nests Solutions Landscape under an unrelated component.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Landscape = the design view. Solutions Landscape = the implementation view (SBBs). Both describe the same enterprise, from different angles.

stem: The TOGAF Technical Reference Model (TRM) is best described as an example of which Enterprise Continuum classification?

options.text: An Organisation-Specific Architecture
A Foundation Architecture
An Industry Architecture
A Solutions Continuum component only, with no Architecture Continuum equivalent

rationale: The TOGAF TRM is explicitly described as an example of a Foundation Architecture — a fundamental, generic architecture upon which other, more specific architectures can be based.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own explicit classification of the TRM, directly stated.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly places it at the most specific end of the Continuum, the opposite of its actual generic classification. C wrongly places it at the industry-specific level. D wrongly denies it has an Architecture Continuum classification at all — the TRM is specifically an Architecture Continuum concept.
explanation.examTip: TRM = Foundation Architecture (most generic). III-RM = Common Systems Architecture (Application Domain, one step more specific than Foundation). Know both classifications precisely.

stem: Which element sits at the centre of the ADM cycle, continuously feeding into every phase?

options.text: Phase A — Architecture Vision
Requirements Management
The Preliminary Phase
Phase H — Architecture Change Management

rationale: Requirements Management sits at the centre of the ADM cycle diagram, continuously operating across all phases — it is not itself a lettered phase.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the defining structural feature of the ADM's clock-face diagram — Requirements Management is central and continuous, not sequential.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Phase A is the starting phase, not the centre. The Preliminary Phase sits outside the cycle entirely. Phase H is the last lettered phase in the cycle, not the centre.
explanation.examTip: Requirements Management is explicitly NOT Phase I or a ninth phase — it's the continuous central hub feeding all phases.

stem: Does the ADM mandate that its phases be performed in a specific, fixed sequence?

options.text: Yes, always Preliminary through H in strict linear order with no exceptions
No — the ADM explicitly does not mandate that phases be performed in any specific sequence, nor does it mandate a waterfall method
Yes, but only for Phases B through D; the rest are flexible
The Standard does not address this question

rationale: The Standard explicitly states the ADM does not mandate that phases must be performed in any specific sequence, and does not mandate a "waterfall" method — flexibility and iteration are core design features.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is directly and explicitly stated — a foundational nuance frequently tested to catch candidates who assume rigid sequencing.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly imposes strict sequencing the Standard explicitly denies. C fabricates a partial-flexibility rule not present in the Standard. D is false — the Standard directly and explicitly addresses this.
explanation.examTip: The phrase 'does not mandate a specific sequence' and 'does not mandate a waterfall method' should immediately register as this exact fact when seen in an exam question.

stem: Which phase is primarily responsible for ensuring conformance with the Target Architecture by implementation projects?

options.text: Phase E — Opportunities & Solutions
Phase F — Migration Planning
Phase G — Implementation Governance
Phase H — Architecture Change Management

rationale: Phase G, Implementation Governance, has the specific objective of ensuring conformance with the Target Architecture by implementation projects — distinct from Phase H, which manages ongoing change after implementation.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is Phase G's specifically stated objective, and a frequently tested distinction from adjacent phases.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Phase E identifies delivery vehicles. Phase F finalises the migration plan. Phase H manages architecture change after implementation — none of these are specifically about conformance during implementation.
explanation.examTip: Phase G = conformance during implementation. Phase H = change management after implementation. Don't conflate the two.

stem: A programme sponsor claims: "Since the ADM diagram shows Phase A leading directly to Phase B, we cannot begin any Phase B activity until Phase A is 100% formally closed." Which best characterises this claim?

options.text: Correct — this is precisely how the ADM must be applied in every case

Incorrect — the sequential, discrete presentation of phases can be misread as implying a deterministic waterfall methodology, which the ADM explicitly does not mandate; phases may run concurrently or iteratively
Correct, but only for Foundational change initiatives, not Bounded ones
Incorrect, because Phase A does not actually precede Phase B in the ADM cycle

rationale: The Standard explicitly warns that its own sequential, discrete phase-by-phase presentation can be misread as implying a deterministic waterfall methodology — in practice, phases may run concurrently, cycle iteratively, or overlap.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly addresses the specific misconception the Standard itself anticipates and warns against.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly validates a rigid waterfall interpretation the Standard explicitly disclaims. C fabricates an engagement-type-specific exception not stated in the Standard. D is factually wrong — Phase A does precede Phase B in the ADM's standard presentation; the actual issue is about strict sequencing, not the phases' relative order.
explanation.examTip: The Standard itself flags that its sequential diagram 'can be read to imply' waterfall — recognising and correcting this misreading is directly exam-tested.

stem: Which three phases are commonly described as the ADM's "bookend" phases, marking the setup, start, and sustaining points of the architecture lifecycle?

options.text: Phase A, Phase E, Phase H
Preliminary, Phase A, Phase H
Phase B, Phase C, Phase D
Phase F, Phase G, Phase H

rationale: Preliminary sets up the Architecture Capability before any cycle begins; Phase A starts every ADM cycle; Phase H sustains the architecture by monitoring for change and triggering new cycles — together these form the recognised "bookend" structure of the ADM lifecycle.

explanation.whyCorrect: These three phases uniquely serve the setup/start/sustain roles across the entire architecture lifecycle, distinct from the core domain-development phases in between.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A omits the Preliminary Phase's setup role. C lists only the domain-development phases (Business/Data-Application/Technology), not the lifecycle bookends. D omits both the setup phase and the cycle-starting phase.
explanation.examTip: Preliminary = setup. Phase A = start of every cycle. Phase H = sustain/trigger new cycles. This three-part memory anchor is a reliable way to keep the ADM's lifecycle structure straight.

stem: Which abstraction level answers the question "why is the architecture needed?"

options.text: Contextual
Conceptual
Logical
Physical

rationale: The Contextual abstraction level answers why the architecture is needed, focusing on the environment, goals, drivers, and objectives motivating the work.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, stated question the Contextual level answers, distinct from the other three levels.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Conceptual answers 'what' (functionality/requirements). Logical answers 'how' (structure). Physical answers 'with what' (implementation assets) — none of these answer 'why.'
explanation.examTip: Why=Contextual, What=Conceptual, How=Logical, With What=Physical. Memorise this exact question-to-level mapping.

stem: The Standard explicitly warns that its use of "why, what, how" in Architecture Abstraction has no connection to a similarly named usage in which other framework?

options.text: The Zachman Framework
ITIL
COBIT
PRINCE2

rationale: The Standard explicitly notes that its why/what/how/with-what abstraction levels have no connection to their use in the Zachman Enterprise Architecture Framework, despite superficially similar terminology.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a direct, explicit disclaimer in the Standard — a deliberate warning against a specific, plausible confusion.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: ITIL, COBIT, and PRINCE2 are all real frameworks TOGAF integrates with, but none of them use a comparable why/what/how terminology the Standard specifically disclaims connection to.
explanation.examTip: This is a named, deliberate disclaimer — candidates with prior Zachman exposure are specifically warned not to assume the terminology transfers.

stem: The Conceptual Abstraction Level can also be referred to by which alternate name(s)?

options.text: Structural abstraction or Framework abstraction
Service abstraction or Behaviour abstraction
Physical abstraction or Implementation abstraction
Governance abstraction or Compliance abstraction

rationale: The Standard explicitly notes the Conceptual Abstraction Level can also be referred to as either service abstraction or behaviour abstraction, since it is modelled using service models representing desired behaviour.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a directly stated alternate-naming fact, useful for recognising Conceptual-level content described using different but equivalent terminology.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A, C, and D are all fabricated alternate names not present in the Standard's actual terminology for the Conceptual level.
explanation.examTip: If you see 'service abstraction' or 'behaviour abstraction' in a question, recognise this as referring to the Conceptual level.

stem: An architect documents a component as "Notification Service: must support multi-channel delivery (email, SMS) with under 500ms latency," without naming any specific vendor or product. Which abstraction level does this represent, and why?

options.text: Physical — because it specifies a measurable requirement
Logical — because it describes implementation-independent structure
Conceptual — because it describes required service behaviour without committing to how it will be structured or implemented
Contextual — because it relates to business goals

rationale: This describes required behaviour (multi-channel delivery, latency) using a service model without addressing structural components (Logical) or implementation choices (Physical) — the defining characteristic of the Conceptual level.

explanation.whyCorrect: The description focuses purely on required behaviour and performance, not on how components are structured (Logical) or which specific technology realises them (Physical) — squarely Conceptual.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly assumes any measurable requirement is automatically Physical — measurability doesn't determine abstraction level. B wrongly assigns it to Logical, which would require describing structural components, not just behaviour. D wrongly assigns it to Contextual, which concerns environment and motivation, not service behaviour specifics.
explanation.examTip: A requirement stated purely in terms of behaviour and performance, without naming components or vendors, is Conceptual — not automatically Physical just because it has numbers attached.

stem: How do the Logical and Physical abstraction levels map to Building Blocks?

options.text: Logical = SBB; Physical = ABB
Logical = ABB; Physical = SBB
Both Logical and Physical map exclusively to ABBs
Neither Logical nor Physical relates to Building Blocks at all

rationale: The Logical level identifies implementation-independent components (ABBs); the Physical level allocates actual implementation choices to realise them (SBBs) — directly mirroring the ABB/SBB distinction.

explanation.whyCorrect: This mapping directly connects the abstraction levels to the Building Block concepts from Lesson 4 — Logical/ABB (what capability) and Physical/SBB (which product).
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A reverses the correct mapping. C wrongly claims both map to ABBs, ignoring the implementation-specific nature of the Physical level. D denies a direct, well-established relationship between abstraction levels and building blocks.
explanation.examTip: Logical=ABB, Physical=SBB is a frequently tested cross-reference between two related but distinct lesson topics — expect questions combining both concepts.

stem: Which best describes the relationship between an Architecture View and an Architecture Viewpoint?

options.text: A View is a high-level summary; a Viewpoint is a detailed technical specification
A Viewpoint specifies the conventions for constructing and using a View; a View is the specific representation produced using that Viewpoint
Views and Viewpoints are interchangeable terms for the same artifact
A Viewpoint is produced by stakeholders; a View is produced by architects

rationale: An Architecture Viewpoint is a specification of the conventions for a particular kind of Architecture View — the template. An Architecture View is a representation of a system from the perspective of a related set of concerns — the specific output produced using that Viewpoint.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the precise, glossary-level definition distinguishing the two — template (Viewpoint) vs. specific output (View).
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A mischaracterises the distinction as being about level of detail rather than template vs. instance. C wrongly denies a genuine, frequently tested distinction. D fabricates a production-role split not present in the Standard.
explanation.examTip: View = what you see. Viewpoint = where you're looking from (the lens/template). This memory anchor consistently resolves confusion.

stem: Using the Standard's own pilot/air-traffic-controller example, which best explains why two stakeholders looking at the same airport system need different Views?

options.text: Because the pilot and controller are looking at two entirely different, unrelated systems
Because each stakeholder's Viewpoint constrains and reduces how they see the overall system, based on their own specific concerns
Because only one of them is authorised to see the full system architecture
Because Views are always identical regardless of stakeholder, so this scenario doesn't actually require two Views

rationale: The Standard's own example shows the pilot's viewpoint includes concerns like passengers and fuel, irrelevant to the controller; the controller's viewpoint includes concerns like other planes, irrelevant to the pilot. Each Viewpoint constrains what's shown, even though both describe the same underlying system.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly reflects the Standard's own illustrative example and its stated point about Viewpoints constraining and reducing what each stakeholder sees.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly claims they're looking at different systems — they're examining the same airport system from different concerns. C fabricates an authorisation-based restriction not part of the example. D denies the entire premise of the example, which specifically demonstrates why different Views are needed.
explanation.examTip: The pilot/controller example is the Standard's own worked illustration — expect it or a close paraphrase directly on the exam.

stem: What is an Architecture Description, as defined by the Standard?

options.text: A single comprehensive diagram covering the entire architecture
The complete set of Views that describes an architecture from all relevant stakeholder perspectives
A synonym for the Architecture Definition Document
A legally binding contract between architects and vendors

rationale: An Architecture Description is the complete set of Views that together describe an architecture from all relevant stakeholder perspectives — not a single document, but a collection of Views.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the precise definition, emphasising that it's a collection (of Views), not one document.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly reduces it to a single diagram, contradicting the multi-View nature. C conflates two distinct concepts. D fabricates a legal-contract characterisation not part of the definition.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Description is a collection of Views — remember it's plural in nature, not a single artifact.

stem: An architect has produced eleven detailed Views for a mid-sized system upgrade, addressing every identified stakeholder concern. A colleague insists more Views should be produced "to be thorough." What principle should guide the response?

options.text: Architecture work should be developed only to the point of being fit-for-purpose — adequately addressing all pertinent stakeholder concerns — and not reiterated indefinitely as an academic exercise
More Views are always better regardless of whether additional stakeholder concerns remain unaddressed
Exactly twelve Views is the minimum required for any TOGAF-compliant architecture
Views should only ever be produced in even numbers for balance

rationale: The Standard explicitly states architecture should be developed only to the point at which it is fit-for-purpose, and not reiterated ad infinitum as an academic exercise — the correct test is whether all pertinent stakeholder concerns are addressed, not an arbitrary volume of Views.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own explicit fitness-for-purpose principle, directly countering the 'more is always better' instinct.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B wrongly validates unlimited View production regardless of actual need. C and D both fabricate arbitrary numeric rules with no basis in the Standard.
explanation.examTip: The correct test for 'enough Views' is stakeholder concern coverage, not volume — recognise and reject the 'more is always better' trap.

stem: Which statement about the reusability of Architecture Viewpoints versus Architecture Views is correct?

options.text: Viewpoints are generic and can be stored in libraries for re-use; a View is always specific to the architecture for which it is created
Views are generic and reusable; Viewpoints are always specific to one architecture
Both Views and Viewpoints are equally reusable across different architectures
Neither Views nor Viewpoints can ever be stored for future re-use

rationale: Architecture Viewpoints are generic and can be stored in libraries (specifically the Reference Library) for re-use across different architectures; an Architecture View is always specific to the particular architecture for which it was created.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the exact stated reusability distinction — Viewpoints are the reusable templates; Views are the one-off specific outputs.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B reverses the correct reusability relationship. C wrongly treats both as equally reusable, denying the genuine distinction. D wrongly denies that Viewpoints specifically can be stored for reuse.
explanation.examTip: Viewpoint = reusable template (can live in a viewpoint library). View = specific, one-time output for this architecture.

stem: What are the two objectives of the Preliminary Phase?

options.text: Develop the Architecture Vision; obtain Statement of Architecture Work approval
Determine the Architecture Capability desired by the organisation; establish the Architecture Capability
Develop Baseline and Target Business Architecture; identify gaps
Finalise the Architecture Roadmap; produce the Implementation and Migration Plan

rationale: The Preliminary Phase's two objectives are: (1) determine the Architecture Capability desired by the organisation, and (2) establish that Architecture Capability.

explanation.whyCorrect: These are the Preliminary Phase's specific, stated objectives — distinct from any lettered ADM phase's objectives.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A describes Phase A's objectives. C describes Phase B's objectives. D describes Phase F's objectives.
explanation.examTip: Determine, then Establish — the two Preliminary Phase objectives, easily confused with Phase A's objectives if not memorised precisely.

stem: In which phase are Architecture Principles first established?

options.text: Phase A — Architecture Vision
The Preliminary Phase
Phase B — Business Architecture
Phase H — Architecture Change Management

rationale: Architecture Principles are established in the Preliminary Phase. Phase A confirms and elaborates them — it does not create them from scratch (unless the Preliminary Phase was skipped).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a frequently tested distinction — candidates often mistakenly believe Phase A creates principles rather than confirming ones already established earlier.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Phase A confirms/elaborates existing principles, it doesn't originate them. Phase B and Phase H are unrelated to initial principle establishment.
explanation.examTip: Principles are established in Preliminary, confirmed/elaborated in Phase A. This ordering is one of the most commonly tested Preliminary Phase facts.

stem: Which three types of tailoring are addressed during the Preliminary Phase?

options.text: Terminology, Process, Content
Budget, Schedule, Scope
Business, Data, Technology
Strategic, Segment, Capability

rationale: The Preliminary Phase addresses three types of tailoring: Terminology tailoring (language/glossary), Process tailoring (adapting steps and checkpoints), and Content tailoring (adapting the Architecture Content Framework).

explanation.whyCorrect: TPC (Terminology, Process, Content) is the specific, named tailoring taxonomy applied during the Preliminary Phase.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B lists unrelated project management concerns. C lists architecture domains, not tailoring types. D lists Architecture Landscape levels, an unrelated concept.
explanation.examTip: TPC — Terminology, Process, Content. This exact three-part tailoring taxonomy is directly and frequently tested.

stem: During Phase A, the team discovers the Architecture Capability established in the Preliminary Phase lacks any process for governing cloud security architecture, now central to the current engagement's scope. What is the correct response?

options.text: Continue Phase A and work around the gap informally, since the Preliminary Phase is already finished
The Preliminary Phase may be formally revisited from the Architecture Vision phase specifically to ensure the Architecture Capability is suitable to address this specific architecture problem
Abandon the current ADM cycle entirely and restart from Phase A with a different team
Escalate directly to the CEO without involving the Architecture Board

rationale: The Standard explicitly states the Preliminary Phase may be revisited from the Architecture Vision phase to ensure the organisation's Architecture Capability is suitable to address a specific architecture problem — exactly the situation described.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own explicit, named provision for this exact situation — a capability gap discovered during Phase A.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly assumes Preliminary Phase work can never be revisited once Phase A begins. C is disproportionate — the whole cycle needn't restart for a targeted capability extension. D fabricates an unsupported executive escalation path bypassing normal governance.
explanation.examTip: Preliminary Phase capability gaps discovered in Phase A trigger a formal, named return to Preliminary — not an informal workaround, and not a full cycle restart.

stem: Which document is a key output of the Preliminary Phase, encompassing the tailored architecture method, tailored content, and Architecture Principles?

options.text: Statement of Architecture Work
Tailored Architecture Framework
Architecture Definition Document
Architecture Roadmap

rationale: The Tailored Architecture Framework is a Preliminary Phase output, including the tailored architecture method, tailored architecture content (deliverables and artifacts), Architecture Principles, and configured/deployed tools.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is one of the Preliminary Phase's specifically named key outputs, distinct from Phase A's Statement of Architecture Work.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Statement of Architecture Work is a Phase A output. Architecture Definition Document is developed and refined across Phases A through F. Architecture Roadmap is first produced in Phase E.
explanation.examTip: Tailored Architecture Framework (Preliminary) vs. Statement of Architecture Work (Phase A) — a commonly confused pair of similarly-named outputs from adjacent phases.

stem: What formally triggers the beginning of Phase A?

options.text: Completion of all Preliminary Phase outputs
A Request for Architecture Work from the sponsoring organisation
An Architecture Board vote
Publication of the Architecture Roadmap

rationale: Phase A starts with receipt of a Request for Architecture Work from the sponsoring organisation to the architecture organisation — this is the explicit trigger.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own stated trigger for Phase A's beginning.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly requires full Preliminary Phase completion, which isn't strictly required before Phase A can begin. C fabricates a formal vote requirement not described as the trigger. D describes a much later Phase E output, unrelated to Phase A's start.
explanation.examTip: Request for Architecture Work = the trigger for Phase A. This is a directly and frequently tested fact.

stem: Which document represents the critical gate output of Phase A, without which the team cannot formally proceed to Phase B?

options.text: The Architecture Vision document
The Capability Assessment
The Approved Statement of Architecture Work
The Communications Plan

rationale: The Statement of Architecture Work, once approved, is the critical gate output authorising the team to proceed to Phase B — distinct from the Architecture Vision, which describes the WHAT and WHY but isn't itself the formal approval document.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the formal approval mechanism specifically identified as the Phase A gate output.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: The Architecture Vision is the WHAT/WHY document but not the formal gate. The Capability Assessment and Communications Plan are both Phase A outputs but neither functions as the formal authorisation to proceed.
explanation.examTip: Statement of Architecture Work = the gate (HOW and WHEN, formal approval). Architecture Vision = the picture (WHAT and WHY). Don't confuse the two.

stem: Which Phase A output is most frequently forgotten by candidates, despite being explicitly listed among Phase A's outputs?

options.text: Architecture Vision
Communications Plan
Statement of Architecture Work
Capability Assessment

rationale: The Communications Plan — specifying when, how, and to whom the EA team communicates throughout the ADM cycle — is a genuine Phase A output frequently overlooked by candidates who focus on the more prominent Architecture Vision and Statement of Architecture Work.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is specifically flagged as a commonly forgotten output in exam preparation, despite being an explicitly listed Phase A deliverable.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Architecture Vision, Statement of Architecture Work, and Capability Assessment are all more prominent and less commonly forgotten Phase A outputs.
explanation.examTip: Make a deliberate point of remembering the Communications Plan as a Phase A output — it's specifically the kind of detail exam distractors exploit.

stem: Business Scenarios are recommended as a technique for which specific purpose in Phase A?

options.text: Finalising the Architecture Roadmap timeline
Discovering and documenting business requirements, and articulating an Architecture Vision that responds to those requirements
Selecting specific technology vendors for Phase D
Auditing compliance during Phase G

rationale: Business Scenarios are the recommended technique for discovering and documenting business requirements in Phase A, and for articulating an Architecture Vision that genuinely responds to those requirements. Multiple Business Scenarios may be used to generate a single Architecture Vision.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the technique's specifically stated purpose — anchored to Phase A requirements discovery and vision articulation.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A describes a Phase E/F activity, unrelated to Business Scenarios' purpose. C describes Phase D technology selection, a different technique entirely. D describes Phase G compliance activity, unrelated to this Phase A technique.
explanation.examTip: Business Scenarios = Phase A (and optionally Phase B) requirements discovery technique — not a Phase C, D, or G tool.

stem: During Phase A, the team discovers the organisation lacks cloud architecture skills needed for the engagement. What is the most appropriate TOGAF response?

options.text: Proceed to Phase B and address the skills gap once Phase D begins
Document the gap in the Capability Assessment and, if necessary, iterate back to the Preliminary Phase to address the shortfall
Descope the entire Technology Architecture domain from the engagement permanently
Immediately terminate the ADM cycle and restart from scratch with new stakeholders

rationale: Phase A capability gaps — identified via the Capability Assessment — may require iterating back to the Preliminary Phase to address the shortfall in Architecture Capability, rather than proceeding regardless or descoping permanently.

explanation.whyCorrect: This reflects the correct mechanism (Capability Assessment documentation, potential Preliminary Phase iteration) for addressing capability gaps found during Phase A.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly defers addressing a foundational skills gap until much later. C is a disproportionate, permanent response to what may be a temporary or addressable gap. D is an extreme overreaction not warranted by a capability gap alone.
explanation.examTip: Capability gaps discovered in Phase A are documented in the Capability Assessment and may trigger a Preliminary Phase iteration — not phase-skipping, permanent descoping, or full cycle termination.

stem: What are the two objectives of Phase B?

options.text: Develop the Baseline Business Architecture; obtain approval to proceed
Develop the Target Business Architecture; identify candidate Architecture Roadmap components based upon gaps between Baseline and Target
Define the business case; identify transformation risks
Develop Business Architecture models; conduct stakeholder sign-off review

rationale: Phase B's two objectives are precisely: develop the Target Business Architecture describing how the enterprise needs to operate, and identify candidate Architecture Roadmap components based on gaps between Baseline and Target.

explanation.whyCorrect: The second objective — identifying candidate roadmap components — is frequently forgotten by candidates who only remember the Target Architecture development objective.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A misdescribes the objectives around Baseline development and approval, not the actual stated pair. C and D both list plausible-sounding but fabricated objective pairs.
explanation.examTip: Both Phase B objectives matter: Target Architecture development AND candidate roadmap component identification via gap analysis — don't stop at just the first half.

stem: Which of the four gap analysis classifications describes something present in the Baseline but no longer needed in the Target?

options.text: Retained
Eliminated
Added
Intentionally Omitted

rationale: "Eliminated" describes something that exists in the Baseline but is not needed in the Target — distinct from Retained (needed in both), Added (new in Target only), and Intentionally Omitted (a known, deliberately deferred gap).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the precise, stated definition of the Eliminated classification within the four-part gap analysis taxonomy.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Retained describes something needed in both states. Added describes something new to the Target only. Intentionally Omitted describes a consciously deferred gap, not simply something no longer needed.
explanation.examTip: Four gap classifications: Retained (both), Eliminated (Baseline only, not needed), Added (Target only, new), Intentionally Omitted (known, deferred gap). Know all four precisely.

stem: At the end of Phase B, gap analysis has produced a list of capability changes needed to reach the Target. What happens to these findings?

options.text: They are formally approved by the Architecture Board as the final Architecture Roadmap
They are documented as candidate Architecture Roadmap components, to be consolidated with Phase C and D findings in Phase E
They are handed directly to the project delivery team to begin implementation planning immediately
They are submitted to the Requirements Repository and considered fully closed at that point

rationale: Phase B's gap analysis findings become candidate Architecture Roadmap components — not the final Roadmap itself. The Architecture Roadmap is fully consolidated in Phase E, combining candidates from Phases B, C, and D.

explanation.whyCorrect: This correctly identifies Phase B's findings as candidates only, feeding into Phase E's later consolidation — not a finalised, standalone Roadmap.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly treats Phase B's output as the final Architecture Board-approved Roadmap, skipping the necessary Phase C/D consolidation. C wrongly hands unconsolidated findings directly to delivery, bypassing Phases C, D, and E entirely. D wrongly treats the findings as fully closed rather than actively feeding forward.
explanation.examTip: Phase B, C, and D all produce candidate roadmap components — only Phase E consolidates them into the actual Architecture Roadmap. Don't confuse 'candidate' with 'final.'

stem: Which modelling technique is best suited to showing how an organisation creates and delivers value end to end for a specific stakeholder?

options.text: Organisation Mapping
Business Capability Mapping
Value Stream Mapping
Use-Case Analysis

rationale: Value Stream Mapping specifically shows how the business creates and delivers value end to end for a customer, stakeholder, or end user — distinct from Business Capability Mapping (what the business CAN do) or Organisation Mapping (who does what).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the technique specifically suited to end-to-end value delivery visualisation, as distinct from capability inventories or organisational structure mapping.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Business Capability Mapping shows abilities, not end-to-end flow. Organisation Mapping shows who performs what role, not value delivery flow. Use-Case Analysis focuses on user-system interaction, not organisation-wide value delivery.
explanation.examTip: If a question asks about visualising end-to-end value delivery for a specific stakeholder, the answer is Value Stream Mapping — a frequently tested technique selection question.

stem: At the end of Phase B, is the Architecture Definition Document considered formally complete and baselined?

options.text: Yes, it is fully finalised at the end of Phase B
No — it remains a draft until all BDAT domains (Phases B, C, D) have contributed to it
Yes, but only the Business Architecture sections are finalised, while other domain sections are permanently excluded
The Architecture Definition Document does not exist until Phase E

rationale: The Architecture Definition Document remains a draft at the end of Phase B — it is not formally baselined until all BDAT domains (developed across Phases B, C, and D) have contributed to it.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly counters the misconception that Phase B alone finalises the Architecture Definition Document.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly claims premature finalisation. C wrongly implies permanent exclusion of other domain content, rather than pending contribution from Phases C and D. D is false — the document exists in draft form from Phase A onward, not only from Phase E.
explanation.examTip: The Architecture Definition Document is a cumulative, multi-phase document — it isn't complete or baselined until Phases B, C, and D have all contributed, a frequently tested nuance.

stem: Why is Phase C titled "Information Systems Architectures" (plural) rather than a single architecture?

options.text: Because it covers both Data Architecture and Application Architecture as its two constituent parts
Because it must be repeated three times for large enterprises
Because it includes Business Architecture and Technology Architecture combined
It's simply a naming convention with no substantive meaning

rationale: The plural naming reflects that Phase C explicitly covers two distinct architecture domains — Data Architecture and Application Architecture — combined into one phase.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the direct, stated reason for the plural naming — two domains within one phase.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B fabricates a repetition requirement unrelated to the naming. C wrongly substitutes different domains (Business/Technology) for the actual pairing (Data/Application). D dismisses meaningful naming that directly signals the phase's scope.
explanation.examTip: The plural 'Architectures' in Phase C's name is a direct clue and frequently tested fact — it signals Data + Application, not a naming coincidence.

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four types of data a Data Architecture should address?

options.text: Data at rest
Data in motion
Data in transit through Phase G
Open data

rationale: The four recognised types of data are: data at rest, data in motion, data in use (at the application border, e.g., GUI), and open data (public disclosures). "Data in transit through Phase G" is a fabricated category.

explanation.whyCorrect: This distractor mimics real terminology ("in motion"/"in transit") but attaches an invalid phase reference not part of the actual four-type taxonomy.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Data at rest, data in motion, and open data are all genuine, named types from the Standard's four-part taxonomy.
explanation.examTip: The four data types are: at rest, in motion, in use, open. Watch for plausible-sounding but fabricated fifth categories combining real terms with invented phase references.

stem: Which conceptual-level term represents a business concept like "Customer" or "Invoice," before any implementation decisions are made?

options.text: Physical Data Component
Logical Data Component
Data Entity
Data Building Block

rationale: A Data Entity is the conceptual-level representation of a business concept (e.g., "Customer," "Invoice") — the first of the ELP progression (Entity → Logical Component → Physical Component).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, stated conceptual-level term in the three-level data hierarchy.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Physical Data Component is the implementation-level term (e.g., database schema). Logical Data Component is the implementation-independent structural level, one step past conceptual. "Data Building Block" is not part of this specific three-level terminology.
explanation.examTip: ELP progression: Data Entity (conceptual) → Logical Data Component (logical) → Physical Data Component (physical).

stem: While mapping applications during Application Architecture work, a team discovers significant undocumented data quality issues affecting several core applications. A team member says these are "out of scope until the formally scheduled Data Architecture sub-phase." Is this correct?

options.text: Yes — rigid phase boundaries mean data issues must wait for a formally scheduled Data Architecture activity
No — the Standard explicitly notes it may be appropriate to drop into a short iteration of Data Architecture if deemed valuable to the scope of the engagement
Yes, but only if the issues were anticipated in the original Statement of Architecture Work
No — Data Architecture issues can only ever be addressed in Phase B, never during Phase C Application work

rationale: The Standard explicitly supports dropping into a short iteration of Data Architecture during Application Architecture work when valuable to the engagement — exactly the situation described, rather than rigidly deferring to a separately scheduled sub-phase.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own explicit allowance for exactly this kind of mid-stream discovery and short-iteration response.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly imposes rigid phase boundaries the Standard explicitly relaxes. C fabricates an anticipation requirement not part of the actual guidance. D wrongly restricts Data Architecture activity to Phase B only, when Phase C explicitly includes Data Architecture as well.
explanation.examTip: Discovering significant data issues during Application work is exactly the situation where a short, valuable Data Architecture iteration is explicitly supported — not something to defer rigidly.

stem: Which artifact is typically the starting point of the Application Architecture phase, providing the foundation for subsequent matrices and diagrams?

options.text: Application Communication Diagram
Application Portfolio Catalog
Application Migration Diagram
Software Distribution Diagram

rationale: The Application Portfolio Catalog is typically the starting point of the Application Architecture phase, providing the foundational inventory of applications on which subsequent matrices and diagrams are built.

explanation.whyCorrect: This reflects the correct construction order — the catalog (inventory) precedes diagrams built from it.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Application Communication Diagram, Application Migration Diagram, and Software Distribution Diagram are all downstream artifacts that depend on an established application inventory, not the starting point itself.
explanation.examTip: Application Portfolio Catalog first, then diagrams and matrices built from it — reversing this order (diagrams before catalog) is a common exam trap.

stem: A planning team wants to sequence the single most technically difficult Technology Architecture work package first, citing team motivation as the only reason. What does the Standard's sequencing guidance suggest?

options.text: This is correct — difficult activities should always be tackled first regardless of reason

Difficult activities should generally be implemented after other activities that most easily deliver missing capability, unless there are compelling reasons otherwise — team motivation alone doesn't meet this bar
Difficulty level has no bearing on sequencing decisions at all
Only the CTO can decide sequencing order for difficult activities

rationale: The Standard specifically states difficult activities should generally be implemented after other activities that most easily deliver missing capability, unless compelling reasons justify otherwise — team motivation alone doesn't constitute such a compelling reason.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the exact stated sequencing principle, including its explicit exception clause ("unless there are compelling reasons").
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly states an absolute 'difficult first' rule the Standard doesn't support. C wrongly denies any sequencing guidance exists at all. D fabricates an executive decision-rights rule not present in the Standard.
explanation.examTip: Difficult activities generally go LAST unless a compelling reason exists — not first, and not irrelevant to sequencing.

stem: A Technology Architect completes Phase D gap analysis and declares the resulting Technology Roadmap "the official Architecture Roadmap for the programme." Is this accurate?

options.text: Yes, once Phase E formally adopts it as-is
No — the Technology Roadmap is described as raw material supporting a more detailed, consolidated, cross-discipline roadmap developed within Phase E, not a finished document Phase E simply adopts
Yes, because Technology Architecture is always the final domain phase
No — Technology Roadmaps have no relationship to Phase E whatsoever

rationale: The Standard describes the initial Technology Architecture roadmap as raw material to support the more detailed, consolidated, cross-discipline roadmap developed in Phase E — Phase E must integrate it with Business, Data, and Application Architecture gap analysis results, not simply adopt it.

explanation.whyCorrect: This precisely characterises the Technology Roadmap's actual status — valuable input, not a finished, ready-to-adopt Architecture Roadmap.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly implies Phase E simply rubber-stamps the Technology Roadmap unchanged. C is true about phase sequencing but doesn't address the Roadmap consolidation question being asked. D wrongly denies any relationship, when the Technology Roadmap specifically feeds into Phase E's work.
explanation.examTip: Technology Roadmap (Phase D) = raw material. Architecture Roadmap (Phase E) = the consolidated, final product integrating all domains' candidates.

stem: Before considering Phase D complete, what must a team specifically check regarding "resolving impacts across the Architecture Landscape"?

options.text: Only whether the budget for Phase D was fully spent
Whether this Technology Architecture impacts, or will be impacted by, other projects (planned or in progress) elsewhere in the organisation
Only whether the Architecture Board has been personally briefed
Nothing — this check is unique to Phase G, not Phase D

rationale: Resolving impacts across the Architecture Landscape specifically requires checking whether this Technology Architecture creates impacts on pre-existing architectures, and whether it impacts or will be impacted by other projects — whether planned or in progress — elsewhere in the organisation.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specifically defined Phase D step, extending beyond the immediate engagement's own scope to check broader organisational impacts.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly narrows the check to budget only. C wrongly narrows it to a single briefing requirement. D wrongly claims this check is exclusive to Phase G, when it's specifically a defined Phase D activity.
explanation.examTip: Resolving Architecture Landscape impacts is a defined Phase D step — checking for effects on OTHER projects, not just this engagement's own scope.

stem: When finalising the Technology Architecture, what does the Standard recommend regarding building block selection?

options.text: Always build every Technology Building Block completely from scratch, regardless of timeline
Select standards for each building block while re-using as much as possible from reference models already available in the Architecture Repository
Only use building blocks recommended directly by the primary technology vendor
Building block selection should be entirely deferred to Phase G

rationale: Finalising the Technology Architecture specifically involves selecting standards for each building block while re-using as much as possible from reference models already available in the Architecture Repository, rather than building everything fresh.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, stated finalisation guidance — re-use is emphasised, not building from scratch or vendor-dependent selection.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly recommends building everything fresh, working against re-use principles the Standard specifically promotes. C wrongly restricts selection to a single vendor's recommendations, contradicting TOGAF's vendor-neutral principle. D wrongly defers a Phase D activity entirely to a much later phase.
explanation.examTip: Re-use from the Architecture Repository is the recommended approach to finalising Technology Architecture building blocks — not building fresh, and not vendor-dictated.

stem: By the end of which phase is the Architecture Definition Document's coverage of all four BDAT domains complete, allowing it to be formally baselined?

options.text: Phase A
Phase B
Phase D
Phase F

rationale: The Architecture Definition Document grows across Phases B (Business), C (Data/Application), and D (Technology) — it is complete across all four BDAT domains and can be formally baselined by the end of Phase D, the last domain-development phase.

explanation.whyCorrect: Phase D is the last of the domain-development phases (B, C, D); once its contributions are added, all BDAT domains are covered.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Phase A only produces a high-level vision, not full domain coverage. Phase B only completes Business Architecture, one of four domains. Phase F occurs after domain development is already complete — it doesn't itself complete BDAT coverage.
explanation.examTip: ADD (Architecture Definition Document) is 'complete' across BDAT domains by the end of Phase D — it grows through B → C → D, then Phase D is where it's ready to baseline.

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of Phase E's three objectives?

options.text: Generate the initial complete Architecture Roadmap
Determine whether an incremental approach is required, and identify Transition Architectures if so
Define the overall Solution Building Blocks (SBBs) to finalise the Target Architecture based on the ABBs
Finalise the detailed Implementation and Migration Plan with costed timelines

rationale: Phase E's three objectives are: generating the Architecture Roadmap, determining need for Transition Architectures, and defining SBBs. Finalising the detailed, costed Implementation and Migration Plan is specifically a Phase F objective.

explanation.whyCorrect: This distractor describes a genuine ADM activity, but attributes it to the wrong phase — it belongs to Phase F, not Phase E.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A, B, and C are all genuine, correctly stated Phase E objectives.
explanation.examTip: Phase E defines SBBs and the initial Roadmap; Phase F finalises the detailed, costed Implementation and Migration Plan. Don't conflate the two adjacent phases' objectives.

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of Phase F's three objectives?

options.text: Finalise the Architecture Roadmap and Implementation and Migration Plan
Ensure the Plan is coordinated with the enterprise's overall change portfolio
Ensure key stakeholders understand the business value and cost of work packages and Transition Architectures
Define the overall Solution Building Blocks needed to finalise the Target Architecture

rationale: Phase F's three objectives are finalising the plan, ensuring portfolio coordination, and ensuring stakeholder understanding of value/cost. Defining SBBs to finalise the Target Architecture is specifically a Phase E objective.

explanation.whyCorrect: This distractor attributes a genuine Phase E objective (SBB definition) incorrectly to Phase F.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A, B, and C are all genuine, correctly stated Phase F objectives.
explanation.examTip: SBB definition belongs to Phase E, not Phase F — a frequently tested distinction between these two adjacent phases' objectives.

stem: Does the time-span between successive Transition Architectures need to be of uniform duration?

options.text: Yes, all Transition Architectures must be spaced at identical intervals for consistency
No — the Standard explicitly states the time-span between successive Transition Architectures does not have to be of uniform duration
Yes, but only if fewer than three Transition Architectures are planned
The Standard does not address Transition Architecture spacing at all

rationale: The Standard explicitly states the time-span between successive Transition Architectures does not have to be of uniform duration — spacing should be driven by what each Transition Architecture delivers and dependencies involved, not forced into equal intervals.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a directly stated, specific clarification against an intuitive but incorrect assumption of uniform spacing.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly imposes a uniformity requirement the Standard explicitly denies. C fabricates an arbitrary numeric exception. D is false — the Standard directly and explicitly addresses this exact question.
explanation.examTip: Transition Architecture spacing is content-driven, not uniform-interval-driven — a frequently tested nuance against an intuitive but wrong assumption.

stem: A Phase F team proposes a "big-bang" simultaneous go-live for all application systems to avoid sequencing complexity. Which architectural risk does this specifically ignore?

options.text: There is no risk — big-bang go-live is always the recommended TOGAF approach

Dependency-driven sequencing (e.g., a data-driven sequence where systems creating data are implemented before systems processing that data) — ignoring this risks systems going live without data or upstream components they depend on
Big-bang implementations are explicitly prohibited by the TOGAF Standard in all circumstances
The only risk is increased project management overhead, with no technical implications

rationale: Migration planning should consider dependency-driven sequencing, such as data-driven sequencing where data-creating systems are implemented before data-processing systems. A big-bang approach risks violating these dependencies, with downstream systems going live before their required upstream components are ready.

explanation.whyCorrect: This reflects the Standard's specific guidance on dependency-aware migration sequencing and the concrete risk of ignoring it.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly validates big-bang as universally recommended, when dependency-driven sequencing is the actual guidance. C wrongly claims an absolute prohibition not stated in the Standard — big-bang isn't banned, but its risks (specifically dependency violations) must be considered. D wrongly minimises this to a project-management-only concern, missing the substantive technical/data risk.
explanation.examTip: Big-bang approaches aren't prohibited outright, but ignoring dependency-driven sequencing (e.g., data-creating before data-processing systems) is the specific risk this creates.

stem: Which best describes what happens to an Architecture Building Block (ABB) as work progresses through Phase E?

options.text: ABBs are discarded entirely once Phase E begins
ABBs are formally realised into Solution Building Blocks (SBBs) as part of Phase E's objective to finalise the Target Architecture
ABBs are converted into Architecture Principles during Phase E
ABBs remain unchanged throughout the entire ADM cycle with no realisation into SBBs ever occurring

rationale: One of Phase E's three objectives is defining the overall Solution Building Blocks (SBBs) needed to finalise the Target Architecture, based on the ABBs already defined in earlier phases — this is where ABBs become concrete SBBs.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly reflects Phase E's specific objective of realising ABBs into SBBs — the concrete implementation choices.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly claims ABBs are discarded, when they specifically inform SBB definition. C fabricates an unrelated conversion into a completely different concept (Principles). D wrongly denies that ABB-to-SBB realisation ever occurs, contradicting Phase E's stated purpose.
explanation.examTip: Phase E is specifically where ABBs (capability, generic) become SBBs (concrete implementation choices) — this ABB→SBB transition is a defining feature of Phase E.

stem: What are Phase G's two objectives?

options.text: Develop the Target Architecture; obtain stakeholder sign-off
Ensure conformance with the Target Architecture by implementation projects; perform appropriate Architecture Governance functions for the solution and implementation-driven Change Requests
Finalise the Architecture Roadmap; coordinate with the enterprise change portfolio
Monitor business growth and decline; trigger new ADM cycles

rationale: Phase G's two objectives are ensuring conformance with the Target Architecture by implementation projects, and performing appropriate Architecture Governance functions for the solution and any implementation-driven Change Requests.

explanation.whyCorrect: These are Phase G's specifically stated objectives, distinct from adjacent phases.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A describes earlier phase activities (Target Architecture development, sign-off). C describes Phase F objectives. D describes Phase H activities, not Phase G's.
explanation.examTip: Phase G = conformance + governance during implementation. Don't confuse with Phase F (finalising plans) or Phase H (post-implementation change management).

stem: A team completes a compliance review of the single project implementing the Target Architecture and declares Phase G's compliance work complete. What is missing?

options.text: Nothing — reviewing the implementing project alone is sufficient

Ensuring compliance is a key aspect of Phase G not only for implementation projects delivering this architecture, but also for other ongoing projects within the enterprise that may be affected by or need to align with it
Only a review by external auditors can complete Phase G compliance work
Compliance review is not actually a Phase G responsibility at all

rationale: The Standard specifically states compliance review in Phase G extends beyond the implementing project to other ongoing projects within the enterprise potentially affected by or needing to align with the architecture.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly identifies the specific scope-expansion the Standard requires — beyond just the primary implementing project.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly declares the narrower review sufficient. C fabricates an external-audit-only requirement. D wrongly denies compliance review is a Phase G responsibility, when it's one of Phase G's two core objectives.
explanation.examTip: Phase G compliance review scope extends to OTHER ongoing projects potentially affected — not just the one project directly delivering this architecture.

stem: Which category of architecture change is driven by a requirement to reduce investment or complexity without affecting architectural intent?

options.text: Re-architecting
Incremental
Simplification
Foundational

rationale: Simplification changes are driven by a requirement to reduce investment or complexity without affecting architectural intent — handled via change management, not requiring a new ADM cycle.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the precise, stated definition of Simplification within the three-category change taxonomy.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Re-architecting is driven by increasing investment for new value, requiring a full new ADM cycle. Incremental derives additional value from existing investment. "Foundational" is an unrelated engagement-classification term, not one of the three change categories.
explanation.examTip: Three change categories: Simplification (reduce investment), Incremental (derive more value from existing investment), Re-architecting (increase investment for new value, full new cycle).

stem: GlobalTech's board announces a major strategic acquisition requiring completely new business capabilities never previously supported. Per the three-category change taxonomy, how should this be classified in Phase H?

options.text: Simplification — handled via routine change management
Incremental — deriving additional value from existing investment
Re-architecting — requiring a new Request for Architecture Work and a full new ADM cycle
This scenario falls outside all three categories and requires no formal classification

rationale: A strategic acquisition requiring entirely new business capabilities is driven by a requirement to increase investment to create new architectural value — the defining characteristic of a Re-architecting change, requiring a full new ADM cycle.

explanation.whyCorrect: New capabilities never previously supported, driven by increased investment for new value, is the textbook Re-architecting scenario.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly minimises a major strategic shift to routine change management. B wrongly treats genuinely new capability as merely 'additional value from existing investment.' D wrongly claims no classification applies, when this is a clear, textbook example of one of the three categories.
explanation.examTip: New business capabilities never previously supported + major investment = Re-architecting, triggering a full new ADM cycle with a new Request for Architecture Work.

stem: Which document, once signed by all developing organisations and the sponsoring organisation, transforms the Architecture Definition Document from a reference into a binding agreement?

options.text: The Communications Plan
The Architecture Contract
The Capability Assessment
The Business Transformation Readiness Assessment

rationale: The Architecture Contract is the joint agreement between development partners and sponsors on the deliverables, quality, and fitness-for-purpose of an architecture — signed by all developing organisations and the sponsoring organisation, transforming the Architecture Definition Document into a binding agreement.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Architecture Contract's specifically stated function — the binding, signed governance mechanism.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Communications Plan governs stakeholder engagement, not contractual binding. Capability Assessment evaluates readiness, not contractual agreement. Business Transformation Readiness Assessment evaluates organisational readiness for change, unrelated to contractual binding.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Contract = the signed, binding agreement. It's what gives governance formal authority over delivery.

stem: Does the Requirements Management process itself prioritise which requirements should be addressed first?

options.text: Yes, prioritisation is Requirements Management's primary function
No — the Requirements Management process does not dispose of, address, or prioritise any requirements; this is done within the relevant phase of the ADM
Yes, but only for requirements affecting Phase A
Requirements Management and prioritisation are the same activity by definition

rationale: The Standard explicitly states the Requirements Management process itself does not dispose of, address, or prioritise any requirements — this happens within the relevant phase of the ADM, by the architects and stakeholders working in that phase.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a directly stated, frequently tested limitation on Requirements Management's actual role.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly assigns prioritisation as Requirements Management's core function, when it's explicitly NOT its role. C fabricates a phase-specific restriction not present in the Standard. D wrongly conflates two genuinely distinct activities.
explanation.examTip: Requirements Management manages the PROCESS (capture, store, feed) — it does not itself decide priority. The relevant ADM phase does that.

stem: Gap analysis reveals a data validation rule present in the Baseline is absent from the Target. Investigation confirms this was accidental, not a deliberate design decision. What is this called, and what must happen?

options.text: An intentional omission — no further action is required
A gap requirement — it must be addressed and the Target Architecture revised accordingly
A compliance breach requiring immediate Architecture Board escalation
A Change Request requiring a completely new Statement of Architecture Work

rationale: A gap requirement is specifically defined as something eliminated by accident, requiring a change to the Target Architecture — distinct from a deliberate, documented intentional omission.

explanation.whyCorrect: This precisely matches the definition of a gap requirement — accidental (not deliberate) elimination requiring remediation.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly labels an accidental omission as "intentional," the opposite classification. C is disproportionate — a gap requirement doesn't automatically constitute a compliance breach requiring Board escalation. D is disproportionate — addressing a gap requirement doesn't require a completely new Statement of Architecture Work.
explanation.examTip: Gap requirement = accidental elimination, requires Target revision. Intentional omission = deliberate, documented decision, no automatic revision required. Don't confuse the two.

stem: Into how many levels of granularity is the Architecture Requirements Repository structured?

options.text: Two: Enterprise-wide and Project-specific
Three: Strategic, Segment, and Capability
Four: Preliminary, Vision, Development, and Governance
The Repository is not structured into levels at all

rationale: The Architecture Requirements Repository is structured into three levels of granularity — Strategic (long-term, whole-enterprise), Segment (programme/portfolio-level), and Capability (individual work package/project-level) — mirroring the Architecture Landscape levels.

explanation.whyCorrect: This three-level structure directly mirrors the Strategic/Segment/Capability Architecture Landscape levels, applied specifically to requirements.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly collapses the structure into an overly simple two-way split. C fabricates ADM-phase names as if they were Repository granularity levels. D wrongly denies any structuring at all.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Requirements Repository levels mirror Architecture Landscape levels: Strategic, Segment, Capability — the same three-tier granularity pattern appears in both.

stem: A stakeholder is unhappy that their requirement change was deprioritised. The Requirements Management team says: "We recorded the change and generated a Requirements Impact Assessment — our job is done regardless of the stakeholder's satisfaction." Is this correct?

options.text: Yes — Requirements Management's responsibility ends once the Impact Assessment is generated
No — Requirements Management specifically needs to determine stakeholder satisfaction with decisions made, and remains accountable for resolving dissatisfaction and determining next steps
Yes, but only if the stakeholder is external to the organisation
No — this issue should be escalated directly to the CEO, bypassing Requirements Management entirely

rationale: The Requirements Management phase specifically needs to determine stakeholder satisfaction with decisions made regarding their requirements, and where dissatisfaction exists, remains accountable to ensure resolution and determine next steps.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly identifies stakeholder satisfaction and dissatisfaction resolution as an explicit Requirements Management accountability, not something outside its scope.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly ends the responsibility prematurely at the Impact Assessment step. C fabricates an internal/external stakeholder distinction not relevant to this accountability.
