D skips the responsibility rather than fulfilling it — CEO escalation isn't the designated first response.
explanation.examTip: Requirements Management remains accountable for stakeholder satisfaction resolution — the Impact Assessment isn't the final step if the stakeholder remains dissatisfied.

stem: A new requirement emerges during Phase D. When assessing its impact, which phases should be considered?

options.text: Only Phase D, the currently active phase
Both the current phase (Phase D) and previous phases (e.g., B and C), since earlier decisions may be affected by later-emerging requirements
Only future phases, since past phases are already complete and unaffected
Only the Preliminary Phase, regardless of which phase the requirement emerged in

rationale: Assessing the impact of changed requirements specifically requires evaluating impact on the current (active) phase and on previous phases — a new requirement discovered later can still have implications for already-completed earlier-phase decisions.

explanation.whyCorrect: This reflects the two-part impact assessment activity — current AND previous phases, not just the currently active one.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly limits the assessment to only the current phase, ignoring potential effects on completed earlier work. C wrongly assumes past phases are always immune to new requirements. D fabricates an irrelevant restriction to only the Preliminary Phase.
explanation.examTip: Impact assessment covers current AND previous phases — 'already completed' doesn't mean 'immune to being affected' by a later-emerging requirement.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between Phase G (Implementation Governance) and Architecture Governance overall?

options.text: Phase G and Architecture Governance are the same thing
Phase G is just one aspect of Architecture Governance, which covers all aspects of architecture development and evolution from the Preliminary Phase through Phase H
Architecture Governance is a subset of Phase G
Phase G entirely replaces the need for Architecture Governance during implementation

rationale: The Standard explicitly states Architecture Governance covers the management and control of all aspects of the development and evolution of Enterprise Architectures — from the Preliminary Phase through Phase H — with Phase G (Implementation Governance) being just one specific aspect of this broader governance scope.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly reflects the explicit, frequently tested distinction between Phase G specifically and the much broader concept of Architecture Governance.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly equates the two. C inverts the actual relationship — Phase G is a subset of Architecture Governance, not the reverse. D wrongly claims Phase G eliminates the need for the broader governance concept.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Governance is the umbrella (Preliminary through Phase H); Phase G is just one piece of it (Implementation Governance specifically). This is one of the most frequently tested governance nuances.

stem: What is the recommended permanent membership size for an Architecture Board?

options.text: One or two senior executives only
Four or five members, with no more than ten
Exactly twenty members, one per business unit
As many representatives as the organisation deems necessary, with no upper limit

rationale: The recommended Architecture Board size is four or five permanent members, with no more than ten — broader representation is achieved through rotation with staggered terms, not an oversized permanent membership.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own specific, stated size recommendation, directly and frequently tested.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly understates the recommended range. C fabricates an arbitrary size formula tied to business unit count. D wrongly claims no upper limit exists, when the Standard specifically caps recommended size at ten.
explanation.examTip: 4-5 recommended, max 10 — a precise, frequently tested numeric fact. Broader representation comes from ROTATION, not a larger permanent Board.

stem: A project's dispensation, granted eighteen months ago, is still being relied upon without any renewal or review. Is this appropriate?

options.text: Yes — once granted, a dispensation remains valid indefinitely as long as the business situation hasn't changed
No — dispensations are not granted indefinitely; they are time-bound, tied to a given period and specific criteria, precisely to trigger renewed Architecture Compliance activity
Yes, but only if the original dispensation request mentioned no expiry date
No — dispensations are automatically revoked after exactly six months in all cases, with no exceptions

rationale: The Standard explicitly states dispensations are not granted indefinitely — they are time-bound and tied to specific criteria, precisely so their expiry triggers renewed Architecture Compliance review, not so they persist indefinitely once granted.

explanation.whyCorrect: This reflects dispensations' deliberately designed time-bound nature as a compliance-triggering mechanism, not a one-time approval.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly assumes indefinite validity contingent only on unchanged business conditions. C fabricates an exception based on whether an expiry was originally mentioned. D fabricates a specific, universal six-month automatic revocation period not stated in the Standard.
explanation.examTip: Dispensations are ALWAYS time-bound by design — this triggers renewed compliance review, not a one-time-forever approval.

stem: Which document is explicitly identified by the TOGAF Standard as "effectively an Architecture Contract between the architecting organisation and the sponsor"?

options.text: The Architecture Definition Document
The Architecture Compliance Assessment
The Statement of Architecture Work
The Architecture Requirements Specification

rationale: The Standard explicitly states the Statement of Architecture Work created in Phase A is effectively an Architecture Contract between the architecting organisation and the sponsor — one of three named types of Architecture Contract across the ADM.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a directly stated, specific characterisation of the Statement of Architecture Work as itself being an Architecture Contract type.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Architecture Definition Document is a technical content deliverable, not itself an Architecture Contract. Architecture Compliance Assessment is a governance review output, not a contract. Architecture Requirements Specification documents requirements, not a contractual agreement.
explanation.examTip: Statement of Architecture Work = BOTH a Phase A deliverable AND the first Architecture Contract of the ADM cycle. This dual identity is frequently tested.

stem: What should Architecture Board meetings specifically include, per the Standard's operational guidance?

options.text: Open, unstructured discussion with no agenda, to encourage free-flowing ideas
Clearly identified agendas with explicit objectives, content coverage, and defined actions, with supporting documentation circulated in advance
Only verbal reports, with no written documentation permitted
Attendance restricted exclusively to the CIO, with no other members present

rationale: Architecture Board meetings should be conducted within clearly identified agendas with explicit objectives, content coverage, and defined actions — with participants receiving supporting documentation in advance and expected to be familiar with it before the meeting.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own specific operational guidance for how Architecture Board meetings should be structured and prepared.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly recommends an unstructured approach the Standard specifically advises against. C fabricates a no-documentation restriction contradicting the advance-materials requirement. D fabricates an attendance restriction inconsistent with the Board's cross-organisational, multi-member composition.
explanation.examTip: Clear agenda + advance documentation + expected pre-reading = the Standard's specific Board meeting operational guidance, not open-ended discussion.

stem: On the Standard's own Stakeholder Power Grid, what is the correct label for a stakeholder with High Power and High Interest?

options.text: Manage Closely
Key Players
Minimal Effort
Keep Satisfied

rationale: The Standard's own Stakeholder Power Grid (Figure 3-2) labels the High Power, High Interest quadrant "Key Players" — not "Manage Closely," which is terminology from a different, more generic stakeholder-management model sometimes used elsewhere.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own specific, named label for this exact quadrant, directly from its own Power Grid figure.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: "Manage Closely" is a plausible-sounding but non-Standard term. "Minimal Effort" is actually the Standard's label for the opposite quadrant (Low Power, Low Interest). "Keep Satisfied" is the Standard's label for High Power, Low Interest.
explanation.examTip: The Standard's own four Power Grid labels are: Key Players (High/High), Keep Satisfied (High Power/Low Interest), Keep Informed (Low Power/High Interest), Minimal Effort (Low/Low) — use these exact terms, not generic project-management equivalents.

stem: What are the four steps of the TOGAF Stakeholder Management process, in order?

options.text: Identify, Classify, Determine Approach, Tailor Engagement Deliverables
Notify, Approve, Escalate, Close
Plan, Execute, Monitor, Review
Discover, Design, Deploy, Decommission

rationale: The four Stakeholder Management steps are: Identify stakeholders (formal and informal), Classify stakeholder positions, Determine the stakeholder management approach (Power/Interest grid), and Tailor engagement deliverables to each stakeholder group.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, named four-step process for Stakeholder Management.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B, C, and D are all plausible-sounding but fabricated process sequences unrelated to the actual named Stakeholder Management steps.
explanation.examTip: ICDT: Identify → Classify → Determine approach → Tailor deliverables. A reliable memory anchor for this four-step process.

stem: A facilities coordinator with no formal architecture role controls physical access to a data centre a migration depends on. A team member says she isn't a stakeholder since she has no formal role. What does stakeholder identification guidance say about this?

options.text: The team member is correct — only people with formal architecture roles count as stakeholders
Stakeholder identification specifically warns against relying too heavily on formal organisational structure, and asks who controls resources — she should be identified as a stakeholder
She should only be added to the stakeholder list if she formally requests inclusion herself
Facilities staff are explicitly excluded from stakeholder consideration in all TOGAF engagements

rationale: Stakeholder identification specifically warns against over-relying on formal organisational structure, and poses questions like "who controls resources?" — someone controlling physical access the migration depends on is exactly this kind of informally influential stakeholder.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly applies the Standard's specific warning against formal-structure-only stakeholder identification.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly restricts stakeholder status to formal roles, contradicting the specific warning against this. C wrongly reverses responsibility — identification is the architecture team's active job, not dependent on self-nomination. D fabricates a blanket exclusion not present in the Standard.
explanation.examTip: Someone controlling critical resources (physical access, specialist knowledge) is a stakeholder regardless of formal title — a frequently tested scenario type.

stem: Which of the Five Qualities specifically means a principle should be sufficiently definitive and precise to support consistent decision-making in complex, potentially controversial situations?

options.text: Understandable
Robust
Stable
Consistent

rationale: Robust specifically means enabling good quality decisions about architectures and plans, and enforceable policies and standards — each principle should be sufficiently definitive and precise to support consistent decision-making in complex, potentially controversial situations.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the exact stated definition of the Robust quality, distinct from the other four.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Understandable concerns clarity for broad comprehension. Stable concerns enduring nature with an amendment process. Consistent concerns balance of interpretation across the principle set — none of these describe decision-making precision in controversial situations specifically.
explanation.examTip: Robust = precise enough to drive consistent decisions and enforceable policies, even in controversial situations. Don't confuse with Understandable (clarity) or Complete (coverage).

stem: Two principles appear to conflict: one promotes data accessibility, the other requires strict security restrictions. A reviewer says one must be deleted. What does the Consistency quality actually require?

options.text: One principle must indeed be deleted whenever any tension exists between two principles
Strict adherence to one principle may require a loose interpretation of another; principles should allow a balance of interpretations rather than being deleted whenever tension exists
The two principles should be merged into a single combined statement covering both concerns
Consistency requires that no two principles may ever address related topics

rationale: The Standard specifically states that strict adherence to one principle may require a loose interpretation of another, and that a set of principles should allow a balance of interpretations rather than being contradictory to the point of violating each other's spirit — tension between principles is expected and managed through balanced interpretation, not resolved by deletion.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly reflects the Standard's own guidance on managing (not eliminating) tension between principles.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly treats any tension as requiring deletion, when balanced interpretation is the actual mechanism. C risks producing an unclear, overly complex combined principle rather than addressing the real issue. D fabricates an unrealistic restriction that principles can never address related topics.
explanation.examTip: Tension between principles (e.g., accessibility vs. security) is normal and managed through balanced interpretation and documented precedence — not resolved by deleting one principle.

stem: Which are the three Architecture Landscape levels, from broadest to most granular?

options.text: Foundation, Common Systems, Organisation-Specific
Strategic, Segment, Capability
Preliminary, Vision, Development
Business, Data, Technology

rationale: The three Architecture Landscape levels are Strategic Architecture (entire enterprise, long-term), Segment Architecture (specific area/division, programme level), and Capability Architecture (specific unit of capability, project level).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, stated three-level Landscape classification.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A lists Enterprise Continuum levels, a different classification scheme entirely. C lists ADM phase names, unrelated to Landscape levels. D lists BDAT architecture domains, an unrelated concept.
explanation.examTip: Strategic/Segment/Capability are Architecture Landscape LEVELS — don't confuse with Enterprise Continuum levels (Foundation/Common Systems/Industry/Organisation-Specific), a different classification entirely.

stem: A team completes classifying the Architecture Landscape into Strategic, Segment, and Capability Levels and declares architecture partitioning also complete. Is this accurate?

options.text: Yes — Levels and Partitions are the same organising concept
No — the Standard explicitly notes Architecture Levels are distinct from Architecture Partitions; completing Level classification doesn't establish ownership and management boundaries
Yes, but only for organisations with fewer than three divisions
No — partitioning applies only to Solutions, never to Architecture

rationale: The Standard explicitly notes architecture levels are distinct from architecture partitions. Levels organise by granularity; partitions establish ownership and management boundaries assigned to specific teams — completing one doesn't complete the other.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly reflects the Standard's own explicit definitional note distinguishing these two related but separate concepts.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly denies a distinction the Standard explicitly makes. C fabricates an organisation-size-based exception. D wrongly claims Architecture partitioning doesn't exist, when the Standard specifically addresses both Architecture and Solutions partitioning as distinct activities.
explanation.examTip: Levels = granularity classification. Partitions = ownership/management boundaries. Completing one doesn't complete the other — a specific, named distinction.

stem: Which four organising characteristics (BDTR) help classify content within the Architecture Landscape?

options.text: Breadth, Depth, Time, Recency
Business, Data, Technology, Requirements
Baseline, Design, Target, Roadmap
Board, Delivery, Team, Review

rationale: The four organising characteristics are Breadth (subject matter), Depth (level of detail), Time (time period covered), and Recency (how current the architecture is) — BDTR.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, named four-characteristic taxonomy for organising Architecture Landscape content.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B, C, and D are all plausible-sounding acronym-style distractors with no basis in the actual BDTR taxonomy.
explanation.examTip: BDTR: Breadth, Depth, Time, Recency — the four organising characteristics for Architecture Landscape content.

stem: Which criterion is described as the "fundamental technique" for structuring both solutions and architectures?

options.text: Time
Maturity/Volatility
Subject Matter (Breadth)
Recency

rationale: Subject Matter (Breadth) is specifically described as the fundamental technique for structuring both solutions and architectures — though Time and Maturity/Volatility are also named additional classification criteria supporting solution partitioning specifically.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specifically stated, named "fundamental technique" designation.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Time (organising around lifecycle timelines) and Maturity/Volatility (shaping investment priorities) are both genuine additional criteria, but neither is designated as the fundamental technique. Recency isn't a named Solutions partitioning criterion at all — it's part of the separate BDTR taxonomy.
explanation.examTip: Subject Matter/Breadth is fundamental; Time and Maturity/Volatility are additional, supporting criteria for Solutions partitioning specifically — don't treat all three as equally 'fundamental.'

stem: An integration architect specifies "Degree 3" interoperability between two systems, without further detail. Why might a technical reviewer ask for more precision?

options.text: "Degree 3" alone is already maximally precise and needs no refinement

The Standard provides four sub-classifications within Degree 3 — 3A (Formal Message Exchange), 3B (Common Data Exchange), 3C (Complete Data Exchange), 3D (Real-time Data Exchange) — for exactly this kind of technical refinement
Degree 3 has been deprecated and Degree 4 should always be used instead
Interoperability degrees are purely conceptual and are never expected to be technically precise

rationale: The Standard specifically refines Degree 3 (Seamless Sharing of Data) into four sub-classifications — 3A through 3D — precisely so degrees of interoperability are technically meaningful for the projects implementing them.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Standard's own specific refinement mechanism for exactly this kind of precision request.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly claims maximal precision already exists at the unqualified Degree 3 level. C fabricates a deprecation that doesn't exist — Degree 3 and Degree 4 serve different purposes, neither replaces the other. D wrongly claims interoperability degrees are never meant to be technically precise, contradicting the entire purpose of the 3A-3D refinement.
explanation.examTip: Degree 3 has four named sub-classifications (3A-3D) specifically for technical precision — a frequently tested refinement mechanism.

stem: A risk initially Critical/Frequent (Extremely High) is mitigated so the effect drops to Marginal, but frequency remains Frequent. A risk owner declares the mitigation successful and closes the risk. What does the Standard's own warning suggest checking first?

options.text: Nothing further — any reduction in effect severity automatically constitutes successful mitigation

The Standard warns that moving from frequent/catastrophic to frequent/critical still delivers an extremely high risk — the actual combined risk category (Frequent + Marginal) must be recalculated using the risk matrix before closing
Only the frequency needs verification; the effect reduction can be trusted without further checks
The risk should automatically be escalated to the CEO regardless of what the combined category shows

rationale: The Standard's own worked example warns that changing a risk from frequent/catastrophic to frequent/critical still delivers an extremely high risk — reducing one factor doesn't guarantee an acceptable residual risk. The actual combined risk category must be recalculated using the classification scheme before declaring mitigation successful.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly applies the Standard's own specific warning example to verify the actual resulting risk category, not just assume success from partial improvement.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly assumes any effect reduction alone is sufficient. C wrongly reverses which factor needs checking. D is a disproportionate response not tied to what the actual combined risk category shows.
explanation.examTip: Always recalculate the COMBINED risk category after mitigation — a partial improvement in one factor (effect or frequency) doesn't automatically produce an acceptable residual risk.

stem: An Enterprise Architect identifies a significant risk, designs a mitigation, and personally decides the residual risk is acceptable, proceeding without further sign-off. What does the Standard say about this?

options.text: This is correct — an architect's own analysis and confidence is sufficient to accept risk

The architect may identify risks and design mitigations, but it is within the governance framework that risks have to be first accepted and then managed — the architect's own confidence doesn't substitute for governance acceptance
The architect must redo the entire risk analysis with a different team before any further action
Risk acceptance is entirely the CFO's sole responsibility, with no Architecture Board involvement

rationale: The Standard explicitly separates two roles: the Enterprise Architect may identify risks and mitigate certain ones, but it is within the governance framework that risks have to be first accepted and then managed — not by the architect unilaterally.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly reflects the Standard's explicit separation of analytical role (architect) from acceptance role (governance framework).
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly validates unilateral architect acceptance. C misdiagnoses the problem as being about analysis quality rather than governance process. D fabricates an exclusive CFO-only acceptance role not described in the Standard.
explanation.examTip: Architects identify and mitigate risk; GOVERNANCE accepts risk. This separation of roles is a frequently tested governance principle.

stem: Which are the three categories of interoperability defined by TOGAF?

options.text: Operational/Business, Information, Technical
Strategic, Segment, Capability
Contextual, Conceptual, Logical
Simplification, Incremental, Re-architecting

rationale: TOGAF defines three categories of interoperability: Operational/Business (how business processes are shared), Information (how information is shared), and Technical (how technical services are shared or connected).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specifically named three-category interoperability taxonomy.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B lists Architecture Landscape levels. C lists Architecture Abstraction levels. D lists Phase H change categories — all genuine TOGAF concepts, but none are the interoperability category taxonomy.
explanation.examTip: Interoperability's three categories (Operational/Business, Information, Technical) are distinct from — and easily confused with — other three-part TOGAF taxonomies. Keep them separate.

stem: Two systems exchange structured data requiring manual compilation and dispatch, intended for both manual and/or automated handling. Which Degree of Interoperability best matches this description?

options.text: Degree 1 — Unstructured Data Exchange
Degree 2 — Structured Data Exchange
Degree 3 — Seamless Sharing of Data
Degree 4 — Seamless Sharing of Information

rationale: Degree 2 (Structured Data Exchange) specifically involves human-interpretable structured data intended for manual and/or automated handling, but requiring manual compilation, receipt, or dispatch — exactly matching this description.

explanation.whyCorrect: The structured nature of the data plus the manual compilation/dispatch requirement precisely matches Degree 2's definition.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Degree 1 involves unstructured data (e.g., free text), not structured data. Degree 3 requires automated sharing via a common exchange model, inconsistent with the manual compilation described. Degree 4 requires universal interpretation through fully co-operating applications, well beyond this scenario.
explanation.examTip: Structured data + still requiring manual compilation/dispatch = Degree 2, not Degree 1 (which is unstructured) or Degree 3 (which is automated).

stem: A Business Transformation Readiness Assessment identifies poor readiness factors and produces improvement actions. Where should these actions specifically be incorporated?

options.text: They are a standalone deliverable with no required connection to any other planning document

They should be formally incorporated into the emerging Implementation and Migration Plan, since the readiness assessment is a key input into strategic migration planning initiated in Phase E and completed in Phase F
They should be handled entirely by HR with no architecture team involvement whatsoever
They only need to be considered starting in Phase G, not before

rationale: Readiness factor risks and improvement actions should be formally incorporated into the emerging Implementation and Migration Plan — the readiness assessment is a key input into the strategic migration planning initiated in Phase E and completed in Phase F.

explanation.whyCorrect: This correctly identifies the specific integration point (Implementation and Migration Plan) and the specific phases (E and F) this feeds into.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly treats the actions as disconnected from broader planning. C wrongly excludes the architecture team, when the Standard frames this as a joint effort between corporate staff, lines of business, and IT/architecture planners. D wrongly defers integration to Phase G, when it should feed into Phase E/F planning much earlier.
explanation.examTip: Readiness assessment actions feed into the Implementation and Migration Plan (Phases E/F), as a joint effort involving IT/architecture planners — not a standalone or HR-only exercise.

stem: What are the three parts of the Architecture Trade-off Method?

options.text: Define Criteria, Identify and Describe Alternatives, Select or Combine
Baseline, Target, Gap Analysis
Discover, Design, Deploy
Contextual, Conceptual, Logical

rationale: The Architecture Trade-off Method has three parts: (1) Define Criteria using Vision, Principles, and Requirements; (2) Identify and Describe Alternatives; (3) Select or Combine — choosing one alternative or merging features from several.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, named three-part method for evaluating architecture alternatives.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B describes the general gap analysis pattern used elsewhere in the ADM, not this specific method. C is a fabricated generic sequence. D lists Architecture Abstraction levels, an unrelated concept.
explanation.examTip: CDC — Criteria, Describe alternatives, Choose or Combine. The three-part Trade-off Method.

stem: A team evaluating three cloud alternatives produces exhaustive, fully detailed technical specifications for each before presenting to stakeholders. What does the Standard's guidance suggest about this level of detail?

options.text: More detail is always better regardless of the decision-support purpose
The Standard specifically instructs creating necessary views to reach proper understanding of impact, but explicitly not going into too much detail at this stage
No architecture views should be produced for any alternative under evaluation
Only the most expensive alternative needs detailed specification

rationale: When describing the architecture for each alternative, the Standard specifically instructs creating necessary views for proper understanding, but explicitly not going into too much detail — the goal is decision-support, not exhaustive specification before a choice is made.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly reflects the Standard's specific caution against excessive detail at the alternatives-evaluation stage.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly validates unlimited detail regardless of purpose. C wrongly eliminates views entirely, when necessary views ARE called for, just not excessive detail. D fabricates an arbitrary cost-based exception to the detail guidance.
explanation.examTip: "Do not go into too much detail" is the Standard's own specific caution when describing alternatives — proportionate to decision support, not exhaustive specification.

stem: A team evaluating alternatives decides to only assess Technology Architecture alternatives, reasoning all domains are interconnected anyway. What does the Standard actually recommend?

options.text: Assessing only one domain is correct when domains are interconnected
Alternatives are commonly defined per domain specifically to simplify analysis, with domain-level alternatives then merged into one overall analysis of the whole architecture
All four domains must always be assessed as one single combined alternative from the start, skipping per-domain analysis entirely
Domain interconnection means alternatives evaluation should never be attempted at all

rationale: The Standard recommends defining alternatives per domain specifically to simplify analysis, with domain-level alternatives then merged into one overall analysis for the whole architecture — domain interconnection is precisely why each domain should be assessed and then merged, not a reason to skip domains.

explanation.whyCorrect: This correctly applies the Standard's specific per-domain-then-merge method, showing why interconnection supports (not undermines) domain-by-domain assessment.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly validates assessing only one domain. C skips the Standard's specific simplification technique of assessing domains separately first. D is an extreme overreaction not supported by the Standard's actual guidance.
explanation.examTip: Per-domain analysis first, then merge into overall analysis — this simplification technique exists precisely because domains ARE interconnected, not despite it.

stem: An alternative under consideration clearly violates an Architecture Principle. Should it be automatically excluded from the alternatives presented to stakeholders?

options.text: Yes, non-compliant alternatives must always be excluded without exception

Not necessarily — including a non-compliant alternative can make the cost of the principle visible and may prompt the Architecture Board to reconsider or reaffirm it; the decision remains with the Board
Yes, and the architect presenting it should face disciplinary action
No — non-compliant alternatives should always be selected over compliant ones

rationale: Presenting a non-compliant alternative deliberately can help extract hidden agendas and requirements, making trade-offs visible — a Board may reconsider or reaffirm the principle, but the final governance decision remains with the Architecture Board, not automatic exclusion.

explanation.whyCorrect: This reflects the deliberate, considered use of trade-off presentation, including non-compliant options, to surface genuine governance decisions.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly assumes automatic exclusion is required. C fabricates a disciplinary consequence with no basis. D wrongly reverses the logic entirely — non-compliance isn't a reason for automatic selection either.
explanation.examTip: Non-compliant alternatives can still be presented deliberately — this surfaces real trade-offs for a genuine governance decision, rather than being automatically excluded.

stem: At which points in the ADM can the Architecture Alternatives and Trade-offs technique be applied?

options.text: Only in Phase E
Any phase in the ADM, and any level of the architecture (Strategic, Segment, Capability)
Only during the Preliminary Phase
Only after the Architecture Roadmap has been finalised

rationale: The technique applies at any phase in the ADM, and at any level of the architecture (Strategic, Segment, Capability) — it feeds into Phase E's roadmap consolidation but is not limited to Phase E alone.

explanation.whyCorrect: This correctly identifies the technique's broad applicability across phases and architecture levels.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly restricts it to Phase E only, when it applies throughout the ADM. C wrongly restricts it to the Preliminary Phase, before any real architecture alternatives would typically exist. D wrongly requires the Roadmap already be finalised, when the technique feeds INTO roadmap decisions, not after them.
explanation.examTip: This technique isn't Phase-E-exclusive — it can be used wherever significant architectural decisions arise, at any level (Strategic/Segment/Capability).

stem: Which four content concepts (BCMD) does the Architecture Content Framework use to describe architectural work products?

options.text: Building Block, Catalog, Matrix, Diagram
Baseline, Change, Migration, Delivery
Business, Capability, Method, Domain
Board, Contract, Meeting, Dispensation

rationale: The four content concepts are Building Block (an entity within the metamodel), Catalog (a list of one type of building block), Matrix (relationships between entities), and Diagram (a graphical rendering).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, named four-concept taxonomy underpinning the Content Framework.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B, C, and D are all plausible-sounding acronym-style distractors unrelated to the actual BCMD content concept taxonomy.
explanation.examTip: BCMD: Building Block → Catalog → Matrix → Diagram. The foundational content concept hierarchy.

stem: An organisation spends months debating whether to adopt the TOGAF Content Framework, Zachman, or DoDAF, treating this as the single most critical decision. What does the Standard say about this choice?

options.text: The choice between alternative Content Frameworks is the single most critical decision and deserves extensive debate

Selecting a Content Framework is essential, but the choice between alternatives is less important — the final framework is usually adapted to fit specific organisation needs regardless of starting point
Only the Zachman Framework is officially endorsed by The Open Group for use with TOGAF
Organisations must use all three frameworks simultaneously to be TOGAF-compliant

rationale: The Standard explicitly states selecting a Content Framework is essential, but the choice of Content Framework is less important, since the final Content Framework is usually adapted to fit specific organisation needs regardless of which one is initially chosen.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly reflects the Standard's specific de-emphasis of framework choice relative to adaptation effort.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly treats framework selection as the critical decision, when adaptation matters more. C fabricates an exclusive endorsement not present in the Standard, which explicitly allows multiple alternative Content Frameworks. D fabricates a simultaneous-adoption requirement that doesn't exist.
explanation.examTip: The choice OF a Content Framework is less important than actually selecting and adapting one — a frequently tested nuance against excessive framework-comparison debate.

stem: Which three specific benefits does the Standard attribute to developing an Enterprise Metamodel?

options.text: Consistency, Completeness, Traceability
Speed, Cost Savings, Vendor Independence
Approval, Compliance, Escalation
Flexibility, Scalability, Portability

rationale: The Enterprise Metamodel specifically helps ensure Consistency (architects capturing compatible entity types), Completeness (a completeness-check for what's covered), and Traceability (relationships between entities properly tracked).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, named three-benefit list the Standard attributes to the Enterprise Metamodel.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B, C, and D are all plausible-sounding but fabricated benefit lists with no basis in the Standard's actual stated Metamodel benefits.
explanation.examTip: Enterprise Metamodel's three benefits: Consistency, Completeness, Traceability — a directly tested, specific list.

stem: An architect produces a document listing every application alongside its business owner and calls it an "Application Interaction Matrix." What is actually wrong with this labelling?

options.text: Nothing — any document about applications qualifies as an Interaction Matrix
A Matrix specifically depicts relationships between two or more entities; a list of applications with owners but no relationships shown is actually a Catalog, not a Matrix
The document should instead be reclassified as a Building Block
Only diagrams can show application-to-owner relationships, never catalogs or matrices

rationale: A Matrix specifically depicts relationships between two or more model entities. A document simply listing applications alongside owners, with no relationships between applications shown, is a Catalog (a list of one type of thing) mislabelled as a Matrix.

explanation.whyCorrect: This correctly applies the defining test for each artifact type (Catalog = list; Matrix = relationships) to identify the actual mislabelling.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly accepts any application-related document as automatically qualifying as a Matrix. C fabricates an unrelated reclassification as a Building Block, a completely different content concept. D fabricates a restriction that only diagrams can show such relationships, when catalogs and matrices serve their own distinct, valid purposes.
explanation.examTip: Catalog = list of one type of thing (even with an attribute like 'owner' attached). Matrix = relationships BETWEEN two or more types of things. A list with one extra column isn't automatically a matrix.

stem: What is the key difference between the Data Entity/Business Function Matrix and the Application/Data Matrix?

options.text: They are two names for the exact same artifact

The Data Entity/Business Function Matrix supports assigning data ownership at the business-function level (governance); the Application/Data Matrix shows which applications technically use which data entities (dependency/migration scope)
The Data Entity/Business Function Matrix is only used in Phase D, while the Application/Data Matrix is only used in Phase A
Only one of the two matrices is a genuine TOGAF artifact; the other is fabricated

rationale: The Data Entity/Business Function Matrix specifically supports assigning data ownership to organisations for governance purposes. The Application/Data Matrix supports understanding technical dependencies — which applications use which data entities — critical for migration scoping.

explanation.whyCorrect: This correctly distinguishes the business-governance purpose of one matrix from the technical-dependency purpose of the other.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly claims identity between two genuinely distinct artifacts serving different purposes. C fabricates phase restrictions not tied to either matrix's actual usage (both relate to Phase C work). D wrongly claims one is fabricated, when both are genuine, distinct Content Framework artifacts.
explanation.examTip: Data Entity/Business Function Matrix = governance/ownership. Application/Data Matrix = technical dependency/migration scope. Frequently confused, genuinely distinct artifacts.

stem: Beyond the ADM's core processes, how many operational management areas does the Standard identify for a mature Architecture Capability?

options.text: Four
Six
Eight
Twelve

rationale: The Standard identifies eight operational areas: Financial Management, Performance Management, Service Management, Risk and Opportunity Management, Resource Management, Communications and Stakeholder Management, Quality Management, and Supplier Management.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, named count and list of eight operational management areas for running a mature Architecture Capability like an operational business unit.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Four, six, and twelve are all plausible-sounding but incorrect counts not matching the Standard's actual eight-area list.
explanation.examTip: Eight operational areas reflect the principle that a mature EA practice should be run like any operational business unit, not just as a technical process — memorise the count and be ready to name several.

stem: Is establishing an Enterprise Architecture Capability considered a one-off project?

options.text: Yes, once established, it is a completed project requiring no further attention

No — establishing the practice should be seen as an ongoing discipline providing context, environment, and resources to govern and enable architecture delivery, not a phase of a project or a one-off project
Yes, but only for organisations with fewer than 100 employees
The Standard takes no position on this question

rationale: The Standard explicitly states establishing the architecture practice should not be seen as a phase of an architecture project, or a one-off project, but rather an ongoing discipline — delivery projects may request changes triggering further ADM cycles to extend it.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly reflects the Standard's explicit framing of the practice as continuous, not a completed, closed project.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly treats establishment as complete and requiring no further attention. C fabricates an organisation-size exception. D is false — the Standard directly and explicitly addresses this question.
explanation.examTip: Establishing the EA practice is explicitly NOT a one-off project — it's an ongoing discipline, frequently triggering further ADM cycles as it evolves.

stem: An organisation measures its Architecture Capability maturity purely by counting documented Architecture Principles. Is this a reliable maturity measure?

options.text: Yes, principle count is a reliable proxy for overall maturity

No — genuine maturity assessment covers factors like governance processes/roles, architecture skills, landscape/standards/reference model quality, and re-use potential — not simply how many principles are documented
Yes, but only if the count exceeds 50 principles
Maturity cannot be measured or assessed at all in TOGAF

rationale: Genuine architecture maturity assessment covers factors like Architecture Governance processes/organisation/roles, architecture skills, breadth/depth/quality of the landscape and repository, and re-use potential — not a narrow output metric like principle count.

explanation.whyCorrect: This correctly identifies the actual multi-factor nature of genuine maturity assessment, contrasting it with the narrow, misleading principle-count proxy.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly validates a narrow, single-metric proxy as reliable. C fabricates an arbitrary numeric threshold with no basis. D wrongly denies maturity assessment is possible, when the Standard specifically recommends adapting an existing maturity model.
explanation.examTip: Recognise 'more X means more mature' as a red flag for an oversimplified maturity claim — genuine maturity assessment is multi-factor (governance, skills, repository quality, re-use), not a single count.

stem: When applying BDAT reflexively to the EA practice itself, what does "Data Architecture" specifically refer to?

options.text: General business data used by core operational systems
The structure of the Enterprise Continuum and Architecture Repository — sometimes referred to as the metamodel of the architecture practice
Customer and financial data governance policies
The Architecture Requirements Repository exclusively

rationale: When BDAT is applied reflexively to the practice itself, Data Architecture specifically refers to the structure of the organisation's Enterprise Continuum and Architecture Repository — sometimes called the metamodel of the architecture practice.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, stated meaning of "Data Architecture" in the context of establishing the practice itself, not general business data.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly applies the term to unrelated general business data. C fabricates an unrelated governance-policy scope. D wrongly narrows the meaning to only one Architecture Repository component.
explanation.examTip: Reflexive BDAT: Data Architecture (of the practice) = the Enterprise Continuum/Repository structure — not general business data.

stem: Which TOGAF Series Guide does the Standard reference for guidance on skills, experience, and competency levels expected of different architecture roles?

options.text: TOGAF Series Guide: Architecture Skills Framework
TOGAF Series Guide: Business Scenarios
TOGAF Series Guide: Digital Enterprise
TOGAF Series Guide: Architecture Maturity Models

rationale: The Standard specifically points to the TOGAF Series Guide: Architecture Skills Framework for guidance on the specific skills, experience, and competency levels expected of different architecture roles (e.g., Enterprise Architect, Business Architect, Data Architect).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specifically named Series Guide addressing role-specific skills and competency guidance.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: Business Scenarios addresses a different technique (requirements discovery in Phase A). Digital Enterprise addresses a different topic area. Architecture Maturity Models addresses capability maturity assessment, a related but distinct topic from role-specific skills.
explanation.examTip: Architecture Skills Framework Series Guide = the reference for role/skill/competency definitions — distinct from other named Series Guides covering different topics.

stem: An organisation already using ITIL for IT service management adopts TOGAF and considers discarding ITIL entirely to avoid redundancy. What does the Standard say about this?

options.text: ITIL should always be discarded once TOGAF is adopted, since running two frameworks is inherently redundant
TOGAF is specifically designed to co-exist with and enhance the operational capabilities of other management frameworks like ITIL, already present in an organisation
TOGAF cannot be used in any organisation that already has ITIL in place
ITIL and TOGAF must always be run with zero coordination between them

rationale: TOGAF is specifically designed to co-exist with and enhance the operational capabilities of other management frameworks already present in an organisation, such as ITIL — addressing IT service management, a different concern from TOGAF's Enterprise Architecture method.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly reflects the Standard's stated co-existence design intent, rather than treating other frameworks as automatically redundant.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly recommends discarding a functioning, differently-scoped framework. C fabricates an incompatibility that doesn't exist. D wrongly recommends zero coordination, when the actual point is that the two frameworks CAN and should be coordinated.
explanation.examTip: TOGAF integrates with, rather than replaces, frameworks like ITIL, COBIT, and PRINCE2 that address different concerns — a frequently tested integration principle.

stem: Which three types of iteration does the ADM support?

options.text: Landscape iteration, Within-cycle iteration, Capability iteration
Business iteration, Data iteration, Technology iteration
Phase A iteration, Phase B iteration, Phase C iteration
Governance iteration, Compliance iteration, Dispensation iteration

rationale: The three types of iteration are: Landscape iteration (multiple ADM cycles populating/extending the Architecture Landscape), Within-cycle iteration (phases running concurrently or looping), and Capability iteration (a new Preliminary Phase pass).

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, named three-type iteration taxonomy.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B lists BDAT-style domain names, unrelated to iteration types. C fabricates per-phase iteration names not part of the actual taxonomy. D fabricates governance-related terms unrelated to iteration types.
explanation.examTip: Three iteration types: Landscape (multiple projects), Within-cycle (phases looping/concurrent), Capability (new Preliminary pass) — a frequently tested taxonomy.

stem: A team applying "Baseline First" iteration finds themselves spending significant effort on Target Architecture details during Iteration 1, which is meant to focus on the Baseline. Is this a process violation?

options.text: Yes, any Target Architecture activity during Iteration 1 of a Baseline First cycle is strictly forbidden
No — the Standard's own iteration-to-phase mapping shows Target activity as a legitimate secondary ('Light') focus during Iteration 1, even though Baseline is the primary ('Core') focus
Yes, and the team must immediately switch their entire approach to Target First
The Standard does not address iteration activity mapping at all

rationale: The Standard's own activity-by-iteration mapping for Baseline First cycles explicitly shows Target Architecture work as a secondary ("Light") focus during Iteration 1, alongside Baseline as the primary ("Core") focus — some Target consideration is expected, not a violation.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly reflects the Standard's own iteration-activity table, correcting the misconception that any Target activity during Baseline-focused iteration is forbidden.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly treats normal, expected secondary activity as a strict violation. C is an overreaction not warranted by expected secondary-focus activity. D is false — the Standard specifically provides this iteration-activity mapping.
explanation.examTip: The Standard's own iteration tables show some secondary ('Light') focus on the non-primary state during any given iteration — this is expected, not a rule violation.

stem: A CIO states a broad objective ("modernise our data capabilities") with no agreed vision, scope, or stakeholder alignment yet. Which class of change initiative does this represent, and what should happen first?

options.text: A Bounded change initiative — immediately elaborate a detailed Target Architecture
A Foundational change initiative — the initial priority is understanding the nature of the problem and bringing structure to its definition, before defining detailed solutions
An Architecture Governance engagement — since the objective is vague, this should be governed rather than developed
This scenario doesn't fit any recognised TOGAF engagement classification

rationale: A known objective without a strictly scoped or agreed vision is a Foundational change initiative. The Standard specifically states the initial priority in this class of engagement is understanding the nature of the problem and bringing structure to its definition — not immediately elaborating detailed solutions.

explanation.whyCorrect: This correctly classifies the scenario (known objective, unscoped) as Foundational and applies the correct sequencing principle (structure the problem first).
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly classifies this as Bounded, which applies to situations with an already-agreed vision/scope. C misapplies Architecture Governance, which concerns governing implementation of an already-defined solution, not undefined problems. D wrongly claims no classification fits, when Foundational is precisely the named category for this situation.
explanation.examTip: Known objective + no agreed scope/vision = Foundational (structure the problem first). Agreed vision/scope already exists = Bounded (elaborate the solution). Don't confuse the two.

stem: Even when stakeholders expect Baseline and Target to be considered in parallel, what does the Standard recommend regarding team focus?

options.text: The team should give completely equal, unwavering 50/50 priority to both at all times
The architecture team should still focus priority on one state to maintain focus and consistency of execution, while giving informal consideration to the other
The team should split into two entirely separate, uncoordinated groups — one for Baseline, one for Target
Parallel stakeholder interest means Baseline and Target should never both be considered by the same team

rationale: The Standard specifically recommends that even in situations where Baseline and Target are expected to be considered in parallel by stakeholders, the architecture team should focus priority on one state to maintain focus and consistency of execution.

explanation.whyCorrect: This directly reflects the Standard's specific recommendation to prioritise one state even under parallel stakeholder expectations.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly recommends an unwavering equal split the Standard specifically advises against. C misapplies the guidance as team fragmentation rather than one team maintaining a primary focus. D wrongly claims the same team can never consider both, when informal consideration of the other state is explicitly expected.
explanation.examTip: Even under parallel stakeholder interest, ONE team maintains a primary focus (Baseline First or Target First) while informally considering the other — not a rigid 50/50 split or team fragmentation.

stem: What is the actual format of the OGEA-102 (Part 2) exam, as clarified in this lesson?

options.text: 40 questions, 60 minutes, single best answer
8 scenario-based questions, 90 minutes, gradient-scored (0/1/3/5) with an overall pass mark AND a per-scenario minimum threshold
100 questions, 120 minutes, true/false format
One extended essay question, unlimited time

rationale: OGEA-102 consists of 8 scenario-based questions over 90 minutes, each scored on a gradient (0/1/3/5), requiring both an overall pass percentage and a minimum score on every individual scenario.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the corrected, accurate exam format specifically clarified after an earlier imprecise description in the material.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A describes the OGEA-101 (Part 1) format, not Part 2. C and D are both fabricated formats with no basis in the actual exam structure.
explanation.examTip: Don't confuse Part 1 (40 questions, single best answer) with Part 2 (8 gradient-scored scenarios, dual pass criteria) — a commonly conflated pair.

stem: What does the MGP-C diagnostic framework check for when evaluating a gradient-scored answer option?

options.text: Mechanism, Governance, Pressure acknowledgment, Contradiction check
Money, Growth, Profit, Cost
Management, Goals, Priorities, Compliance
Motivation, Guidance, Practice, Certification

rationale: MGP-C checks: does the option name the correct Mechanism (TOGAF phase/artifact)? Does it route to the correct Governance body? Does it acknowledge the legitimate Pressure in the scenario? Does it Contradict anything the Standard explicitly states (a disqualifier)?

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, named four-part diagnostic framework taught for evaluating gradient-scored answer options.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B, C, and D are all plausible-sounding but fabricated acronym expansions unrelated to the actual MGP-C framework.
explanation.examTip: MGP-C: Mechanism, Governance, Pressure, Contradiction — apply all four checks to any option before selecting it as your answer.

stem: A candidate spends only 3 minutes each on the first five of eight Part 2 scenarios, to "bank time" for the final three. Why is this risky, given the exam's actual scoring structure?

options.text: It isn't risky — banked time can always be reallocated later without consequence

Because of the per-scenario minimum threshold, a single very poor scenario can fail the candidate even if the overall percentage would otherwise pass — banked time on later scenarios cannot retroactively fix an early floor-level failure
It is risky only because it violates a strict rule requiring exactly equal time per scenario
It isn't risky, since the exam has no per-scenario minimum, only an overall pass mark

rationale: Because the exam requires both an overall pass mark and a per-scenario minimum threshold, rushing through early scenarios risks producing at least one answer poor enough to fail that individual threshold — a failure banked time on later scenarios cannot fix.

explanation.whyCorrect: This correctly identifies the specific mechanism (per-scenario minimum threshold) that makes uneven time allocation genuinely risky.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly claims no consequence exists for rushed early answers. C fabricates a strict equal-time rule that isn't the actual reason time-banking is risky. D is factually wrong — the exam does have a per-scenario minimum threshold, which is exactly what makes this risky.
explanation.examTip: Because of the per-scenario minimum threshold, allocate roughly equal, full time to every scenario — a single rushed, poor scenario can sink an otherwise passing overall score.

stem: Which of the following is identified as one of the four common trap answer patterns in Part 2 scenarios?

options.text: Rigid/bureaucratic — over-applies rules, ignoring TOGAF's explicit flexibility
Always-correct — an option that is always the best answer regardless of context
Vendor-neutral — an option specifically avoiding any mention of technology
Governance-free — an option deliberately bypassing all Architecture Board involvement in every case

rationale: Rigid/bureaucratic is one of four named trap patterns — sounding safe by over-applying rules, but actually ignoring TOGAF's explicit flexibility. Other named traps include Pragmatic-but-ungoverned, Disproportionate escalation, and Technically-correct-but-incomplete.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is one of the four specifically named trap patterns candidates should learn to recognise.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B, C, and D are all fabricated pattern names not among the four actually taught trap types.
explanation.examTip: Four trap patterns: Rigid/bureaucratic, Pragmatic-but-ungoverned, Disproportionate escalation, Technically-correct-but-incomplete. Recognising these speeds up eliminating wrong options.

stem: What is the recommended technique to avoid being anchored by the framing of the four answer options in a Part 2 scenario?

options.text: Read all four options twice before forming any opinion
Write your own one-sentence answer using TOGAF vocabulary BEFORE reading any of the four options, then match your answer against them
Always select the shortest option, since brevity avoids anchoring bias
Skip reading the scenario text and go directly to the options

rationale: Writing your own one-sentence answer using TOGAF vocabulary before reading the options prevents the options — including deliberately constructed distractors — from anchoring your reasoning; you then match your own answer against the four given.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the specific, named anti-anchoring technique taught for approaching gradient-scored scenarios.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A doesn't address the anchoring risk at all — reading options twice doesn't prevent them from shaping your reasoning. C fabricates an unreliable length-based heuristic. D is nonsensical — skipping the scenario text would make forming any answer impossible.
explanation.examTip: Form your own answer BEFORE reading the options — this is the specific technique to avoid anchoring on well-constructed but potentially misleading distractors.

stem: Which reference model specifically addresses whether an application can be moved to a different underlying technology platform?

options.text: The Integrated Information Infrastructure Reference Model (III-RM)
The Technical Reference Model (TRM)
The Enterprise Continuum
The Architecture Content Framework

rationale: The TRM specifically addresses platform portability — whether an application can be moved to a different underlying platform — via its two key interfaces: the Application Platform Interface and Communications Infrastructure Interface.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the TRM's specifically stated concern — platform-layer portability.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: III-RM addresses application-level information sharing, a different concern. The Enterprise Continuum is a classification scheme, not a portability-focused reference model. The Architecture Content Framework describes content categorisation, unrelated to portability specifically.
explanation.examTip: TRM = platform portability (can it move?). III-RM = application interoperability (can it talk to others?). Keep these two reference models' concerns distinct.

stem: Which two interfaces does the TRM define as critical boundaries for portability?

options.text: Application Platform Interface and Communications Infrastructure Interface
Business Interface and Data Interface
Governance Interface and Compliance Interface
Vision Interface and Roadmap Interface

rationale: The TRM defines the Application Platform Interface (between Application Software and the Application Platform) and the Communications Infrastructure Interface (between the Application Platform and the Communications Infrastructure/network) as its two critical portability boundaries.

explanation.whyCorrect: These are the specifically named two interfaces underpinning the TRM's portability concept.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: B, C, and D are all fabricated interface pairs with no basis in the TRM's actual structure.
explanation.examTip: API (Application Platform Interface) sits above CII (Communications Infrastructure Interface) — standards-based design at both boundaries is what enables genuine portability.

stem: In III-RM terms, what is a "Brokering Application"?

options.text: An application that directly supports business processes and end users
A specific type of Infrastructure Application whose role is to mediate and translate information exchange between Business Applications not originally designed to interoperate
A synonym for a Technical Reference Model component
A governance body approving architecture contracts

rationale: A Brokering Application is a specific type of Infrastructure Application in III-RM whose specific role is mediating and translating information exchange between Business Applications that were never designed to talk to each other directly.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the precise, stated definition of Brokering Application within III-RM's three-category model.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A describes a Business Application, a different III-RM category. C wrongly conflates III-RM terminology with TRM. D fabricates an unrelated governance-body definition.
explanation.examTip: III-RM's three application categories: Business (direct support), Infrastructure (shared services), Brokering (a type of Infrastructure Application specifically mediating between Business Applications).

stem: A junior architect asks: "If our cloud platform gives us portability between providers, doesn't that automatically mean our applications can share data seamlessly too?" What is the correct response?

options.text: Yes — platform portability and application-level data sharing are effectively the same capability

No — portability (TRM's concern) is a platform-layer property; seamless data sharing (III-RM's concern) is a different, application-layer/semantic property. Two applications can each be portable and still be unable to share data meaningfully without compatible data definitions or a brokering mechanism
Yes, but only for applications built after 2020
No, because portability and data sharing are entirely unrelated with no connection whatsoever

rationale: Platform portability and application-level data sharing are genuinely distinct architectural properties addressed by different reference models — TRM (platform layer) and III-RM (application/semantic layer). Achieving one does not guarantee the other.

explanation.whyCorrect: This correctly separates the two distinct architectural concerns and explains why portability doesn't guarantee interoperability.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly conflates two distinct properties. C fabricates an arbitrary, irrelevant date-based exception. D overcorrects — while distinct, the two properties aren't wholly unrelated; a well-chosen, standards-based platform can still ease integration even though it doesn't guarantee it.
explanation.examTip: Portability (TRM) ≠ Interoperability (III-RM). Being portable across platforms doesn't automatically mean applications can meaningfully exchange data — a frequently tested distinction.

stem: Where do TRM and III-RM sit within the Enterprise Continuum?

options.text: They are examples of Organisation-Specific Architecture, unique to each enterprise
They are examples of Foundation/Common Systems Architecture — generic, reusable reference models toward the generic end of the Continuum, meant to be specialised for an organisation's use
They are components of the Governance Repository
They replace the Architecture Continuum entirely for any technology-focused engagement

rationale: TRM is an example of Foundation Architecture, and III-RM an example of Common Systems Architecture (Application Domain) — both sitting toward the generic end of the Enterprise Continuum, as reusable reference models to be specialised, not built from scratch as organisation-specific.

explanation.whyCorrect: This correctly places both models at the generic end of the Continuum, as worked examples to be specialised.
explanation.whyOthersWrong: A wrongly places them at the most specific end, opposite their actual generic classification. C wrongly assigns them to an unrelated Architecture Repository component. D wrongly claims they replace the entire Architecture Continuum for any technology engagement.
explanation.examTip: TRM = Foundation Architecture. III-RM = Common Systems Architecture (Application Domain). Both generic, reusable, specialise-don't-rebuild-from-scratch reference models.
